units.la: HABVI ego 10. & 11. Aprilis huius anni 1590. Colloquium, viris quibusdam magnis ac doctis praesentibus, cum Ioanne Badio Rodingensi, Caluinianae Sectae Ministro, cuius summam vt ad hunc modum describerem, in causa fuit rumor quidam, ab hominibus istius Sectae sparsus, quem paucis diebus, vt sunt gloriosuli, sursum deorsum, & quaqua versum inter suos propagarunt; nimirum adeo fortiter ac strenuè Badium causam suam egisse, vt me penitus prostrato, victoriam ex vtriusque diei congressu reportarit. Quo nomine Caluiniani nescio quas spirant glorias, & suauiter admodum se mutuò titillant; vt adeò Ioanni, ob rem praeclarè gestam, triumphum in Republica sua decreuisse videantur. Placuit igitur, dum memoria recens fuit, illius Colloquij summariam Narrationem ad hunc modum contexere; non eo consilio quidem, vt typis in publicum ederetur, sed vt eam apud me, velut in certos vsus repositam, asseruarem.
units.tr: I held a colloquy on 10 and 11 April of this year 1590, with some distinguished and learned men present, against John Badius of Roding, minister of the Calvinist sect. The cause of my writing a summary of it in this form was a rumour spread by people of that sect. Within a few days, as these boasters do, they passed it up and down and everywhere among their own, namely that Badius had argued his cause so forcefully and vigorously that, I having been utterly overthrown, he carried off the victory from the encounter of both days. On account of this the Calvinists breathe some kind of glory and tickle one another most pleasantly, so that they seem to have decreed John a triumph for his well-performed deed in their commonwealth. It pleased me, therefore, while the memory was still fresh, to put together a summary narrative of that colloquy in this way. My purpose was not that it be published in print, but that I might keep it by me, as if stored away for certain uses.

units.la: Quia verò Caluinistae nugari de hoc Colloquio, falsosque rumores spargere non desinunt; imò & illud studio habere videntur, vt huiusmodi fallaci strophâ perturbent simpliciorum quorundam animos, eosque à Catholica Religione paulatim auertant; mutaui sententiam, eorumque consilijs acquieui, qui narrationem hanc typis diuulgandam censuerunt: vt mendaciorum fumi scilicet, quos illorum vanitas, ac sinistra narratio passim suscitauit, illata veritatis luce dissipentur.
units.tr: But since the Calvinists do not cease to babble about this colloquy and to spread false rumours, and indeed seem to aim at disturbing the minds of some simpler folk by such deceitful tricks and gradually turning them away from the Catholic Religion, I have changed my mind and given way to the counsel of those who judged that this narrative should be published, so that the clouds of falsehood which their vanity and their sinister account have raised everywhere may be dispelled by the light of truth brought to bear.

units.la: Accepi ego à fide dignis, esse inter Caluinianos, qui confidenter, ac plenis faucibus, iactare ausint, me superatum argumentorum vi, Badio dedisse manus, & in illius sententiam concessisse; futurumque certò, vt antequam annus elabatur, publicè ad Caluinii castra transeam.
units.tr: I have received from trustworthy people that there are among the Calvinists those who boldly and with full throats dare to boast that I, overcome by the force of their arguments, have given my hand to Badius and gone over to his opinion, and that it will certainly come to pass that before the year runs out I shall publicly pass over to the camp of Calvin.

units.la: Quid non audent isti, quibus mentiri non est periculum? Ego vero manus dederim homini, qui non semel inter colloquendum obmutuit: qui nonnunquam victus evidentia rei propositæ, digito, vel manu potius, compescuit labellum, et oculos in sinum reflexit: qui timiditatem ac ὑποκρισιν (insitum a natura vitiosum pudorem) aliquoties ad excusandum sese prætexuit: qui in Eucharistico negocio, solida, eademque dilucida Christi verba, vel euertere strophis sophisticis, vel ad naturalium principiorum gnomonem, ritu prope gentilium, reuocare conatus est: qui eadem Christi Seruatoris verba non secus examinare instituit, ac si vel Platonis ea, vel philosophi cuiusdam essent? qui in controversiis fidei legitimum, atque Spiritu sancto per Apostolos demonstratum, intelligenda, atque declaranda Scripturæ medium, quod à me prolatum est, nec euertere potuit, nec voluit tamen amplecti? Huic ego manus dederim, inquam? Ab hoc eo vel adductus sim, vel adactus, ut de transfugio cogitem: ut aciem illam castrorum ordinatam, in qua meo loco Domino exercituum militaui hactenus, abiectis armis relinquere, atque ad confusam Babylonem aduersariorum, qui perpetuo totis castris inter se tumultuatur, transire in animo habeam?
units.tr: What do those men not dare, for whom lying carries no danger? As for me, would I give my hand to a man who more than once fell silent in the course of the disputation; who, sometimes overcome by the evidence of the matter put before him, quieted his lip with a finger, or rather with a hand, and turned his eyes back into his bosom; who on several occasions pretended timidity and ὑπόκρισις (hypocrisy), a shame naturally ingrained in him as a fault, as an excuse for himself; who in the matter of the Eucharist tried either to overturn the solid and equally clear words of Christ with sophistical twists, or to recall them to the rule of natural principles, almost in the manner of the Gentiles; who set about examining the same words of Christ our Saviour just as if they were the words of Plato or of some philosopher; who, in controversies of faith, could neither overthrow nor was willing to embrace the lawful means of understanding and explaining Scripture, which the Holy Spirit has shown through the Apostles, and which I put forward? Would I, I ask, give my hand to this man? Am I to be led or driven by him to think of desertion, and to intend to abandon that well-ordered battle line, in which I have hitherto served the Lord of hosts in my appointed place, and to pass over to the confused Babylon of the adversaries, who are in constant uproar among themselves through their whole camp?

units.la: At satis intelligo, quorsum huiusmodi contumeliosas voces spargat, homines vaferrimi: nimirum, ut eam de me suspicionem nostrorum mentibus inferant, quasi aliud quiddam in animo reconditum habeam, quam publica voce profiteor: ut laborum meorum fructum, (si quis est, quem ego diuinæ benignitati semper acceptum retuli) hoc artificio, velut ex insidijs, eleuent aut interuertant.
units.tr: But I understand well enough, the most crafty men, why they spread such abusive words: namely, to put that suspicion of me into the minds of our people, as if I had some other thing hidden in my heart than what I openly profess; so that by this trick, as if from an ambush, they may lift up or overturn the fruit of my labours, if there is any, for which I have always acknowledged the credit to the divine goodness.

units.la: Ego vero semel e Flacianorum pedicis, quibus Lutheranorum scholæ me, vel à primis annis induerant, per Dei gratiam eluctatus sum; iamque fixi anchoram in tutissimo Ecclesiæ Catholicæ portu, ex quo, Deo volente, nulli me Caluinistarum, Lutheranorum, Anabaptistarum, Schuuenckfeldianorum, & quorumcunque demum Ecclesiæ hostium, insidiæ, fraudes, machinationes, deturbabunt: Id quod non mei, viriumque mearum, sed solius gratiæ diuinæ fiducia dictum intelligi volo. Nec quicquam mororum ista istorum vel obtrectationes, vel virulentas calumnias, vel furiosos latratus, quibus à multis annis sic satis assuevi. Spargant de me, quicquid lubet, modò ne sui similem, hoc est, Caluinianum dicere unquam vere possint, quod nefas, supplex rogo Dominum, ut à me clementer auertat, neque eò vel insania, vel caecitatis unquam prolabi me patiatur, ut Christi veritatem fucatis Caluini mendaciis permutare velim.
units.tr: As for me, I have by the grace of God once for all struggled free from the fetters of the Flacians, into which the schools of the Lutherans had bound me from my earliest years. Now I have cast my anchor in the safest harbour of the Catholic Church, from which, God willing, the snares, frauds and machinations of none of the Calvinists, Lutherans, Anabaptists, Schwenckfeldians, or whatever enemies of the Church there are, will drive me out. I want this to be understood as said not in confidence in myself or in my own powers, but in confidence in divine grace alone. Nor do these men's detractions, virulent calumnies or raving barks trouble me at all, to which I have for many years now been sufficiently accustomed. Let them say of me whatever they please, provided they can never truly say that I am like them, that is, a Calvinist. That would be a crime, which I humbly beg the Lord to turn away from me in his mercy, and never allow me to fall into such madness or blindness, that I should wish to exchange the truth of Christ for the painted lies of Calvin.

units.la: Interea miror ego vanitatem istorum hominum, qui futilibus huiusmodi nugis in re seria tantopere delectantur. Faciunt certè, ut illud propheticum in eos quadret: Posuimus mēdacium spem nostram, & mendacio protecti sumus. Qua de re nihil lubet amplius, nisi hoc unum: Si Caluinistarum res eo loca sunt, ut mendaciis spargendis necesse habeant vestire nuditatem suam, non est ab ijs vehementer metuendum. Vale. Coloniae Agrippinae, 10. Augusti. Anno post incarnatum Verbum 1590.
units.tr: Meanwhile I marvel at the vanity of these men, who take such delight in trifles of this kind in a serious matter. They certainly make that prophetic saying fit them: "We have made lies our hope, and we are protected by falsehood." Concerning this matter I wish to add nothing further, except this one thing: if the affairs of the Calvinists are in such a state that they must clothe their nakedness by spreading lies, there is no great need to fear them. Farewell. Cologne of Agrippina, 10 August, in the year after the Word was made flesh, 1590.

units.la: ANno Christi 1590. 10. April. vocatus sum, nomine amplissimi Senatus Colonien. ad carcerem publicum, quem Franconum turrim dicunt, vt cum Concionatore quodam, Ioanne Badio Rodingesi, de rebus nonnullis conferrem. Eratis Cocionator captus ante dies aliquot, cum contra Magistratus Edicta, clancularia concionem haberet. Veni ad carcerem circa horam quartam pomeridianam, ibique congregatos inueni primarios aliquot in hac Republica viros, Hilbrandum Sudermannum, & Ioannem Hardenradium, Consules; tum Gulielmum Hacksteinium, ac Petrum Crantium, Iuris Doctores, huius Reipublicae Syndicos; demum Bartholdum Questenbergium, & Ioannem Lennepium, Senatorij ordinis viros.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1590, on 10 April, I was summoned, on behalf of the most distinguished Senate of Cologne, to the public prison, which they call the Franconian Tower, to confer with a certain preacher, John Badius of Roding, on several matters. The preacher had been arrested some days earlier, because he had preached secret sermons against the edicts of the magistrate. I came to the prison about the fourth hour in the afternoon, and there I found gathered several leading men of this commonwealth: Hilbrand Sudermann and John Hardenrath, consuls; then William Hacksteyn and Peter Krantz, doctors of law and syndics of this commonwealth; and finally Bartholomew Questenberg and John Lennep, men of the senatorial order.

units.la: Iussus est e custodia prodire Badius, cui Doctor Gulielmus Hacksteinius, alter Syndicorum, in memoriam reuocauit, quod diebus superioribus respondere noluerit ad capita quaedam, quae nomine amplissimi Senatus illi proposita fuerant. Quia vero pro sui defensione, rationibus partim politicis, partim vero Theologicis vsus sit; Amplif. Senatum politicas ipsius rationes diligenter expendisse, pendisse, atque de ijs quidem iam certi aliquid habere constitutum, quemadmodum suo tempore sit auditus. Quod autem ad rationes Theologicas attineat, eas alterius fori esse: Itaque ne sibi putaret iniuriam fieri, noluisse Ampliss. Senatum hac parte quicquam constituere, antequam de ijs cum viro Ecclesiastico cotulisset. Atque in hunc finem me, Pastorem D. Cuniberti, vocatum esse, vt quia persuasum habeat, laedi conscientiam suam, seque contra legem charitatis delinquere, si ad interrogata responderet, de conscientia sua, deque charitatis lege mecum conferret.
units.tr: Badius was ordered to come out of custody. Doctor William Hacksteyn, the second of the syndics, reminded him that on the previous days he had refused to answer certain articles which had been put to him on behalf of the most distinguished Senate. He had defended himself partly on political grounds and partly on theological grounds. The most distinguished Senate had carefully weighed his political arguments, and had already reached a definite decision on them, as would be made known at the proper time. As for his theological arguments, however, these belonged to another forum. So that he should not think he was being wronged, the Senate had resolved not to decide anything on this point until he had consulted a churchman about them. For this purpose I, the pastor of St. Cunibert's, had been summoned, so that, since he was persuaded that his conscience was violated and that he would sin against the law of charity if he answered the questions put to him, he might confer with me about his conscience and the law of charity.

units.la: Ille principio assurgens, protestabatur, se natura timidum esse, & difficulter, in praesentia tantorum virorum, animi sensa eloqui posse; facturum tamen periculum, vt mentem suam explicet. Deinde paucis ea repetebat, quae diebus superioribus acta fuerant: Rogabat etiam Dominos praesentes, ne id contumacia interpretarentur, quod ad interrogata non responderet eo modo, quo Senatus vellet. Obstare conscientiam suam, & charitatem proximi; Nisi id esset, lubenti se animo imperata facturum.
units.tr: Badius rose first and declared that he was by nature timid, and that in the presence of such distinguished men he could find it hard to express the feelings of his mind; yet he would make the attempt to explain his mind. He then briefly repeated what had happened on the previous days. He also asked the gentlemen present not to interpret it as stubbornness that he did not answer the questions in the way the Senate wished. His conscience and his neighbour's charity stood in the way; otherwise he would gladly do what was commanded.

units.la: Ego primum quaesiui, quam Religionem profiteretur? Responsum est; Confessionem Augustanam, vti ea posterioribus annis, à Philippo Melanthone declarata est. Adiecit ipse, Quia Religionis Pax, quam vocant, in Imperio sancita esset, eius beneficio sibi quoque, tanquam Augustanam Confessionem profitenti, licuisse in hac urbe docere.
units.tr: I first asked which religion he professed. The answer was: the Augsburg Confession, as it was set out in later years by Philip Melanchthon. He added himself that, since the peace of religion, as they call it, had been sanctioned in the Empire, by its benefit he too, as one who professed the Augsburg Confession, had been permitted to teach in this city.

units.la: Fassus fuerat pridie, (quemadmodum illi per Dominos Syndicos in memoriam redigebatur) in eo se sensu Confessionem Augustanā amplecti ac profiteri, in quo Fridericus Palatinus Elector quondam, & filius eius Casimirus hactenus, eandem in Palatinatu professi fuerint. Dixi, eum esse germanum Caluinismum: Quod vt aperte demonstrarem, subieci; In Comitijs Augustanis anno 1530. duas esse Confessiones Imperatori oblatas, alteram à Saxone, Landgrauio, atque aliis Imperij Ordinibus Lutheranis; alteram vero à quatuor ciuitatibus Zwinglianis, Argentorato, Constantia, Memminga, & Lindauia, quas cæteri Protestantes nullo pacto in societatem suæ Confessionis recipere voluerint: Quod confirmaui, narrata quadam historia de Bucero, ex Comitijs Augustanis, Zwinglianorum nomine Coburgum ad Lutherum misso, atque à communione reiecto; quam longum esset hoc loco intexere. Interrogaui deinde; Vtram istarum Confessionum amplectereretur, Lutheranam ne, an Zwinglianam? Hic vero nonnihil cunctabatur. Cum vrgerem, ab aliis demum ipsius loco responsum est, quod ipse pridie dixerat, Eam, cuius auctor esset Philippus Melanthon. Addidit ipse, Melanthoni hanc eandem Confessionem, de consensu eorundem Ordinum, à quibus in Comitijs Augustanis oblata sit, postea declarare ac mutare licuisse.
units.tr: The day before, he had confessed (as the syndics reminded him) that he embraced and professed the Augsburg Confession in the sense in which Frederick, the former Elector Palatine, and his son Casimir, had hitherto professed it in the Palatinate. I said that this was pure Calvinism. To demonstrate this clearly, I added that at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 two confessions had been presented to the Emperor: one by the Elector of Saxony, the Landgrave, and the other Lutheran estates of the Empire; the other by four Zwinglian cities, Strasbourg, Constance, Memmingen and Lindau. The other Protestants had by no means been willing to admit these into fellowship with their confession. I confirmed this by recounting a story about Bucer from the Diet of Augsburg, sent on behalf of the Zwinglians to Luther at Coburg and rejected from communion; to relate it fully here would take too long. I then asked: which of these confessions did he embrace, the Lutheran or the Zwinglian? At this he hesitated somewhat. When I pressed him, at last others answered in his place, as he himself had said the day before, that he embraced the one whose author was Philip Melanchthon. He added himself that Melanchthon had been permitted afterwards to declare and change this same confession, with the consent of the same estates by whom it had been presented at the Diet of Augsburg.

units.la: Respondi, primum Augustanæ Confessionis auctorem, Melanthonem solum non esse: Lutherum ipsum, doctrinam suam septendecim capitibus comprehensam suppeditasse Melanthoni; eum vero postmodum hæc ipsa doctrinæ capita paulo fusius tractasse; Quæ Lutherus itidem, antequam in Comitijs offerretur, viderit, ac suo iudicio confirmarit. Atque hanc esse Confessionem illam Augustanam, Imperatori Carolo Quinto à Protestantibus oblatam; quam Melanthoni deinceps mutare nequaquam licuerit, propterea, quod nec ipsum solum auctorem agnoscat; & si agnosceret, non ipsius tamen, aut Lutheri, sed Protestatium Ordinum nomine, in publico Imperij Conuetu sit oblata. Non diffiteri me, quin Melanthon in articulo de coena, postremis annis ab hac Confessione Lutherana, ad alteram illam Zwinglianam defecerit: Verum si deinde, posteaquā mutarit animum, Confessionem quoq; Protestantium pro libitu mutare voluerit, eam porrò non Augustanam, sed Philippicam potius.
units.tr: I replied, first, that Melanchthon was not the sole author of the Augsburg Confession: Luther himself had supplied Melanchthon with his doctrine, comprised in seventeen articles; and Melanchthon afterwards treated these same articles of doctrine somewhat more fully. Luther likewise saw them, before they were offered at the Diet, and confirmed them by his judgment. This is the Augsburg Confession which was presented to the Emperor Charles V by the Protestants, and which Melanchthon was by no means permitted to change afterwards; for it is not acknowledged to have Melanchthon alone as its author, and even if it were, it was presented not in his name or Luther's, but in the name of the Protesting estates, in the public assembly of the Empire. I do not deny that Melanchthon, in the article on the Supper, in his last years departed from this Lutheran confession to that other, the Zwinglian one. But if he afterwards, having changed his mind, wished to change the confession of the Protestants at his pleasure, then it should be called not the Augsburg Confession but rather the Philippic.

units.la: Acta Colloquij Altenburgensis, sol. 520 & alibi. Chytraeus in historia Augustanæ Conf. pa. 32. potius dicendam esse, quæ Augustæ nunquam fuerit.
units.tr: Acts of the Colloquy of Altenburg, p. 520 and elsewhere. Chytraeus, in the history of the Augsburg Confession, p. 32: it should rather be called the one which was never at Augsburg.

units.la: Hoc loco D. Consul Sudermanus, Siue Augustana dicatur, (inquit) siue Philippica, satis intelligimus, eā ipsam esse, quam hic profitetur. Ille vero ad hæc omnia negry quidem, quod aiunt. Subiūxi ego; Nunquam omnes Imperij ordines Lutheranos in eam mutatione consensisse, quæ iuxta Melanthonis mentem in Palatinatu instituta sit: Et si consenserint, (quod sine mendacio affirmari nequeat) id publicam defectionem potius, quàm declarationem dici oportere. Extare Lutheranorum Theologorum scripta, in quibus huiusmodi mutationes in Augustana Confessione, defectio à puriore doctrina, & falsi crimen appellentur.
units.tr: At this point Consul Sudermann said: "Whether it is called Augsburg or Philippic, we understand well enough that it is the one he professes here." But Badius denied all of this, as they say. I replied: the Lutheran estates of the Empire never agreed to the change which was instituted in the Palatinate according to Melanchthon's mind; and even if they had agreed (which cannot be affirmed without falsehood), this ought to be called a public defection rather than a declaration. There are writings of Lutheran theologians in which such changes in the Augsburg Confession are called defection from the purer doctrine and the crime of falsehood.

units.la: Neque vero, inquam, vos, qui Caluini ductum sequimini, in hoc vno tantum capite de Cœna, ab Augustanæ Confessionis Protestantibus dissidetis, verum & in multis alijs; verbi causa, de Peccato originis, de Baptismate, de Sacramētorum numero ac virtute, de persona Christi, de Prædestinatione, &c. Adeò vt Iacobus Andreæ in præfatione libri cuiusdam, quem admonendi causa, de Lutheri Bibliis in Palatinatu corruptis edidit, sedecim errores enumeret, quibus ea ipsa Lutheri Biblia à vestris contaminata esse quiritatur.
units.tr: Indeed, I said, you who follow the lead of Calvin dissent from the Protestants of the Augsburg Confession not only on this one point about the Supper, but also on many others: for example, on original sin, on baptism, on the number and power of the sacraments, on the person of Christ, on predestination, and so on. So much so that Jacob Andreae, in the preface to a book which he published as a warning about Luther's Bibles corrupted in the Palatinate, lists sixteen errors by which he complains that those same Bibles of Luther were contaminated by yours.

units.la: Ille ad nomen Iacobi Andreæ falsè ridens, Nosti, inquit, qualis fuerit Iacobus Andreæ, quàm multas ille turbas concitarit. Quam eius vocem omnes suaui risu excepe-runt, quod primarium scilicet Augustanæ confessionis Apostolum, adeò cōtemptim habere videretur. Ego vero, Non ignoro, inquam, qui vir fuerit Iacobus Andreæ, & quas turbas ille dederit: Hoc tamen ex ijs, quæ dicta sunt, manifestum est, nimirum iniquè fecisse te, quod ad Confessionem Augustanam prouocaris, eoque nomine iure te conuentus clancularios egisse dixeris.
units.tr: He, laughing falsely at the name of Jacob Andreae, said: "You know what sort of man Jacob Andreae was, and how many disturbances he stirred up." All of them received this remark with a pleasant laugh, because they evidently thought little of the chief apostle of the Augsburg Confession. But I said: "I am not ignorant of what sort of man Jacob Andreae was, or what disturbances he caused. It is clear, however, from what has been said, that you have acted unjustly in appealing to the Augsburg Confession, and that, on that account, you have rightly been called to account, as you yourself have said, for secret assemblies."

units.la: Cæterum eandem rem & alia quadā ratione probaui.
units.tr: Otherwise I proved the same point by another method as well.

units.la: Dixerat pridie, (quemadmodum Syndici referebant) se in Palatinatu ab Heidelbergensi Concilio, in Verbi Ministrum ordinatum esse: Quæsitus autem, cur ibidem in loco vocationis suæ non manserit? Responderat, Ludovicum Electorem Ministros omnes, qui ad ipsius de Religione sententiam accedere noluerint, à docendi functione remouisse, ijsque mandasse, vt alio sedes transferrent. Huius igitur mandati occasione, se quoque è Palatinatu discessisse, ea mente tamen, vt aliquando (vbi mitior aura spirauerit) isthuc reuerteretur, suumq; munus, ac docendi ministerium resumeret. Hæc cum à Syndicis commemorata essent; quæsiui ego, An non Ludouicus Palatinus Elector Augustanæ Confessionis fuerit? Ille, quanquā negare non audebat, affirmare tamen expresse noluit. Tu ego: Procul dubio fuit, inquam. Quādo igitur te, tuique similes, ob diuersam Religionem è Palatinatu expulit, qua fronte tu hic ad eam Confessionem prouocasti? quis non videat, te sub Augustanæ Confessionis nomine fraudem moliri?
units.tr: The day before, as the syndics reported, he had said that in the Palatinate he had been ordained a minister of the Word by the Heidelberg council. Asked why he had not remained in the place of his calling there, he had answered that Elector Ludwig had removed from their teaching office all the ministers who would not accede to his opinion about religion, and had ordered them to move their seats elsewhere. On the occasion of this order, he too had left the Palatinate, with the intention, however, of returning there sometime, when a milder breeze should blow, and of resuming his office and ministry of teaching. When the syndics had recounted this, I asked: "Was not Ludwig, the Elector Palatine, of the Augsburg Confession?" Though he did not dare to deny it, he would not expressly affirm it. I said: "Without doubt he was, I say. Since, then, he expelled you and those like you from the Palatinate on account of a different religion, with what face do you now appeal to that confession here? Who does not see that you are attempting a fraud under the name of the Augsburg Confession?"

units.la: Excipiebat Dominus Sudermannus Consul, & paucis narrabat historiam mutationis illius, quam Friderico Palatino Electore mortuo, filius illius, ac successor Ludouicus instituerit. Dicebat, fuisse se tum in Palatinatu, ac principia mutationis oculis suis vidisse. Clausa fuisse templa Principis Electoris mandatu, neque licuisse deinceps Concionatoribus illis, qui sub Friderico docuerat, officio suo fungi; quod ipse Badius ignorare non posset, vt qui eodem tempore è Palatinatu quoque discedere coactus fuerit. Ad hæc ille, pudore suffusus tacuit.
units.tr: Consul Sudermannus took up the matter and briefly described the change that Frederick, the Palatine Elector, instituted after his death, and that his son and successor, Ludwig, carried through. He said he had been in the Palatinate at the time and had seen the beginnings of the change with his own eyes. The churches were closed by the Elector's order, and the preachers who had taught under Frederick were no longer allowed to carry out their office. Badius himself could not be ignorant of this, since he too had been forced to leave the Palatinate at the same time. To this he said nothing, overcome with shame.

units.la: Ego vero & illud porro subiungebam; Quod si Confessionem Augustanam syncere profiteretur, non licuisse tamen illi sub statu Imperij Catholico, contra Magistratus Edicta, eam ipsam priuatim exercere; cum Religionis Pacem, ad quam prouocaret, super Status ipsos, non super singula subditorum capita, fundatam costet.
units.tr: I added this further: even if he sincerely professed the Augsburg Confession, he was not permitted, under the Catholic state of the Empire and against the edicts of the magistrates, to practise it privately. The Peace of Religion, to which he appealed, is clearly founded on the states themselves, not on the individual heads of subjects.

units.la: Quærebam cuidētiæ causa, si ego vigore Constitutionis illius, quam Pacem Religionis vocant, Heidelbergæ in Palatinatu, vel in vrbe quadam Imperij Lutherana, id facere conarer, quod ille hoc loco aliquandiu fecisset, an id laturus essem impunè?
units.tr: I asked, for the sake of inquiry, whether, if I tried under the authority of that constitution which they call the Peace of Religion to do in Heidelberg in the Palatinate, or in some Lutheran imperial city, what he had been doing here for some time, I would get off unpunished.

units.la: Ad hæc ille nihil admodum: Responderat tamen diebus superioribus, quemadmodum Syndici referebant; Aliam esse hac parte conditionem vrbium, in quibus populus eligeret magistratum, quàm Principum eorum, qui Status Imperij sunt ex natiuitate. Quam vocem, tanquam occultum seditionis flabellum, vti reuera est, omnes acceperūt. Cùm enim huiusmodi discrimen in promiscuam plebem sinistrè spargitur, facilè nimirum fit, vt incauti, qui nō possunt in hisce rebus discernere, contra magistratum animentur ac concitentur. Voluit ille quidem excusare ac mollire dictū, verùm friuolè. Tum Dominus Hardenradius Consul, Talia, inquit, inculcatis vestris hominibus, vt scilicet persuasum habeant, se rectè facere, cùm contra magistratum insurgunt, atque huiusmodi prohibitos in Imperio clanculariosconuentus agūt. Quod si vel Ratisbonæ, vel Noribergæ, tale quid tentaris, procul dubio longè seuerius tecum ageretur.
units.tr: To this he replied with almost nothing. Yet on earlier days, as the syndics reported, he had answered that in this respect the situation of cities was different, where the people elect the magistrate, from that of those princes who are states of the Empire by birth. Everyone took this remark, as it truly is, for a hidden bellows of sedition. For when such a distinction is maliciously spread among the common people, it easily happens that the incautious, who cannot tell these matters apart, are stirred up and incited against the magistrate. He wanted to excuse and soften what he had said, but feebly. Then Consul Hardenradius said: "You impress such things on your people, namely so that they believe they do right when they rise against the magistrate, and hold such secret gatherings, which are forbidden in the Empire. If you had attempted anything of the kind at Regensburg or Nuremberg, without doubt you would have been dealt with far more severely."

units.la: Quæsiui ego demum, cùm reuera Caluinianus esset, qua conscientia nomen Augustanæ Confessionis præ se ferret? Quomodo, inquam, in articulo mortis, & in extre mo iudicio hoc nomine coram Deo consistes, quod titulo ac larua confessionis illius indutus, cuius reuera hostis es, simpliciores fraudulenter ad Caluinismum ducis? Ad hæc ille subticuit.
units.tr: Finally I asked: since he was really a Calvinist, with what conscience did he display the name of the Augsburg Confession? How, I said, will you stand before God at the point of death and at the last judgment under this name, when, wearing the title and mask of that confession, of which you are truly an enemy, you lead simpler folk fraudulently into Calvinism? To this he said nothing.

units.la: Ventum est deinde ad ipsius conscientiam, & charitate proximi, quam vtramque lædi persuasum habebat, si legitimè ad Amplis. Senatus interrogata responderet. Iussus est à Dominis Syndicis nūc proferre rationes, quibus in eam sententiam inductus esset. Cumque ille, quantum ego colligere potui, de industria se reprimeret, neq; tum ego colligere potui, de industria se reprimeret, neq; proferret quicquam, interrogaui demum ego: An non Amplissimum Senatum Colonienfem, pro vero huius vrbis magistratu agnosceret? Respondit, quanquam cun stabundus, Ita. Quæsiui denuo: An non, dum in hac vrbe vixisset, obedientiâ sese eidem legitimo magistratui debere, ex conscientiæ obligatione putaret? Respondit, Ita, si nihil contra Deum mandaret; Alioquin Deo magis obediendum esse, quàm hominibus. Quæsiui tertiò: An igitur Amplifs. huius vrbis Senatus, vnquam ipsi mandarit aliquid, quod legi charitatis, aut diuino mandato contrarium fuerit? Ad hanc quæstionem subticuit.
units.tr: We then came to his conscience and to love of neighbour, both of which he believed would be harmed if he answered the questions of the most distinguished Senate lawfully. The syndics ordered him to now state the reasons that had led him to that opinion. Although, as far as I could gather, he deliberately restrained himself and would say nothing, I finally asked: did he not acknowledge the most distinguished Senate of Cologne as the true magistracy of this city? He replied, though hesitantly, "Yes." I asked again: while he lived in this city, did he not think that, by an obligation of conscience, he owed obedience to that same lawful magistracy? He said, "Yes, provided it commanded nothing against God; otherwise God must be obeyed rather than men." I asked a third time: has the most distinguished Senate of this city ever commanded him anything contrary to the law of love or to a divine command? To this question he was silent.

units.la: Admonitus aliquoties à Dominis Syndicis, vt aperiret syncere mentem suam, ac causas proderet pertinacis illius silentij, quo iam aliquamdiu Magistratum elusisset; Nihil amplius protulit, nisi, proximum suum læde, si voluntati Senatus obtemperaret: Neque vero hac in re opus esse suo indicio, posse Magistratum omnia, quæ ex ipso scire vellet, aliunde resciscere. Facturum se contra conscientiam, si ea proderet, per quæ deinde proximo suo detrimentum adferri sciret. Itaque rogare se, ne hac parte grauius vrgeretur.
units.tr: Although the syndics often admonished him to disclose his mind sincerely and to give the reasons for the stubborn silence by which he had for some time eluded the magistrate, he produced nothing more than this: he would harm his neighbour if he obeyed the will of the Senate. Nor was there any need for his own testimony in this matter, since the magistrate could learn elsewhere everything it wished to know from him. He would act against his conscience if he disclosed things by which, he knew, harm would afterwards come to his neighbour. He therefore asked that he not be pressed more hard on this point.

units.la: Quæsiui ego rursum: An Senatus, quem pro legitimo huius vrbis magistratu agnosceret, ipsius quoque proximus esset, nec ne? Respondit, esse. Cur igitur, inquam, quando proximi tui rationem habere vis, magis respiciendum putas ad paucos quosdam priuatos, qui magistratui debitam obedientiam negant, quàm ad eos, quos ad Reipublicæ gubernacula collocauit Dominus, quorum interest ad conseruandam pacem publicam, ea scire, quæ à te quæruntur.
units.tr: I asked again: is the Senate, which he acknowledged as the lawful magistracy of this city, also his neighbour or not? He said it was. Why then, I said, when you wish to have regard for your neighbour, do you think more weight should be given to a few private persons who deny due obedience to the magistrate than to those whom the Lord has set at the helm of the commonwealth? It is their concern, for preserving public peace, to know the things that are being asked of you.

units.la: Respondit ille, Non pendere Reipublicæ salutem ex hoc negocio, neq; lædi Senatus auctoritatem, si non prodat ea, quæ Magistratus ipsius indicio scire vellet. Imò ve-rò, inquam, læditur. Antea fassus es, obedientiâ te debere Magistratui huius vrbis, nisi quid contra Deum mandet. Igitur vel obtemperandum nunc est, vel certè demon- strandū, mandari aliquid, quod cum diuina lege pugnet. Iam & salus Reipublicæ læditur, quando nimirum occultantur ea consilia, eæque actiones, quibus perturbari pacem publicam, ac seditiones excitari, aliarum vrbium exempla testantur: Et tu quidem tacitè Senatum huius vrbis accusas impietatis atq; tyrannidis, impiettatis quidem, quod eam Religionem foueat, quam tu cum Idololatria coniunctam esse sentis, quæ summa est, & omnium maxima impietas; tyrannidis verò, quod Edicta sanciat, quibus Idololatria & impietas stabiliatur, ac subditi, ab ea alieni, per vim opprimantur; quæ, quin germana tyrannis sit, negari non potest.
units.tr: He replied that the safety of the commonwealth did not depend on this matter, nor was the Senate's authority harmed if he did not disclose what the magistrate wished to know from him. "Indeed," I said, "it is harmed. You admitted earlier that you owe obedience to the magistrate of this city unless it commands something against God. So either obedience must now be given, or it must certainly be shown that something is commanded which conflicts with divine law. Moreover, the safety of the commonwealth is harmed when those plans and actions are concealed by which, as the examples of other cities testify, public peace is disturbed and seditions are stirred up. And you, indeed, tacitly accuse the Senate of this city of impiety and tyranny: of impiety, because it fosters that religion which you judge to be joined with idolatry, which is the greatest and worst of all impieties; of tyranny, because it sanctions edicts by which idolatry and impiety are established, and subjects who are alien to it are oppressed by force. That this is genuine tyranny cannot be denied."

units.la: Excepit ille, Nequaquam se tyrannidis aut impietatis accusare Senatum. Posse fieri, vt magistratus ex sinistra persuasione iudicio nonnunquam aberret, dum hæc aut illa, præter æquitatis rationem statuit: Quemadmodum euenerit Constantino Magno Imperatori, quem Arriani quondam in Athanasium vehementer concitarint. Neque verò huiusmodi lapsus eorum, qui in magistratu sunt, impietatis ac tyrannidis nomine censendos esse, quando non accedit habitus.
units.tr: He retorted that he did not accuse the Senate of tyranny or impiety at all. A magistrate, he said, could from a mistaken persuasion sometimes err in judgment, deciding this or that beyond the reason of equity, just as it happened to the Emperor Constantine the Great, whom the Arians once vehemently stirred up against Athanasius. Nor should such lapses of those who hold office be counted as impiety and tyranny, when there is no settled habit of it.

units.la: Ego, cùm Constantini mentionem faceret, narrauì ex Historia Ecclesiastica, qua stropha piissimus Imperator, cùm magno concordiæ sarciendæ studio flagraret, ab Arrio circumuentus, in Arrianos aliquando propensior factus fit. Quam historiam hoc loco breuitatis studio nō infero. Subiunxi deinde, Eum hoc exēplo non sufficienter ab huius vrbis Senatu tyrannidis atque impietatis crimē remouere: Quandoquidem omnia, quæ Senatus hac parte contra Sectarios ageret, non temerè, vel ex informatione sinistra, sed maturo consilio, ac deliberato ageret; imò, (quemadmodum Syndici suggerebant) hanc tuendæ Religionis Catholicæ rationem, à piis maioribus per manus traditam haberet: Vt adeò hæ actiones, proeul dubio, ex habitu quodam administrandae Reipu-blicae proficiscantur. Itaq; non esse, quod imprudentem Constantini credulitatem ac lapsum, cum maturis huius magistratus actionibus comparet.
units.tr: When he mentioned Constantine, I related from the Ecclesiastical History by what trick that most pious emperor, though burning with a great desire to restore concord, was deceived by Arius and at one time became more inclined towards the Arians. I do not set out that story here for the sake of brevity. I then added that by this example he did not sufficiently clear the Senate of this city of the charge of tyranny and impiety. For whatever the Senate does in this respect against the sectaries, it does not do rashly or from false information, but with mature counsel and deliberation; indeed, as the syndics pointed out, it holds this way of defending the Catholic religion handed down by its pious ancestors. So these actions surely proceed from a settled habit of governing the commonwealth. Therefore there was no reason to compare Constantine's imprudent credulity and lapse with the mature actions of this magistracy.

units.la: Hortabatur cum inter conferendum Doctor Hack-steinius, vt nunc proferret D. Cypriani sententiam, quam ad cautae suae defensionem, in examine superiori protulisset; Vrgebam idem & ego. Verum ille perpetuo, quicquid diceremus, tergiuersatus est, nec vnquam vel D. Cypriani nomen appellare voluit. Demum ego, quia nihil afferebat, Cyprianus, inquâ, nulla in re tibi suffragatur. Fuit is Episcopus Catholicus, & causam egit coram magistratu gentili. Si quid eo rerum statu dixit, id ad te nihil pertinet: Quando inter D. Cyprianum, & te; tum inter Senatum huius vrbis Catholicum, & magistratum illum gentilem, nulla penitus est comparatio.
units.tr: Doctor Hacksteinius, during our conversation, urged him to now bring forward the opinion of St Cyprian, which he had put forward in defence of his caution at the earlier examination, and I pressed the same point. But he kept evading whatever we said, and never once wished even to name St Cyprian. At last, since he offered nothing, I said: "Cyprian supports you in no respect. He was a Catholic bishop, and he pleaded his cause before a pagan magistracy. If he said anything in that state of affairs, it has nothing to do with you. For there is no comparison at all between St Cyprian and you, nor between this Catholic Senate of the city and that pagan magistrate."

units.la: Vrgebant cum, cùm ita perpetuo restitaret, alijs quoq; rationibus, Consul Hardenradius & Syndici. Quaerebat, cur ad eum modum tergiuersaretur? Quid huiusmodi subterfugijs Amplissimum Senatum ac seipsum quoque distineret? Ipsum fateri hoc pertinaci silentio, quod male fecerit. Nam si bene se fecisse putaret, cur tantopere de fugeret lucem? Cur actiones suas secretas esse vellet, easque tanto studio celare contenderet? Imo quo magis hac parte subterfugeret, eo graviores habere causas Senatu, vt consilia contra Reipublicae salutem in iis conuenticulis agitata suspicetur. Neque vero eam suspicionem omnino vanam esse, quando per huiusmodi clancularios conuentus, insignes nonnunquam Respublicae penitus euersae sint. Haec, & id genus alia cum obijcerentur, ille nihil admodum respondit; nisi quod diceret, se suos auditores semper ad obedientiam, ac pacem colendam hortatum fuisse, neque hoc spectasse vnquam, vt seditionem concitaret.
units.tr: Since he kept resisting in this way, Consul Hardenradius and the syndics urged him with other arguments too. They asked why he evaded in such a manner, and why he kept the most distinguished Senate, and himself as well, at a distance with such subterfuges. By this stubborn silence he was in effect confessing that he had done wrong: for if he thought he had acted well, why did he so greatly shun the light? Why did he want his actions to be secret and strive so eagerly to conceal them? Indeed, the more he evaded on this point, the more serious reasons the Senate had to suspect that plans against the safety of the commonwealth were being hatched in those conventicles. Nor was that suspicion at all vain, since notable commonwealths have sometimes been utterly overthrown by such secret gatherings. When these and other things of this kind were put to him, he answered almost nothing, except that he had always exhorted his hearers to obedience and to the keeping of peace, and had never aimed at stirring up sedition.

units.la: Ad quam vocem Dominus Hardenradius Consul, fciliscilicet,inquit,id fatis experimur in vestri sodalitij homi nibus,qui ita fe gerunt erga Senatum, vt omnia illorum inobedientiam spirare videantur: Vnde liquidò con- stare potest,quid agatur in vestris coetibus, & qualia in ijs consilia pertractentur:In quibus proculdubio inter alia Senatum falsò, & contra conscientiam traducitis, quasi Christo Seruatori praecludat viam, & Idololatriam in hac vrbe foueat;vt scilicet causam habere videatur,cùm sese magistratui ad eum modum opponunt. Ad quae ille paululum submurmuras,nihil amplius respondit,quàm quod antea quoque dixerat, quod nunquam publi- cos excitare motus in animo habuerit.
units.tr: At this remark Lord Hardenradius, the Consul, said: "We experience this indeed, namely in the men of your fellowship, who so conduct themselves toward the Senate that all of them seem to breathe disobedience. From this it can clearly be established what is going on at your gatherings and what plans are discussed in them. In them, without doubt, among other things, you slander the Senate falsely and against your conscience, as though it blocks the way to Christ the Saviour and fosters idolatry in this city, so that you may seem to have a reason when you thus set yourselves against the magistrate." To this he muttered a little and answered nothing more than what he had said before: that he had never intended to stir up public disturbances.

units.la: Tum ego,vt hoc,inquam,concedatur,quod tu conci- tare auditores tuos contra Senatum non intenderis, cer- tum est tamen experientia magistra, vbicunque contra magistratus Edicta, huiusmodi secreti conuentus à ve- stris habiti sunt,ibi semper perturbationem publicae pa- cis, ac magistratus oppressionem demum subsecutam. Quod exempla florentissimarum vrbium in vicino Bel- gio satis testificantur. Addidit Dominus Consul Suder- mannus exemplum vrbis Aquisgranensis, quae eadem via in magnas difficultates coniecta sit. Et in Belgio quidem, (inquit Dominus Consul) voluistis omnes, vti vobis vi- debatur, à iugo Romani Pontificis eximere. At quid fa- ctum est? Scilicet vestris conatibus multò profundius, quàm vnquam antea,Belgas in Pontificis Romani serui tutem coniecistis. Itaque nihil valent conatus vestri, ne- que tolerari debent,aut possunt. Admonemur ex omni parte,multas in vrbe nostra Sectas pullulare; necessariū esse, vt diligenter prospiciamus rebus nostris, ne quid ab ijs detrimenti Reipublicae nostrae inferatur.
units.tr: Then I said: "Granted, let it be conceded that you did not intend to stir up your hearers against the Senate. Experience, the teacher of all things, nonetheless makes it certain that wherever such secret meetings held by your people have been held against the edicts of the magistrate, there the disturbance of public peace and the oppression of the magistrate have always followed. The examples of the most flourishing cities in neighbouring Belgium bear sufficient witness to this." Consul Sudermannus added the example of the city of Aachen, which was thrown into great difficulties by the same route. "And in Belgium indeed," said the Lord Consul, "you all wished, as it seemed to you, to free yourselves from the yoke of the Roman Pontiff. But what happened? Clearly, by your efforts you have thrust the Belgians into the slavery of the Roman Pontiff far more deeply than ever before. Therefore your efforts are worth nothing, and ought not, or cannot, be tolerated. We are warned on every side that many sects are sprouting up in our city, and it is necessary that we take careful thought for our affairs, lest any harm come to our commonwealth from them."

units.la: Ad haec verba ego,rogata venia,interlocutus,quod de Sectis dicitur,inquam,id verissimum est; quemadmodū fatis experimur,qui curam animarum in hac vrbe geri- mus.Lutherani rariores sunt,& deficiunt indies;quidam illoillorum ad nos redeunt, quidam vero paulatim in nas-fam pertrahuntur à Caluinistis; Qui numero superat Lu-theranos. Iam & Svvenckfeldiani quoq; incrementa su-munt. Anabaptistarum vero gens etiam augetur. Quin & Domus charitatis, quæ ex Anabaptistarū secibus, tan-quam riuus quidam, promanauit, pedé in hac vrbe iam-pridem fixit.
units.tr: To these words I replied, having first asked pardon: "As to what is said about sects, I say that this is most true, as we who have the care of souls in this city experience. The Lutherans are fewer and are failing day by day; some of them are returning to us, while others are being drawn gradually into the Calvinists' net, and the Calvinists now outnumber the Lutherans. Already the Schwenckfeldians too are increasing. The race of the Anabaptists is also growing. Indeed the House of Charity, which flowed out of the Anabaptist sects like a certain stream, has long since set foot in this city."

units.la: Excepit Ioannes Lennepius, & Currum quoque ster-corum, (id nouum quoddam Libertinorum genus est) huc aduectum dixit, quemadmodum à fide dignis acce-perit. Tum Dominus Sudermannus Consul, Bene, inquit, Si igitur nos quemlibet pro libitu suo agere patere-mur, & demum aliqua fieret in Religione mutatio; quid Cæsarea Maiestas, quid Rex Hispaniarum, quid Ponti-sex, quid Iuliacensis Princeps, vicinus noster dicturus es-set? Procul dubio hoc pacto ciuitas nostra in plurima pe-ricula coniiceretur. Hæc à Domino Consule cum vehe-mentia quadam dicebantur; Ille vero omnia silentio transmittebat.
units.tr: John Lennep took up the point and said that a cart of dung too had been brought here, a new kind of Libertine (for that is what they are), as he had received from trustworthy sources. Then Consul Sudermannus said: "Good. If, then, we were to allow each person to act as he pleases, and at last some change in religion were to follow, what would his Caesarean Majesty, what the King of Spain, what the Pontiff, what the Prince of Jülich, our neighbour, have to say? Without doubt in this way our city would be thrown into the greatest dangers." These things were said by the Consul with a certain vehemence; but he himself let everything pass in silence.

units.la: Inter colloquendū, cum obijceretur, huiusmodi clan-culariọs conuentus semper motus publicos, ac seditio-nes subditorum contra magistratum peperisse; atque ille nonnihil obmurmuraret, quæsiuit ex illo Ioannes Len-nepius, vt vel vnicum proferret exemplum, vbi secus ac-cidisset? Ad quam vocem, oculis in sinum defixus, peni-tus obmutuit. Tum ego, quid igitur, inquam, magistratus huius vrbis aliud à vobis exspectare potest, quàm vt, qđ alibi per hoc medium perpetrastis, idem & hic quoque conemini paulatim, vbi satis virium accreuerit?
units.tr: In the course of the conversation, when it was objected that such secret meetings had always produced public disturbances and seditions of subjects against the magistrate, and when he muttered something in protest, John Lennep asked him to produce at least one single example where things had turned out otherwise. At this he fixed his eyes on his lap and fell completely silent. Then I said: "What else, then, can the magistrate of this city expect from you, than that you will try little by little here, once you have gathered enough strength, to do the same thing that you have carried out elsewhere by this means?"

units.la: Intuli quoque sermonem de ipsius vocatione; cuius rei occasio fuit, quod conscientiam suam informatam esse Dei verbo diceret. Quæsiui, qua conscietia ipse, cùm nec à Deo vocatus esset, nec ab hominibus, qui potesta-tem eius rei haberet, huius vrbis ciuibus subrepsisset? Nō est, inquam, in hac celebri ac populosa vrbe, vel vnus ho-mo, qui mo, qui non habeat suum Pastorem, per legitimæ vocationis viam à Deo constitutū: Inter quos & ego me quoque, licet omnium infimum, connumero. Nobis igitur, qui Pastores in hac vrbe sumus, creditæ sunt, ac commissæ oues huius gregis, quibus diuini verbi, ac Sacramentorum pabulum hactenus ministrauimus. Eam ad rem, per Dei gratiam, tua, tuíque similium opera non indigemus.
units.tr: I also brought the talk round to his own calling. The occasion for this was that he said his conscience was informed by the Word of God. I asked by what conscience he himself, since he had been called neither by God nor by men who had authority in this matter, had crept in among the citizens of this city. "There is not," I said, "in this famous and populous city a single person who does not have his own minister, appointed by God through the path of lawful calling; and among these I count myself too, though the least of all. To us, therefore, who are ministers in this city, the sheep of this flock have been entrusted and committed, and to them we have hitherto supplied the food of the divine Word and the Sacraments. For this task, by the grace of God, we do not need your work or that of people like you."

units.la: Quomodo igitur in iudicio Dei facinus hoc defendes, quod, cùm peregrinus sis, nec legitimè vocatus, oues nostras dissipas, easque contra Magistratus Edicta in angulum conuocatas, à nobis auertis? Tū quod nos, qui legitimi Pastores sumus, in conuenticulis istis traducis, quin absentes calumnijs ac mendacijs oneras, & nec admonitos, nec auditos condemnas? Quod si nos, qui Coloniæ curam animarum gerimus, non recte fungeremur officio nostro, tuarum partium fuisset, nos admonere prius, & redarguere, quàm ad eum modum, contra Senatus voluntatem, prohibitos conuentus agere. Hæc ego; Ille vero ne verbo quidem vnquam conatus est, vel nostrā vocationem oppugnare, vel tueri suam.
units.tr: "How, then, will you defend this wrong before the judgment of God, that, being a stranger and not lawfully called, you scatter our sheep and, gathering them into corners against the edicts of the magistrate, draw them away from us? And further, that you slander us, who are the lawful ministers, in these little conventicles, and, while we are absent, load us with calumnies and lies, and condemn us without having admonished or heard us? If we who have the care of souls in Cologne were not performing our office rightly, it would have been your part first to admonish us and refute us, rather than to hold forbidden meetings in this way against the will of the Senate." Such was my speech. He, however, never once tried by a single word either to attack our calling or to defend his own.

units.la: Adiunxi demum & illud; Ipsos aduersarios non ferre, vt quisquam inter eos huiusmodi furtiuos conuentus agat, vel secretò docendi auctoritatem vsurpet. Et Lutherus quidem, inquam, consulit, vt tenebriones illi, qui passim repunt per domos, & contra magistratus voluntatem, insciis veris pastoribus, clam aliud doctrinæ genus spargunt, quàm publicè viget, non tolerentur vllo pacto; imò si desistere nolint, demum magistro Hansoni (quo nomine carnificem designat) commendentur. Atque hoc non tantùm intelligi vult de seductoribus, qui prauis dogmatibus simpliciorum animos imbuunt, verùm de ijs quoque, qui veri doctores sunt, ac doctrinam Euangelij profitetur: Hos, inquit, tametsi vel Angeli sint, vel meri Gabrieles de cœlo, tamè, si contra vtriusq; magistratus, Ecclesiastici nimirum, & ciuilis, volùtatem clam docere
units.tr: Finally I added this too: that the adversaries themselves do not put up with anyone among them conducting such furtive meetings or secretly claiming the authority to teach. "And Luther indeed," I said, "advises that those shady fellows who crawl everywhere through houses, and against the will of the magistrate, without the knowledge of the true ministers, spread secretly a kind of teaching other than that which flourishes publicly, must not be tolerated in any way; indeed, if they refuse to desist, they should at last be handed over to Master Hans (by which name he designates the executioner). And he wishes this to be understood not only of seducers who imbue the minds of simple people with false doctrines, but also of those who are true teachers and profess the doctrine of the Gospel. These, he says, even if they are angels, or mere Gabriels from heaven, nevertheless, if they resolve to teach secretly against the will of both magistrates, the ecclesiastical and the civil, must be restrained and punished."

units.la: C docere instituant, coercendos esse ac puniendos; Etiam cum inter Papistas, ut ipse loquitur, aut haereticos, huiusmodi quid tentare volunt. Quae ratio à Lutheranis etiā hactenus observatur: Quemadmodum demonstrari potest exeplis Principum, ac urbium quarundam in Imperio, quae publice Lutheri doctrinam, sub Augustanae Confessionis nomine, profitentur. Haec omnia ille, quemadmodum & superiora, silentio transmittebat.
units.tr: "Even when they wish to attempt such a thing among Papists, as he himself puts it, or heretics. This principle has been observed by the Lutherans up to the present, as can be shown from the examples of princes and certain cities in the Empire, which publicly profess Luther's doctrine under the name of the Augsburg Confession." All these things he let pass in silence, just as he had the earlier ones.

units.la: Sub finem iterum sermo incidit de Edictis Magistratus nostri, deque rebus ijs, quas ipsius indicio scire vellet Amplissimus huius urbis Senatus, quę tacitè, si in sententia sua persistat, tyrannidis ab eo accusari, Doctor Crantius aperte demonstrabat: Ad cuius verba ille, rugata nonnihil fronte, quàm amarulentè, inquit, de hac re loquitur D. Doctor: Nunquam ego tyrannidis Amplissimū Senatū insimulatui. Eam hominis insolentiam indignè ferens Doctor Crantius, humaniter tamen respondit, Iniquè sibi amarulentiam obijci: Non hoc se dicere, quod expressis verbis Senatum tyrannidis accusarit; Verùm id ex ipsius actionibus & verbis necessario sequi: Quam rem idem Doctor Cratius ad eum modum declarauit, ut ille contra ne mutire quidem potuerit.
units.tr: Towards the end the talk turned again to the edicts of our magistrate, and to those matters which the most distinguished Senate of this city wished to know from his own disclosure. Doctor Crantius openly showed that, if he persisted in his opinion, he would be accusing the Senate of tyranny by his silence. At these words he, his brow wrinkled somewhat, said: "How bitterly the Lord Doctor speaks about this matter! I have never accused the most distinguished Senate of tyranny." Doctor Crantius, indignant at the man's insolence, nevertheless replied politely: that it was unjust to charge him with bitterness; he was not saying that he had accused the Senate of tyranny in express words, but that this necessarily followed from its actions and words. Doctor Crantius explained this matter in such a way that he could not even mutter a word against it.

units.la: Obieci ego denuò & illud, (quod antea quoque per occasionem attigeram.) Concionatores istius partis, de quorum numero & ipse sit, in huiusmodi conuenticulis, graui admodum iniuria nos afficere; cùm absentes acerbè ac contumeliosè traducant, & Religionem Catholicam, quam profitemur, velut impiā, & foeda cū Idololatria coniunctā, abominandū in modū detestentur: Quod tametsi iam expresse fateri nolit, nequeat tamē inficiari, nisi conscientiae testimonio reclamare velit. Eā verò criminatione, non ad nos pertinere tātum, verum nostros etiam, eosdemque ipsorum maiores, à quibus Catholica Religio ad nos peruenerit, simul nobiscum inuoluerè. Et quia nobis absentibus tam atrox iniuria inferatur, vt adeo adeò nostram, maiorumque nostrorum innocentiam, aduersus huiusmodi calũnias ac mendacia tueri nequeamus, rem totam quidem Deo, iusto iniuriarum omnium vindici, committendam esse; cui proculdubio grauissimam aliquado rationem hoc nomine sint reddituti.
units.tr: I raised again also that point which I had touched on before in passing: that the preachers of his party, of whose number he himself is one, do us very great wrong in such conventicles, since they bitterly and insultingly slander us in our absence, and detest the Catholic religion which we profess as impious and joined with foul idolatry, in an abominable manner. Although he is now unwilling to admit this openly, he cannot deny it unless he wishes to contradict the testimony of his own conscience. Moreover, this accusation has involved not only us but also our forebears, through whom the Catholic religion came down to us, together with us. And since so atrocious a wrong is done to us in our absence, so that we cannot defend our innocence and that of our forebears against such calumnies and lies, the whole matter must indeed be committed to God, the just avenger of all wrongs, to whom without doubt they will one day render a most grave account for this.

units.la: Hæc ego, & id genus alia quædam in eandem sententiam cùm dicerem, ille se nonnihil repressit: Tandem vero, Non dissiteor, inquit, Religionem vestram, tanquam erroneam, à nobis reprehendi: Quod si hac parte in errore sum, instrui cupio; præbebo me docilem, tu te præbeas doctorem. Respodi, Nescire me, an cum in finem à Magistratu vocatus sim. Præterea tempus colloquendo iam effluxisse, (imminebat enim vespera) vt si in hunc campum ingrediendum sit, id nunc, vel hoc etiam nomine fieri non possit. Iam & alios esse me doctiores, tum in facultate Theologica, tum inter Pastores quoque confratres meos, qui commodius ac melius agere doctorum partes, ac errantem instituere possint. Quanquam ego quidem non existimem, quod hac parte candidè, atque ex animo loquatur. Si enim ea mente esset, vt syncerè cuperet instrui, potuisse iampridem illum toto illo tempore, quo hic cõmoratus fuerit, vel me, vel alium quempiam è Pastoribus hoc nomine conuenire. Tandem à præsentibus Dominis humaniter & amicè monebatur, vt deliberaret secum in diem crastinum, ac posita demum perunicacia, legitimè ad interrogata responderet. Ille ad hæc suo more tergiuersari, ac prætendere cõscientiam suam, & legem charitatis de non lædendo proximo: Mea conscientia, inquit, hoc non fert; alius fortasse posset facere, ego non possum. Deinde repetita protestatione, qua initio quoque fuerat vsus, excusauit timiditatem suam; atq; ita hac vice dimissus est, & reductus in carcerem.
units.tr: I said these things and others of the same kind to that effect, and he restrained himself somewhat. At last he said: "I do not deny that you reprehend our religion as erroneous. But if I am in error in this matter, I wish to be instructed; I will show myself teachable, and you should show yourself a teacher." I replied that I did not know whether I had been summoned for this very purpose by the magistrate. Besides, the time for conversation had already run out (evening was coming on), so that if we were to enter upon this field, it could not be done now, or at least not on this occasion. Moreover, there are others more learned than I, both in the theological faculty and among my fellow ministers, who could more conveniently and better play the part of teachers and instruct one who is in error. Yet I did not think he was speaking candidly and from the heart in this matter. For if he were minded to be sincerely instructed, he could have sought out me, or some other of the ministers, for this purpose at any time during the whole period he had stayed here. At last the gentlemen present admonished him kindly and in a friendly way that he should deliberate with himself until the next day, and, laying aside his obstinacy at last, answer the questions put to him lawfully. He, in his usual manner, evaded these things and pleaded his conscience and the law of charity not to injure one's neighbour: "My conscience," he said, "does not bear this; another perhaps might do it, I cannot." Then, repeating the protest he had also used at the beginning, he excused his timidity; and so he was dismissed for this time and led back into prison.

units.la: Postea visum quibusdam fuit, non futurum abs re, (modò de voluntate Amplissimi Senatus fieri possit) si de vno atque altero Religionis capite, amica cum illo collatio instituere tur; præsertim, quia se docile futurū promisisset. Dixi ego, si publico nomine Magistratus, atq; ex professo cum homine sit agendū, necessariū esse, vt id fiat ordinaria via, de consilio Theologicæ facultatis; vel per Dominum Suffraganeum, qui vnum atque alterum è Pastoribus assumere possit. Exististimatum fuit, satius esse, vt quemadmodum iam factum sit, obiter atque priuatim, per modum amicæ collocutionis tentetur, an reipsa præstare velit, quod verbis præ se tulisset. Ad eam igitur rem ego quidem operam meam detuli; verùm hac conditione, vt quicquid huius futurum esset, id fieret præsentibus viris aliquot fide dignis: propterea quod non semel talium hominum calumnias ac mendacia post huiusmodi priuatas collocutiones, expertus eram. Placuit igitur, vt, si ea res Amplissimo Senatui non displiceret, postridie ad horam secundam pomeridianam, eodem loco rursum conueniremus. Atque hæc fere primi diei collatio fuit.
units.tr: Afterwards it seemed good to some that it would not be out of place (provided it could be done with the will of the most distinguished Senate) if a friendly conference were arranged with him on one or two heads of religion, especially since he had promised that he would be teachable. I said that if the matter were to be conducted in the name of the magistrate and openly, it was necessary that it be done in the ordinary way, with the advice of the theological faculty, or through the Lord Suffragan, who could take one or two of the ministers along. It was judged better, as has in fact already been done, that it first be attempted casually and privately, by way of friendly conversation, whether he would actually do what he had professed in words. I therefore did indeed offer my service for this business, but on this condition: that whatever came of it should take place in the presence of several trustworthy men, because I had more than once experienced the calumnies and lies of such men after private conversations of this kind. It was therefore agreed that, if the matter did not displease the most distinguished Senate, we should meet again in the same place the next day at two o'clock in the afternoon. And this was roughly the conference of the first day.

units.la: ALTERIVS DIEI COLLATIO.
units.tr: THE SECOND DAY'S CONFERENCE.

units.la: POstridie, qui fuit vndecimus Aprilis, hora secunda pomeridiana, vti constitutum erat, ad carcerem rediij. Conuenerunt eò, qui pridie adfuerat; (excepto Ioanne Lennepio) & præter eos Balthasar à Berchem, Theodorus Ploger, Michael Ludgen, Hermannus à Viddig, Senatorij ordinis viri; tum Anthonius Rinck, patritius Coloniensis. Vocatus iterum est Ioannes Badius Ministèr Caluinianus; Cumque suo loco consedisset, Doctor Hackfteinius inter cætera, quæ breuiter illi proposuit Amplissimi Senatus nomine, illa quoque verba repetijt, quod pridie docilem se fore promisisset, si ego doctoris partes agerem. Exististimatum igitur fuisse, non futurum abs re, si fieret eius rei periculum. In eum itaq; finem me, Pastorem D. Cuniberti, nunc denuo vocatum adesse, vt placida scilicet, atque amica inter nos de Religione collatio institueretur.
units.tr: On the next day, which was the eleventh of April, at two o'clock in the afternoon, as had been agreed, I returned to the prison. Those who had been present the day before came together, except John Lennep, and besides them Balthasar von Berchem, Theodore Ploger, Michael Ludgen and Hermann von Viddig, members of the senatorial order, and also Anthony Rinck, a patrician of Cologne. John Badius, the Calvinist minister, was summoned again. When he had taken his seat in his place, Doctor Hackfteinius, among other things that he briefly put to him in the name of the most distinguished Senate, also repeated the words that Badius had promised the day before that he would be teachable if I played the part of the teacher. It was therefore thought that it would not be out of place to put this to the test. To that end I, the pastor of St. Cunibert, have now been called here again, so that a calm and friendly conference about religion might be held between us.

units.la: Ego deinde Badium hortabar, vt eam sumeret in colloquendo libertatem, qua vsurus esset, si vel Heidelbergæ mecum ageret, vel alibi in medio Palatinatu. Faciebā illi quoque potestatē deligendi, quam vellet, materiam, de qua collatione instituii cuperet. Demū, vt inter colloquendū vtras vellet, siue opponētis, siue respōdentis partes agere, id illi quoq; liberum relinquebā. Ille deligebat Articulum de Cœna Domini. Rogaui, Quia multiplex esset de hoc Articulo controuersia, quam istius materiæ partem inter nos disceptari cuperet? Respondit eam, in qua de veritate quæritur, vt quæ primaria esset. Dixi, Magni quoque momenti disputationem esse de Sacrificio, ac Sacerdotio; cur non illam desumeret? Badius ad hæc, Placere nunc priorem, quam dixerit; altera illam postea quoque discutiendam sumi posse. Itaq; ego hac in parte ipsius voluntati acquieui.
units.tr: I then urged Badius to take the same freedom in conversing that he would use if he were dealing with me at Heidelberg or anywhere else in the middle of the Palatinate. I also gave him the choice of whatever subject he wished to take up for the conference. Finally, I left it to him to take whichever role he wanted during the discussion, that of opponent or that of respondent. He chose the article on the Lord's Supper. I asked, since the controversy on this article is manifold, which part of this subject he wanted us to dispute. He answered that it should be the part in which the question is about the truth, since that is the primary one. I said that the dispute about sacrifice and priesthood is also of great importance; why did he not take that up? To this Badius replied that he preferred the first subject, as he had said, and the other could be discussed afterwards. So in this matter I acquiesced to his wish.

units.la: Et principio quidē à me petijt, vt se Dominis præsenti bus excusarem; quos diebus superioribus dicto quodam de pane Eucharistico videretur offendisse. Cùm enim de Eucharistia sermo per occasionem inciderit, eos nō admodum æquis animis accepisse, quod veteres communi pane, ad hoc mysterium peragendum vsos fuisse dixerit.
units.tr: And at the beginning he asked me to excuse him to the gentlemen present, whom, it seemed, he had offended on the previous days by a certain remark about the Eucharistic bread. For when talk of the Eucharist had come up on that occasion, they had not taken it very calmly that he had said the ancients used common bread to perform this mystery.

units.la: Respondi, Non existimare me, quod eo dicto quenquam offenderit; quando Catholicorum omnium consensu satis constet, panem illum, qui ad altare defertur, antequam consecretur, omnino communem esse: Post consecrationem verò iam non amplius dici, vel esse communem panem, sed verum Christi corpus.
units.tr: I replied that I did not think he had offended anyone by that remark, since it is sufficiently established by the consent of all Catholics that the bread which is brought to the altar, before it is consecrated, is indeed common bread; but after consecration it is no longer called or be common bread, but the true body of Christ.

units.la: Ille sermone continuato, ad confirmandum ea, quæ dixerat, Græcorum etiam morem adducebat, quos notum est, vti pane fermentato, cùm sacra mysteria peragunt. Ex quibus verbis intelligebam, quod communis panis nomine, cuiuscunq; generis panem domesticum intelintelligeret, siue fermentatus is sit, siue non sit. Respon-debam igitur ad exemplum Græcorum; Aliam esse consuetudinem Ecclesiæ Latinæ, quæ scilicet azymo pane ad sacrificium peragendum vteretur: Eam vero consuetudinem, procul dubio in ipsius Christi Seruatoris exemplo fundari, quem satis certè cõstaret azymo pane vsum, cum hoc mysterium institueret; quando Iudæis eo tempore, quo Paschalem agnum comedebant, fermētatum panem in domibus habere non licuerit.
units.tr: Continuing his speech, to confirm what he had said he also cited the custom of the Greeks, who, as is well known, use leavened bread when they celebrate the sacred mysteries. From these words I understood that by the name of common bread he meant any kind of household bread, whether leavened or not. I therefore replied, following the example of the Greeks, that the Latin Church has a different custom, namely that it uses unleavened bread to celebrate the sacrifice; and that custom is undoubtedly founded on the example of Christ the Saviour himself, who is certainly known to have used unleavened bread when he instituted this mystery, since at that time the Jews, when they ate the Passover lamb, were not permitted to have leavened bread in their houses.

units.la: Excepit rursum, & nominato D. Gregorio, tum Paulo quoque Diacono, de pane nummulario mentionem intulit, in eũ finem, opinor, vt quemadmodum azymi panis vsum, adducto Græcorum more, arroserat, ita formā quoque rotundam eiusdem Eucharistici panis improbaret. Dixi, talia nihil admodũ facere ad rem; præstare igitur, vt missis ijs, quæ minutiora essent, ad causam ipsam aggrederetur. Idem hortabatur Domini Syndici; qui & illud adijciebant, Se nequaquam indigne tulisse, quod pridie de communis aut fermentati panis vsu dixerit; verum id sibi mirum accidisse potius, quod citauerit pro se D. Gregorium, cum quo reuera tamen in Religione nihil haberet commune.
units.tr: He again took up the matter, and after naming Saint Gregory and then Paul the Deacon, he mentioned coin-shaped bread, I think with the aim of disapproving the round form of this Eucharistic bread, just as he had attacked the use of unleavened bread by citing the custom of the Greeks. I said that such points had almost nothing to do with the matter; he should therefore set aside these smaller questions and come to the cause itself. The gentlemen syndics also urged the same, adding that they had not at all taken it amiss that he had spoken the day before about the use of common or leavened bread; rather, what seemed strange to them was that he had cited Gregory in his favour, although in religion he really had nothing in common with him.

units.la: Igitur cum sermonem in pauca contulisset, propius tandem ad rem ipsam accessit, & pro libertate sibi concessa quæsiuit, quæ mea esset de Eucharistia sententia? Respondi, credere me cum vniuersa Ecclesia Catholica, in Eucharistiæ Sacramento, verũ illud, ac naturale Christi corpus esse, quod de Virgine natum sit, ac pro nobis in mortem traditum. Atque hanc fidei meæ professionem fundaui super ipsius Christi verbis, quæ sunt: Accipite, & manducate, hoc est Corpus meum, quod pro vobis tradetur: Cum satis constet, non panem, sed illud idem corpus pro nobis esse traditū, quod antea natū est ex Maria Virgine. Ille, Se nequaquā id credere, aperte profitebatur. Tu ego; Ergo hic oritur contradictio, dum, quod ego constanter
units.tr: So, after he had reduced his talk to a few points, he at last came closer to the matter itself, and, using the freedom given to him, asked what my opinion was about the Eucharist. I replied that I, with the whole Catholic Church, believe that in the Sacrament of the Eucharist there is the true and natural body of Christ, which was born of the Virgin and given into death for us. And I based this profession of my faith upon the very words of Christ: "Take, eat; this is my body, which is given for you." Since it is well established that it is not bread but that same body which was given for us, which was previously born of the Virgin Mary. He openly declared that he did not believe this. I said: "Then here arises a contradiction, since what I constantly affirm you deny to be true. But since I defend the affirmative side and you the negative, it will be your part to attack, with reasons brought forward, the very thing that I have laid down and, as it were, fixed firmly."

units.la: Exod. 12.
units.tr: Exod. 12.

units.la: Marc. 14. 1. Cor. 11. stanter affirmo, tu verum esse negas. Cæterum, quia ego partem affirmantem defendo, tu negantem; tuarum partium erit, idipsum, quod à me constitutum est, & quasi defixum, rationibus in medium prolatis oppugnare.
units.tr: Mark 14. 1 Cor. 11. I firmly affirm it, and you deny that it is true. But since I defend the affirmative side and you the negative, it will be your part to attack, with arguments brought forward, the very thing that I have laid down and, as it were, fixed firmly in place.

units.la: Postulauit deinde, vt declararem mentem meam, quo nimirum modo Christi verū corpus in Eucharistia præsens esse crederem? Eo, inquam, quem dilucida ipsius Christi verba; Hoc est Corpus meum, quod pro vobis tradetur; in vero natiuoque sensu, secundum τὸ ῥητὸν accepta postulant. Ergo statuis, inquit, fieri transubstâtiationem panis in Christi corpus? Tum ego; Imò vero; Credo fieri quod ipsa Christi verba requirunt, siue id cum Ecclesia Catholica transubstantiationem, siue transelemetationem, vel conuersionem appelles.
units.tr: He then asked me to explain my meaning: in what precise manner did I believe the true body of Christ to be present in the Eucharist? In that manner, I said, which the plain words of Christ himself, This is my body, which shall be given for you, demand that we accept in their true and natural sense, according to the literal meaning [τὸ ῥητόν]. So, he said, you hold that the bread is transubstantiated into the body of Christ? Then I said: Indeed. I believe that what Christ's own words require takes place, whether you call it transubstantiation with the Catholic Church, or transelementation, or conversion.

units.la: Interrogauit deinde, qua virtute huiusmodi transubstantiationem fieri crederem? Dixi, virtute verborum Christi Seruatoris, quæ iuxta D. Ambrosij dictum, in hoc mysterio operatoria essent, vt efficerent, quod Christus ijs pronunciaret. Respondit ille, Si ita crederem, dissentire me à Concilio Tridentino, quod Transubstantiationem non Christi verbis, sed benedictioni tribueret. Excepi ego, nequaquam à Concilio Tridentino me dissentire, verum idem prorsus dicere ac profiteri, quod ab eo sit definitum. Ille contra in sententia persistebat; cumque hoc vrgeret prolixius, aliâ scilicet esse meam hac de re, quàm Concilij Tridentini sententiam; Ego demum, pronoco, inquam, ad ipsius Concilij definitionem. Separas tu benedictionē à Christi verbis, quam ego iuxta mentē Concilij, cum ijs esse coniunctam affirmo. Ergo, inquit ille, tibi nō constas, cùm antea solis Christi verbis transubstantiandi virtutem tribueris, quam nunc verbis simul ac benedictioni adscribis. Respondi: Ego verò benedictionem à verbis Institutionis nunquam separaui, quemadmodum tu fraudulenter ac veteratorie colligis, quasi dum conuersionis vim Christi verbis attribuo, ea re be-
units.tr: He next asked by what power I believed such a transubstantiation takes place. I said: by the power of the words of Christ the Saviour, which, according to the saying of Saint Ambrose, are operative in this mystery, so that they bring about what Christ pronounces. He replied that if I believed this, I was dissenting from the Council of Trent, which ascribes transubstantiation not to the words of Christ but to the blessing. I objected that I did not dissent at all from the Council of Trent, but said exactly the same thing and professed what it had defined. He persisted in his opinion, and when he pressed this at greater length, namely that my view on this matter differed from the judgement of the Council of Trent, I at last appealed, I said, to the definition of the Council itself. "You separate the blessing from the words of Christ, whereas I affirm, according to the mind of the Council, that they are joined with them." "Then," he said, "you are not consistent, since earlier you attributed the power of transubstantiation to the words of Christ alone, and now you ascribe it to the words together with the blessing." I answered: "I have never separated the blessing from the words of institution, as you deceitfully and cunningly infer, as if, by attributing the power of conversion to the words of Christ, I thereby

units.la: { } rebenedictionem ab ijsdem seiungam; quod falsissimū esse contendo.
units.tr: separated the blessing from them; which I maintain is most false."

units.la: Rogauit denuò:Qua tandem igitur virtute conuersio nem panis in Christi corpus fieri dicerem?Respondi, vir tute verborum Christi, velut antea quoque asseruerim, quibus perficiatur benedictio vel consecratio, cōcurren te omnipotentia Dei,quæ nimirum efficiat, vt verum sit, quod ijsdem verbis pronunciatur.Repetij dictū B. Am brofij,Christi sermonem in hisce mysterijs operatorium esse dicentis.Ad quæ ille nihil amplius, nisi scio, inquit, Ambrosium id dicere in libris de Sacramentis.
