units.tr: He asked again: "By what power, then, do you say the conversion of the bread into the body of Christ takes place?" I answered: by the power of the words of Christ, as I said before, by which the blessing or consecration is effected, the omnipotence of God concurring, which of course brings it about that what is pronounced in those words is true. I repeated the saying of Saint Ambrose, that the word of Christ is operative in these mysteries. To this he replied nothing more than: "I know that Ambrose says this in his books on the Sacraments."

units.la: Deinde, cùm paululum, quasi deliberandus, siluisset, adiecit & illud,dissentire me quoque à Pontificijs Doctoribus,quorum nonnulli, (nominabat vero Ambrosium Catharinum)non solis Christi verbis, sed toti actioni co-plexim, transubstantiandi virtutem tribuerent. Addere Catharinum,multa hoc modo deuitari posse incommo-da,quę suboriantur, si solis Christi verbis conuersionem panis in Christi corpus effici dicas.
units.tr: Then, after he had been silent for a little while, as if deliberating, he added that I also dissent from the Papist teachers, some of whom (he named Ambrose Catharinus) ascribe the power of transubstantiation not only to the words of Christ but to the whole action taken together. He added that Catharinus pointed out that many inconveniences which arise can be avoided in this way, if you say that the conversion of the bread into the body of Christ is effected by the words of Christ alone.

units.la: Respōdi, Catharinum de summa rei nequaquam dis-sentire à Concilio Tridentino. Ipsum credere procul dubio,quod verum Christi Iesu corpus,ac verus sanguis, per conuersionem panis ac vini, reuera in Eucharistiæ Sacramento adsint; tum quod eadem conuersio benedi-ctioni vel cōsecrationi fit adscribenda. Cæterū quibus verbis illa Eucharistiæ consecratio præcisè fiat, an ad eā præter verba Christi, alia quoque,quæ in Canone præce-dunt,necessariò requirantur, id à Theologis nonnullis disputari quidem; verum ea moderatione, vt substantia-lia tamen huius articuli nihil lædantur. Instabat ille, disceptationem hanc ad substantialia quoque pertinere. Id vero,quia simpliciter asserebat,eodem modo, ac toti-dem pene verbis à me negatum est.
units.tr: I replied that Catharinus does not at all differ from the Council of Trent on the substance of the matter. Undoubtedly he believes that the true body and true blood of Christ Jesus are really present in the Sacrament of the Eucharist through the conversion of the bread and wine; and that this same conversion is to be ascribed to the blessing or consecration. As to which words the consecration of the Eucharist is effected precisely, and whether other words besides the words of Christ, those which precede them in the Canon, are necessarily required for it, some theologians do indeed dispute this; but with such moderation that the substantials of this article are nonetheless left unharmed. He insisted that this dispute also pertained to the substantials. But since he asserted this simply, I denied it in almost as many words.

units.la: Atque hoc loco parum abfuit, quin in aliam disputa-tionem ingrederemur; cùm ille per hanc occasionem, pripriuata Catholicorum quorundam Theologorum cer-tamina mihi obijceret, in primis vero illud, quod ante Concilium Tridentinum, inter viros doctissimos Domi-nicum à Soto, & Ambrosium Catharinum fuisse, vtriusque scripta testantur. Ad quam ipsius obiectionem res-pondi: Hanc semper in Ecclesia consuetudinem hacte-nus viguisse, vt quoties controuersia surgeret inter do-ctos, quae ad Religionis substantiam pertineret, eam v-traque pars ad cognitionem Ecclesiae, ac Conciliorum generalium definitionem reijceret; Sin vero leuior esset, quàm vt Religionis fundamenta contingeret, tum salua fidei vnitate, atque Ecclesiae obedientia, ita velitatam, vt licet vtraque pars abundaret in suo sensu, neutra tamen contra Ecclesiam insurgeret. Exempli loco disceptatio-nem adduxi, quae de mendacio quondam inter D D. Hie-ronymum & Augustinum exorta est; tum eam quoque, quae ante complures annos, inter quosdam Theologos, de virtute atque operatione Baptismatis in infantibus exarsit. Excepit ille; Catharinum, quamuis in Concilio Tridentino praesens fuerit, tamen post Concilij definitio-nem in sententia sua, de Eucharistiae consecratione per-stitisse. Tum ego; si verum hoc sit, opinionem esse priua-tam hominis, quae rei summam in hoc articulo, veram scilicet corporis Christi praesentiam, & transubstantiatio-nem non euertat.
units.tr: At this point we came close to entering upon another disputation, since he, on this occasion, threw in my face the private quarrels of certain Catholic theologians, and especially that which, before the Council of Trent, arose between the most learned men Dominicus à Soto and Ambrosius Catharinus, as the writings of both attest. To this objection of his I replied: it has always been the custom in the Church until now that whenever a controversy arises among learned men concerning matters that pertain to the substance of religion, each side refers it to the judgment of the Church and the definition of the general councils. But if the question is too minor to touch the foundations of religion, then, with the unity of faith and obedience to the Church preserved, it is so tolerated that, although each side abounds in its own opinion, neither rises up against the Church. As an example I cited the dispute that once arose between the doctors Jerome and Augustine concerning lying, and also the one that some years ago flared up among certain theologians concerning the power and operation of Baptism in infants. He took up the point: granted that Catharinus was present at the Council of Trent, nevertheless he persisted in his opinion concerning the consecration of the Eucharist after the Council's definition. Then I said: if this is true, it is the private opinion of one man, which does not overturn the sum of the matter in this article, namely the true presence of Christ's body and transubstantiation.

units.la: Demum, misso Catharino, veram ac Catholicam de Eucharistia sententiam, quam ego profes-sus eram, op-pugnare coepit; idq; duplici via; partim argumentando, partim vero suo more pressius examinando verba Chri-sti, super quibus ego meam, & Ecclesiae Catholicae sen-tentiam fundaram.
units.tr: Finally, setting Catharinus aside, he began to attack the true and Catholic doctrine concerning the Eucharist, which I had professed; and he did so in two ways: partly by arguing, and partly by examining more closely, in his usual manner, the words of Christ, on which I had founded my own view and that of the Catholic Church.

units.la: Formabat igitur huiusmodi argumentum: Verum Christi corpus factum est ex Maria Virgine: At corpus Christi, quod vos in Eucharistia praesens esse dicitis, fit ex pane. Ergo non est verum Christi corpus. Ego resumpto argu-
units.tr: He therefore framed an argument of this kind: The true body of Christ was made from the Virgin Mary; but the body of Christ, which you say is present in the Eucharist, is made from bread. Therefore it is not the true body of Christ. I took up the argument again.

units.la: SVMMARIA DESCRIPTIO PRIVATI COLLOQVII, QVOD EGO CASPARVS VLENBERGIVS LIPPIENSIS, Pastor & Canonicus ad D. Cunibertum, cum Ioanne Badio Rodingensi, Ministro Calviniano habui.
units.tr: THE BRIEF SUMMARY OF A PRIVATE CONFERENCE WHICH I, CASPAR VLENBERG OF LIPPSTADT, PASTOR AND CANON AT ST. CUNIBERT'S, HELD WITH JOHANN BADIUS OF RÖDINGEN, A CALVINIST MINISTER.

units.la: PRIMI DIEI COLLATIO.
units.tr: THE FIRST DAY'S CONFERENCE.

units.la: ANno Christi 1590. 10. April. vocatus sum, nomine amplissimi Senatus Colonien. ad carcerem publicum, quem Franconum turrim dicunt, vt cum Concionatore quodam, Ioanne Badio Rodingesi, de rebus nonnullis conferrem. Eratis Concionator captus ante dies aliquot, cum contra Magistratus Edicta, clancularia concionem haberet. Veni ad carcerem circa horam quartam pomeridianam, ibique congregatos inueni primarios aliquot in hac Republica viros, Hilbrandum Sudermannum, & Ioannem Hardenradium, Consules; tum Gulielmum Hacksteinium, ac Petrum Crantium, Iuris Doctores, huius Reipublicae Syndicos; demum Bartholdum Questenbergium, & Ioannem Lennepium, Senatorij ordinis viros.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1590, on 10 April, I was summoned, on behalf of the most honourable Senate of Cologne, to the public prison called the Franconian tower, to confer with a certain preacher, Johann Badius of Rödingen, about several matters. The preacher had been taken some days earlier, because he had held a sermon in secret, against the edicts of the magistrate. I came to the prison about the fourth hour in the afternoon, and there I found gathered several leading men of this commonwealth: Hilbrand Sudermann and Johann Hardenrath, consuls; then Wilhelm Hacksteiner and Peter Krantz, doctors of law and syndics of this commonwealth; and finally Bartholomäus Questenberg and Johann Lennep, men of the senatorial order.

units.la: Iussus est è custodia prodire Badius, cui Doctor Gulielmus Hacksteinius, alter Syndicorum, in memoriam reuocauit, quod diebus superioribus respondere noluerit ad capita quaedam, quae nomine amplissimi Senatus illi proposita fuerant. Quia vero pro sui defensione, rationibus partim politicis, partim vero Theologicis vsus sit; Amplif. Senatum politicas ipsius rationes diligenter expendisse, pendisse, atque de ijs quidem iam certi aliquid habere constitutum, quemadmodum suo tempore sit auditus. Quod autem ad rationes Theologicas attineat, eas alterius fori esse: Itaque ne sibi putaret iniuriam fieri, noluisse Amplis. Senatum hac parte quicquam constituere, antequam de ijs cum viro Ecclesiastico conculisset. Atque in hunc finem me, Pastorem D. Cuniberti, vocatum esse, ut quia persuasum habeat, laedi conscientiam suam, seque contra legem charitatis delinquere, si ad interrogata responderet, de conscientia sua, deque charitatis lege mecum conferret.
units.tr: Badius was ordered to be brought out of custody. Doctor Wilhelm Hacksteiner, the other syndic, reminded him that on the previous days he had refused to answer certain articles which had been put to him in the name of the most honourable Senate. Since, however, in his own defence he had used arguments partly political and partly theological, the most honourable Senate had weighed his political arguments carefully, and had already reached some firm decision on them, as would be made known at the proper time. As for his theological arguments, however, these belonged to another forum. So, lest he think he was being wronged, the most honourable Senate had not wished to decide anything in this part of the matter before consulting with a churchman. And to this end I, the pastor of St. Cunibert's, had been summoned, so that, since he was persuaded that his conscience would be violated and that he would offend against the law of charity if he answered the questions put to him, he might confer with me about his conscience and about the law of charity.

units.la: Ille principio assurgens, protestabatur, se natura timidum esse, & difficulter, in praesentia tantorum virorum, animi sensa eloqui posse; facturum tamen periculum, ut mentem suam explicet. Deinde paucis ea repetebat, quae diebus superioribus acta fuerant: Rogabat etiam Dominos praesentes, ne id contumacia interpretarentur, quod ad interrogata non responderet eo modo, quo Senatus vellet. Obstare conscientiam suam, & charitatem proximi; Nisi id esset, lubenti se animo imperata facturum.
units.tr: He first rose and protested that by nature he was timid, and that in the presence of such great men he could express the feelings of his mind only with difficulty; nevertheless he would make the attempt to explain his mind. Then he briefly repeated what had happened on the previous days. He also asked the gentlemen present not to interpret it as obstinacy that he did not answer the questions in the way the Senate wished. His conscience and the charity owed to his neighbour stood in the way; otherwise he would gladly do what was commanded.

units.la: Ego primum quaesiui, quam Religionem profiteretur? Responsum est; Confessionem Augustanam, uti ea posterioribus annis, à Philippo Melanthone declarata est. Adiecit ipse, Quia Religionis Pax, quam vocant, in Imperio sancita esset, eius beneficio sibi quoque, tanquam Augustanam Confessionem profitenti, licuisse in hac urbe docere.
units.tr: I first asked what religion he professed. The answer was: the Augsburg Confession, as it was set out in later years by Philip Melanchthon. He added himself that, since the Religious Peace, as they call it, had been sanctioned in the Empire, by its benefit he too, as one professing the Augsburg Confession, had been permitted to teach in this city.

units.la: Fassus fuerat pridie, (quemadmodum illi per Dominos Syndicos in memoriam redigebatur) in eo se sensu Confessionem Augustanã amplecti ac profiteri, in quo Fridericus Palatinus Elector quondam, & filius eius Casimirus hactenus, eandem in Palatinatu professi fuerint. Dixi, eum esse germanum Caluinismum: Quod ut aperte demonstrarem, subieci; In Comitijs Augustanis anno 1530. duas esse Confessiones Imperatori oblatas, alteram à Saxone, Landgrauio, atque aliis Imperij Ordinibus Lutheranis; alteram vero à quatuor ciuitatibus Zvvinglianis, Argentorato, Constantia, Memminga, & Lindauia, quas caeteri Protestantes nullo pacto in societatem suae Confessionis recipere voluerint: Quod confirmaui, narrata quadam historia de Bucero, ex Comitijs Augustanis, Zvvinglianorum nomine Coburgum ad Lutherum misso, atque à communione reiecto; quam longum esset hoc loco intexere. Interrogaui deinde; Vtram istarum Confessionum ampleCteretur, Lutheranam ne, an Zvvinglianam? Hic vero nonnihil cunctabatur. Cùm vrgerem, ab alijs demum ipsius loco respōsum est, quod ipse pridie dixerat, Eam, cuius auctor esset Philippus Melanthon. Addidit ipse, Melanthoni hanc eandem Confessionem, de consensu eorundem Ordinum, à quibus in Comitijs Augustanis oblata sit, postea declarare ac mutare licuisse.
units.tr: He had admitted the day before (as the syndics reminded him) that he embraced and professed the Augsburg Confession in the sense in which Frederick, the former Elector Palatine, and his son Casimir had professed it in the Palatinate until now. I said that this was genuine Calvinism. To demonstrate this clearly, I went on: at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 two confessions were presented to the Emperor, one by the Elector of Saxony, the Landgrave, and the other Lutheran estates of the Empire; the other by four Zwinglian cities, Strasbourg, Constance, Memmingen and Lindau, whom the other Protestants by no means wished to admit into fellowship with their confession. I confirmed this by recounting a story about Bucer, sent from the Diet of Augsburg to Luther at Coburg on behalf of the Zwinglians, and rejected from communion; but it would take too long to weave that in here. I then asked: which of these confessions did he embrace, the Lutheran or the Zwinglian? He hesitated somewhat at this. When I pressed him, others at last answered in his place, as he himself had said the day before, that it was the one whose author was Philip Melanchthon. He added himself that Melanchthon had been permitted afterwards to declare and alter this same confession, with the consent of the same estates by whom it had been presented at the Diet of Augsburg.

units.la: Respondi, primum Augustanae Confessionis auctorem, Melanthonem solum non esse: Lutherum ipsum, doctrinam suam septendecim capitibus comprehensam suppeditasse Melanthoni; eum vero postmodum haec ipsa doctrinae capita paulo fusius tractasse; Quae Lutherus itidem, antequam in Comitijs offerretur, viderit, ac suo iudicio confirmarit. Atque hanc esse Confessionem illam Augustanam, Imperatori Carolo Quinto à Protestantibus oblatam; quam Melanthoni deinceps mutare nequaquam licuerit, propterea, quod nec ipsum solum auctorem agnoscat; & si agnosceret, non ipsius tamen, aut Lutheri, sed Protestatium Ordinum nomine, in publico Imperij Conuentu sit oblata. Non differeri me, quin Melanthon in articulo de coena, postremis annis ab hac Confessione Lutherana, ad alteram illam Zvvinglianam defecerit: Verum si deinde, posteaquam mutarit animum, Confessionem quoq; Protestantium pro libitu mutare voluerit, eam porro non Augustanam, sed Philippicam potius
units.tr: I replied that Melanchthon alone was not the first author of the Augsburg Confession: Luther himself had supplied Melanchthon with his doctrine, comprised in seventeen articles; and Melanchthon afterwards had treated these same articles of doctrine somewhat more fully; and Luther too had seen these before they were presented at the Diet, and had confirmed them by his judgement. And this is the Augsburg Confession which was offered by the Protestants to the Emperor Charles V; and Melanchthon was by no means permitted to alter it afterwards, since it does not acknowledge him as its sole author; and even if it did, it was presented not in his name, or Luther's, but in the name of the Protestant estates, at the public assembly of the Empire. I do not deny that Melanchthon, in the article on the Supper, in his last years departed from this Lutheran Confession to that other, Zwinglian, one. But if afterwards, having changed his mind, he wished to alter the Protestant confession at his pleasure, then it should not be called the Augsburg Confession, but rather the Philippic

units.la: Chytraeus in historia Augustanae Conf. pag.32. potius dicendam esse, quæ Augustæ nunquam fuerit.
units.tr: Chytraeus, in his history of the Augsburg Confession, p. 32. rather, which was never at Augsburg.

units.la: Hoc loco D. Consul Sudermānus; Siue Augustana dicatur, (inquit) siue Philippica, satis intelligimus, eā ipsam esse, quam hic profitetur. Ille vero ad hæc omnia ne gry quidem, quod aiunt. Subiūxi ego; Nunquam omnes Imperij ordines Lutheranos in eam mutationē consensisse, quæ iuxta Melanthonis mentem in Palatinatu instituta sit: Et si consenserint, (quod sine mendacio affirmari nequeat) id publicam defectionem potius, quàm declarationem dici oportere. Extare Lutheranorum Theologorum scripta, in quibus huiusmodi mutationes in Augustana Confessione, defectio à puriore doctrina, & falsi crimen appellantur.
units.tr: At this point Consul Sudermann said: "Whether it is called Augsburg or Philippic, we understand well enough that it is the very one he professes." But he did not give so much as a grunt, as they say, in reply to all this. I added: the Lutheran estates of the Empire never consented to that alteration which was instituted in the Palatinate according to Melanchthon's mind; and even if they had consented (which cannot be affirmed without lying), this ought to be called a public defection rather than a declaration. There are extant writings of Lutheran theologians in which such alterations of the Augsburg Confession are called defection from the purer doctrine and the crime of falsehood.

units.la: Neque vero, inquam, vos, qui Caluini ductum sequimini, in hoc vno tantùm capite de Cœna, ab Augustanæ Confessionis Protestantibus dissidetis, verùm & in multis alijs; verbi causa, de Peccato originis, de Baptismate, de Sacramētorum numero ac virtute, de persona Christi, de Prædestinatione, &c. Adeò vt Iacobus Andreæ in præfatione libri cuiusdam, quem admonendi causa, de Lutheri Bibliis in Palatinatu corruptis edidit, sedecim errores enumeret, quibus ea ipsa Lutheri Biblia à vestris contaminata esse quiritatur.
units.tr: Nor, I said, do you who follow Calvin's lead differ from the Protestants of the Augsburg Confession only in this one article on the Supper, but also in many others: for example, on original sin, on baptism, on the number and power of the sacraments, on the person of Christ, on predestination, and so on. So much so that Jacob Andreae, in the preface of a certain book which he published as a warning, concerning Luther's Bibles corrupted in the Palatinate, enumerates sixteen errors by which he complains that those very Bibles of Luther were contaminated by your people.

units.la: Ille ad nomen Iacobi Andreæ falsè ridens, Nosti, inquit, qualis fuerit Iacobus Andreæ, quàm multas ille turbas concitarit. Quam eius vocem omnes suaui risu exceperunt, quod primarium scilicet Augustanæ confessionis Apostolum, adeò cōtemptim habere videretur. Ego vero, Non ignoro, inquam, qui vir fuerit Iacobus Andreæ, & quas turbas ille dederit: Hoc tamen ex ijs, quæ dicta sunt, manifestum est, nimirum iniquè fecisse te, quod ad Confessionem Augustanam prouocaris, eoque nomine iure te conuentus clancularios egisse dixeris.
units.tr: He, laughing falsely at the name of Jacob Andreae, said: "You know what sort of man Jacob Andreae was, how many disturbances he stirred up." All of them received this remark with a pleasant laugh, because it apparently treated the chief Apostle of the Augsburg Confession with contempt. But I said: "I am not ignorant of what sort of man Jacob Andreae was, or what disturbances he caused. Yet it is clear from what has been said that you act unjustly in appealing to the Augsburg Confession, and that on this ground you have rightly been called to account as one who works in secret."

units.la: Cæterum eandem rem & alia quadā ratione probaui.
units.tr: Otherwise I proved the same point by another line of argument as well.

units.la: Dixerat pridie, (quemadmodum Syndici referebant) se in Palatinatu ab Heidelbergensi Concilio, in Verbi Ministrum ordinatum esse: Quæsitus autem, cur ibidem in loco vocationis suæ non manserit? Responderat, Ludovicum Electorem Ministros omnes, qui ad ipsius de Religione sententiam accedere noluerint, a docendi functione removisse, ijsque mandasse, ut alio sedes transferrent. Huius igitur mandati occasione, se quoque e Palatinatu discessisse, ea mente tamen, ut aliquando (ubi mitior aura spirauerit) isthuc reuerteretur, suumque munus, ac docendi ministerium resumeret. Hæc cum a Syndicis commemorata essent; quæsiui ego, An non Ludovicus Palatinus Elector Augustanæ Confessionis fuerit? Ille, quanquam negare non audebat, affirmare tamen expresse noluit. Tu ego: Procul dubio fuit, inquam. Quado igitur te, tuisque similes, ob diuersam Religionem e Palatinatu expulit, qua fronte tu hic ad eam Confessionem prouocasti? quis non videat, te sub Augustanæ Confessionis nomine fraudem moliri?
units.tr: He had said the day before (as the syndics reported) that in the Palatinate he had been ordained as a minister of the Word by the Heidelberg council. Being asked why he had not remained in that place of his calling, he had answered that Elector Ludwig had removed from their teaching office all the ministers who would not agree with his opinion on religion, and had ordered them to transfer their seats elsewhere. On the occasion of this order, he too had left the Palatinate, with the intention, however, of returning there at some time (when a milder breeze should blow) and resuming his office and his ministry of teaching. When the syndics had recounted this, I asked: was not Ludwig, the Elector Palatine, of the Augsburg Confession? He, although he did not dare to deny it, nevertheless was unwilling to affirm it expressly. I then said: "Without doubt he was, I said. Since, then, he expelled you and those like you from the Palatinate on account of a different religion, with what face do you now appeal to that Confession here? Who does not see that you are contriving a fraud under the name of the Augsburg Confession?"

units.la: Excipiebat Dominus Sudermannus Consul, & paucis narrabat historiam mutationis illius, quam Friderico Palatino Elector e mortuo, filius illius, ac successor Ludovicus instituerit. Dicebat, fuisse se tum in Palatinatu, ac principia mutationis oculis suis vidisse. Clausa fuisse templa Principis Electoris mandatu, neque licuisse deinceps Concionatoribus illis, qui sub Friderico docuerat, officio suo fungi; quod ipse Badius ignorare non posset, ut qui eodem tempore e Palatinatu quoque discedere coactus fuerit. Ad hæc ille, pudore suffusus tacuit.
units.tr: Consul Sudermann took up the matter and briefly described the change that the Elector Ludwig, son and successor of the late Frederick the Palatine, had introduced. He said that he had been in the Palatinate at the time and had seen the beginnings of the change with his own eyes. By the Elector's command the churches had been closed, and those preachers who had taught under Frederick were no longer allowed to carry out their office. Badius himself could not be unaware of this, since he too had been forced to leave the Palatinate at the same time. At this, Badius, overcome with shame, fell silent.

units.la: Ego vero & illud porro subiungebam; Quod si Confessionem Augustanam syncere profiteretur, non licuisse tamen illi sub statu Imperij Catholico, contra Magistratus Edicta, eam ipsam priuatim exercere; cum Religionis Pacem, ad quam prouocaret, super Status ipsos, non super singula subditorum capita, fundatam costet.
units.tr: I added something further. Even if he sincerely professed the Augsburg Confession, it was not permitted under the Catholic government of the Empire to practise that religion in private against the edicts of the magistrates. The Peace of Religion, to which he appealed, was founded on the agreement of the states themselves, not on the individual heads of subjects.

units.la: Quærebam cuidētiæ causa, si ego vigore Constitutionis illius, quam Pacem Religionis vocant, Heidelbergæ in Palatinatu, vel in vrbe quadam Imperij Lutherana, id facere conarer, quod ille hocloco aliquandiu fecisset, an id laturus essem impunè?
units.tr: I asked, for the sake of clarity, whether, if I relied on the authority of that enactment which they call the Peace of Religion, I attempted in Heidelberg in the Palatinate, or in some Lutheran city of the Empire, to do what he had done here for some time, I would go unpunished.

units.la: Ad hæc ille nihil admodum: Responderat tamen diebus superioribus, quemadmodum Syndici referebant; Aliam esse hac parte conditionem vrbium, in quibus populus eligeret magistratum, quàm Principum eorum, qui Status Imperij sunt ex natiuitate. Quam vocem, tanquam occultum seditionis flabellum, vti revera est, omnes acceperūt. Cùm enim huiusmodi discrimen in promiscuam plebem sinistrè spargitur, facilè nimirum fit, vt incauti, qui nō possunt in hisce rebus discernere, contra magistratum animentur ac concitentur. Voluit ille quidem excusare ac mollire dictū, verùm friuolè. Tum Dominus Hardenradius Consul, Talia, inquit, inculcatis vestris hominibus, vt scilicet persuasum habeant, se recte facere, cùm contra magistratum insurgunt, atque huiusmodi prohibitos in Imperio clancularios conuentus agūt. Quod si vel Ratisbonæ, vel Noribergæ, tale quid tentaris, procul dubio longè seuerius tecum ageretur.
units.tr: To this he replied nothing of substance. Yet in the previous days, as the consuls reported, he had said that the situation in cities was different in this respect, where the people elected the magistrate, from that of those princes who are by birth members of the states of the Empire. Everyone took up this remark as a hidden bellows of sedition, which indeed it is. When such a distinction is carelessly spread among the common people, it easily happens that the unwary, who cannot discern these matters, are stirred up and roused against the magistrate. He tried to excuse and soften what he had said, but feebly. Then Consul Hardenradius said: "You drum such things into your people, so that they are persuaded they act rightly when they rise against the magistrate, and hold such secret meetings, which are forbidden in the Empire. If you had attempted anything of the kind at Regensburg or Nuremberg, you would undoubtedly have been treated far more severely."

units.la: Quæsiui ego demum, cùm revera Caluinianus esset, qua conscientia nomen Augustanæ Confessionis præ se ferret? Quomodo, inquam, in articulo mortis, & in extremo iudicio hoc nomine coram Deo consistes, quod titulo ac larua confessionis illius indutus, cuius revera hostis es, simpliciores fraudulenter ad Caluinismum ducis? Ad hæc ille subticuit.
units.tr: Finally I asked: since he was in truth a Calvinist, with what conscience did he bear the name of the Augsburg Confession? How, I asked, will you stand before God under this name at the hour of death and at the last judgment, when, dressed in the title and mask of that confession, of which you are in truth an enemy, you fraudulently lead the simpler folk to Calvinism? At this he kept silent.

units.la: Ventum est deinde ad ipsius conscientiam, & charitate proximi, quam vtramque lædi persuasum habebat, si legitimè ad Amplis. Senatus interrogata responderet. Iussus est à Dominis Syndicis nūc proferre rationes, quibus in eam sententiam inductus esset. Cumque ille, quantum ego colligere potui, de industria se reprimeret, neq; proferret quicquam, interrogaui demum ego: An non Amplissimum Senatum Colonienfem, pro vero huius vrbis magistratu agnosceret? Respondit, quanquam cunctabundus, Ita. Quaesiui denuo: An non, dum in hac vrbe vixisset, obedientiâ sese eidem legitimo magistratui debere, ex conscientiae obligatione putaret? Respondit, Ita, si nihil contra Deum mandaret; Alioquin Deo magis obediendum esse, quàm hominibus. Quaesiui tertiò: An igitur Amplifs. huius vrbis Senatus, vnquam ipsi mandarit aliquid, quod legi charitatis, aut diuino mandato contrarium fuerit? Ad hanc quaestionem subticuit.
units.tr: Then the discussion turned to his conscience and to love of neighbour, both of which, he was convinced, would be harmed if he answered the questions lawfully put to him by the most distinguished Senate. The consuls ordered him to now state the reasons that had led him to that opinion. Since he, as far as I could gather, deliberately restrained himself and said nothing, I finally asked: did he not acknowledge the most distinguished Senate of Cologne as the true magistracy of this city? He answered, though hesitantly, "Yes." I asked again: while he had lived in this city, did he not think, from a sense of conscience, that he owed obedience to this lawful magistracy? He answered, "Yes, provided it commanded nothing against God; otherwise God must be obeyed rather than men." I asked a third time: then had the most distinguished Senate of this city ever commanded him anything contrary to the law of love or to a divine command? To this question he kept silent.

units.la: Admonitus aliquoties à Dominis Syndicis, vt aperiret syncere mentem suam, ac causas proderet pertinacis illius silentij, quo iam aliquamdiu Magistratum elusisset; Nihil amplius protulit, nisi, proximum suum laedi, si voluntati Senatus obtemperaret: Neque vero hac in re opus esse suo indicio, posse Magistratum omnia, quae ex ipso scire vellet, aliunde rescisci. Facturum se contra conscientiam, si ea proderet, per quae deinde proximo suo detrimentum adferri sciret. Itaque rogare se, ne hac parte grauius vrgeretur.
units.tr: Repeatedly admonished by the consuls to disclose his mind sincerely and to give the reasons for the stubborn silence with which he had for some time been eluding the magistracy, he said nothing more except that his neighbour would be harmed if he obeyed the will of the Senate. There was no need, he said, for his own testimony in this matter, since the magistracy could learn elsewhere everything it wished to know from him. He would be acting against his conscience if he disclosed the things by which, as he knew, harm would then come to his neighbour. Therefore he asked that he not be pressed more heavily on this point.

units.la: Quaesiui ego rursum: An Senatus, quem pro legitimo huius vrbis magistratu agnosceret, ipsius quoque proximus esset, nec ne? Respondit, esse. Cur igitur, inquam, quando proximi tui rationem habere vis, magis respicien-dum putas ad paucos quosdam priuatos, qui magistratui debitam obedientiam negant, quàm ad eos, quos ad Reipublicae gubernacula collocauit Dominus, quorum interest ad conseruandam pacem publicam, ea scire, quae à te quaeruntur.
units.tr: I asked him again: whether or not the Senate, which he acknowledged as the lawful magistracy of this city, was also his neighbour? He replied that it was. "Why then," I said, "since you wish to have regard for your neighbour, do you think greater regard should be paid to a few private persons who deny the obedience owed to the magistracy, than to those whom the Lord has placed at the helm of the state, and whose interest it is, for the preservation of public peace, to know the things that are asked of you?"

units.la: Respondit ille, Non pendere Reipublicae salutem ex hoc negocio, neq; laedi Senatus auctoritatem, si non prodat ea, quae Magistratus ipsius indicio scire vellet. Imò vero, inquam, laeditur. Antea fassus es, obedientiâ te debere Magistratui huius vrbis, nisi quid contra Deum mandet.
units.tr: He replied that the safety of the commonwealth did not depend on this business, nor was the authority of the Senate harmed if he did not disclose what the magistracy wished to learn from him. "On the contrary," I said, "it is harmed. You have already admitted that you owe obedience to the magistracy of this city, unless it commands something against God."

units.la: Igitur vel obtemperandum nunc est, vel certè demon-strandū, mandari aliquid, quod cum diuina lege pugnet: Iam & salus Reipublicæ læditur, quando nimirum occultantur ea consilia, ęqueque actiones, quibus perturbari pacem publicam, ac seditiones excitari, aliarum urbium exempla testantur: Et tu quidem tacitè Senatum huius urbis accusas impietatis atq; tyrannidis; impiettatis quidem, quod eam Religionem foueat, quam tu cum Idololatria coniunctam esse sentis, quæ summa est, & omnium maxima impietas; tyrannidis verò, quod Edicta sanciat, quibus Idololatria & impietas stabiliatur, ac subditi, ab ea alieni, per vim opprimantur; quæ, quin germana tyrannis sit, negari non potest.
units.tr: Therefore either you must now obey, or else it must be clearly shown that something is commanded which conflicts with divine law. And the safety of the commonwealth is indeed harmed when those plans and actions are concealed by which, as the examples of other cities attest, public peace is disturbed and seditions are stirred up. And you, in fact, tacitly accuse the Senate of this city of impiety and tyranny: of impiety, because it fosters that religion which you think is joined with idolatry, which is the greatest and worst of all impieties; and of tyranny, because it sanctions edicts by which idolatry and impiety are established, and subjects alienated from it are oppressed by force. That this is genuine tyranny cannot be denied.

units.la: Excepit ille, Nequaquam se tyrannidis aut impietatis accusare Senatum. Posse fieri, vt magistratus ex sinistra persuasione iudicio nonnunquam aberret, dum hæc aut illa, præter æquitatis rationem statuit: Quemadmodum euenerit Constantino Magno Imperatori, quem Arriani quondam in Athanasium vehementer concitarint. Neque verò huiusmodi lapsus eorum, qui in magistratu sunt, impietatis ac tyrannidis nomine censendos esse, quando non accedit habitus.
units.tr: He answered that he by no means accused the Senate of tyranny or impiety. It could happen that a magistrate sometimes errs in judgement from a mistaken persuasion, while he decides this or that contrary to the reasons of equity, as happened to the Emperor Constantine the Great, whom the Arians once vehemently stirred up against Athanasius. Nor should such lapses of those who hold office be counted under the name of impiety and tyranny, when there is no settled habit of such conduct.

units.la: Ego, cum Constantini mentionem faceret, narraui ex historia Ecclesiastica, qua stropha pissimus Imperator, cum magno concordiæ farciendæ studio flagraret, ab Arrio circumuentus, in Arrianos aliquando propensior factus fit. Quam historiam hoc loco breuitatis studio non infero. Subiunxi deinde, Eum hoc exemplo non sufficienter ab huius urbis Senatu tyrannidis atque impietatis crime remouere: Quandoquidem omnia, quæ Senatus hac parte contra Sectarios ageret, non temere, vel ex informatione sinistra, sed maturo consilio, ac deliberato ageret; imò, (quemadmodum Syndici suggerebant) hanc tuendæ Religionis Catholicæ rationem, à pijs maioribus per manus traditam haberet: Vt adeò hæ actiones, proeul dubio, ex habitu quodam administrandæ Reipu-blicæ proficiscantur. Itaq; non esse, quod imprudentem Constantini credulitatem ac lapsum, cum maturis huius magistratus actionibus comparet.
units.tr: When he mentioned Constantine, I related from ecclesiastical history how that most wicked emperor, although he burned with a great zeal for fostering concord, was circumvented by Arius and at last became more inclined towards the Arians. I do not bring in that history here for the sake of brevity. I then added that by this example he did not sufficiently clear the Senate of this city of the crime of tyranny and impiety, since everything which the Senate did in this matter against the sectaries it did not rashly, nor from some mistaken information, but with mature deliberation. Indeed, as the consuls had suggested, it held this way of defending the Catholic religion handed down from its pious ancestors. Thus these actions undoubtedly proceed from a settled habit of administering the commonwealth. Therefore there was no reason to compare the imprudent credulity and lapse of Constantine with the mature actions of this magistracy.

units.la: Hortabatur cum inter conferendum Doctor Hack-steinius, vt nunc proferret D. Cypriani sententiam, quam ad cautæ suæ defensionem, in examine superiori protu-lisset; Vrgebam idem & ego. Verum ille perpetuò, quic-quid diceremus, tergiuersatus est, nec vnquā vel D. Cy-priani nomen appellare voluit. Demum ego, quia nihil afferebat, Cyprianus, inquā, nulla in re tibi suffragatur. Fuit is Episcopus Catholicus, & causam egit coram magistratu gentili. Si quid eo rerum statu dixit, id ad te nihil pertinet: Quando inter D. Cyprianum, & te; tum inter Senatum huius vrbis Catholicum, & magistratum illum gentilem, nulla penitus est comparatio.
units.tr: Doctor Hackstein urged him during the discussion to now produce the opinion of St Cyprian, which he had put forward in the earlier examination in defence of his cause. I pressed the same request. But he kept evading whatever we said, and never once wished even to name St Cyprian. At last, since he offered nothing, I said: "Cyprian, I tell you, supports you in nothing. He was a Catholic bishop, and he pleaded his case before a pagan magistracy. Whatever he said in that state of affairs has nothing to do with you. Between Cyprian and yourself, and between the Catholic Senate of this city and that pagan magistracy, there is no comparison at all."

units.la: Vrgebant eum, cum ita perpetuò restitaret, alijs quoq; rationibus, Consul Hardenradius & Syndici. Quærebāt, cur ad eum modum tergiuersaretur? Quid huiusmodi subterfugijs Amplissimum Senatum ac seipsum quoque distineret? Ipsum fateri hoc pertinaci silentio, quod male fecerit. Nam si bene se fecisse putaret, cur tantopere de fugeret lucem? Cur actiones suas secretas esse vellet, eas-que tanto studio celare contenderet? Imò quò magis hac parte subterfugeret, eò graviores habere causas Senatū, vt consilia contra Reipublicæ salutem in iis conuenticu lis agitata suspicetur. Neque vero eam suspicionem omnino vanam esse, quando per huiusmodi clancularios conuentus, insignes nonnunquam Respublicæ penitus euersæ sint. Hæc, & id genus alia cùm obijcerentur, ille ni hil admodum respondit; nisi quod diceret, se suos audi-tores semper ad obedientiam, ac pacem colendam hor-tatum fuisse, neque hoc spectasse vnquam, vt seditionem concitaret.
units.tr: Since he kept resisting in this way, the consul Hardenradius and the consuls' assistants pressed him with other arguments as well. They asked why he evaded in such a manner. Why did he distract the most distinguished Senate, and himself too, with such subterfuges? By this stubborn silence he was confessing that he had done wrong. For if he thought he had acted well, why did he so greatly shun the light? Why did he want his actions to be secret, and strive so eagerly to conceal them? Indeed, the more he fled in this matter, the greater reasons the Senate had to suspect that plans against the safety of the commonwealth were being devised in those conventicles. Nor was that suspicion altogether groundless, since through such secret meetings distinguished commonwealths have sometimes been utterly overthrown. When these and similar things were thrown at him, he answered nothing of substance, except that he had always exhorted his hearers to obedience and to the cultivation of peace, and had never aimed at stirring up sedition.

units.la: Ad quam vocem Dominus Hardenradius Consul, sciliscilicet,inquit,id fatis experimur in vestri sodalitij homi nibus,qui ita fe gerunt erga Senatum, vt omnia illorum inobedientiam spirare videantur: Vnde liquido con- stare potest,quid agatur in vestris coetibus, & qualia in ijs consilia pertractentur:In quibus proculdubio inter alia Senatum falsò, & contra conscientiam traducitis, quasi Christo Seruatori praecludat viam, & Idololatriam in hac vrbe foueat;vt scilicet causam habere videatur,cùm sese magistratui ad eum modum opponunt. Ad quæ ille paululum submurmuras,nihil amplius respondit,quàm quod antea quoque dixerat, quod nunquam publi- cos excitare motus in animo habuerit.
units.tr: To this remark Lord Hardenrad the Consul replied: "We have experience of this in the men of your society, who conduct themselves towards the Senate in such a way that all of them seem to breathe disobedience. From this it can clearly be established what is done at your gatherings and what sort of plans are discussed in them. In them, no doubt among other things, you falsely and against your conscience misrepresent the Senate, as if it blocks the way to Christ the Saviour and fosters idolatry in this city, so that you may seem to have a reason for setting yourselves against the magistrate in the way you do." To these words he muttered a little and made no further reply than what he had said before, that he had never intended to stir up public disturbances.

units.la: Tum ego,vt hoc,inquam,concedatur,quod tu conci- tare auditores tuos contra Senatum non intenderis, cer- tum est tamen experientia magistra, vbicunque contra magistratus Edicta, huiusmodi secreti conuentus à ve- ftris habiti sunt,ibi semper perturbationem publicæ pa- cis, ac magistratus oppressionem demum subsecutam. Quod exempla florentissimarum vrbium in vicino Bel- gio fatis testificantur. Addidit Dominus Consul Suder- mannus exemplum vrbis Aquifgranenfis, quæ eadē via in magnas difficultates coniecta fit. Et in Belgio quidē, (inquit Dominus Consulj voluistis omnes, vti vobis vi- debatur, à iugo Romani Pontificis eximere. At quid fa- ctum est? Scilicet vestris conatibus multò profundius, quàm vnquam antea,Belgas in Pontificis Romani feru tutem coniecistis.Itaque nihil valent conatus vestri, ne- que tolerari debent,aut possunt. Admonemur ex omni parte,multas in vrbe nostra Sectas pullulare; neceffariū esse,vt diligenter prospiciamus rebus nostris, ne quid ab ijs detrimenti Reipublicæ nostræ inferatur.
units.tr: Then I said: "Granted that you did not intend to stir up your hearers against the Senate, it is nonetheless certain, as experience teaches, that wherever secret gatherings of this kind have been held by your people against the edicts of the magistrate, there the public peace has always been disturbed and the magistrate in the end overthrown. The examples of the most flourishing cities in the neighbouring Netherlands bear ample witness to this." Consul Sudermann added the example of the city of Aachen, which was thrown into great difficulties by the same route. "And in the Netherlands indeed," said Consul Sudermann, "you all wished, as it seemed to you, to free yourselves from the yoke of the Roman Pontiff. But what happened? Of course, by your efforts the Belgians were cast into the servitude of the Roman Pontiff far more deeply than ever before. Therefore your attempts are worth nothing and ought not, nor can they, be tolerated. We are warned on every side that many sects are sprouting up in our city, and it is necessary that we take careful thought for our affairs, lest any harm from them be inflicted on our commonwealth."

units.la: Ad hæc verba ego,rogata venia,interlocutus,quod de Sectis dicitur,inquam,id verissimum est; quemadmodū fatis experimur,qui curam animarum in hac vrbe geri- mus.Lutherani rariores sunt,& deficiunt indies;quidam illoillorum ad nos redeunt, quidam vero paulatim in naf- fam pertrahuntur à Caluinistis;Qui numero superat Lu- theranos. Iam & Svvenckfeldiani quoq; incrementa su- munt. Anabaptistarum vero gens etiam augetur. Quin & Domus charitatis, quae ex Anabaptiftarū fecibus, tan- quam riuus quidam, promanauit, pede in hac vrbe iam- pridem fixit.
units.tr: To these words I replied, with leave asked: "As to what is said about sects, I say that it is most true, as we know well enough who have the cure of souls in this city. The Lutherans are fewer and are dwindling day by day; some of them return to us, but some are gradually drawn into the net by the Calvinists, who now outnumber the Lutherans. Already the Schwenckfeldians too are gaining ground. The race of the Anabaptists is also growing. Indeed the House of Charity, which flowed out of the dregs of the Anabaptists like a certain stream, has long since set foot in this city."

units.la: Excepit Ioannes Lennepius, & Currum quoque ster- corum, (id nouum quoddam Libertinorum genus est) huc aduectum dixit, quemadmodum à fide dignis acce- perit. Tum Dominus Sudermannus Consul, Bene, in- quit, Si igitur nos quemlibet pro libitu suo agere patere- mur, & demum aliqua fieret in Religione mutatio; quid Caesarea Maiestas, quid Rex Hispaniarum, quid Ponti- sex, quid Iuliacensis Princeps, vicinus noster dicturus es- set? Procul dubio hoc pacto ciuitas nostra in plurima pe- ricula conijceretur. Haec à Domino Consule cum vehe- mentia quadam dicebantur; Ille vero omnia silentio transmittebat.
units.tr: John Lennep took up the point and said that a cart of dung (this is a new kind of Libertine) had also been brought here, as he had received from trustworthy sources. Then Consul Sudermann said: "Good. If, therefore, we allowed each person to act as he pleases, and in the end some change were made in religion, what would the Imperial Majesty, what would the King of Spain, what would the Pontiff, what would our neighbour the Prince of Jülich say? Without doubt in this way our city would be cast into very great dangers." These things were said by the Consul with some vehemence; but he himself let everything pass in silence.

units.la: Inter colloquendū, cum obijceretur, huiusmodi clan- cularios conuentus semper motus publicos, ac seditio- nes subditorum contra magistratum peperisse; atque ille nonnihil obmurmuraret, quaesiuit ex illo Ioannes Len- nepius, vt vel vnicum proferret exemplum, vbi secus ac- cidisset? Ad quam vocem, oculis in sinum defixus, peni- tus obmutuit. Tum ego, quid igitur, inquam, magistratus huius vrbis aliud à vobis exspectare potest, quàm vt, qd' alibi per hoc medium perpetraftis, idem & hic quoque conemini paulatim, vbi satis virium accreuerit?
units.tr: In the course of the conversation, when it was objected that such secret gatherings had always produced public disturbances and seditions of subjects against the magistrate, and he muttered something in reply, John Lennep asked him to produce at least one example where things had turned out otherwise. At this, fixing his eyes on his breast, he fell completely silent. Then I said: "What else, then, can the magistrate of this city expect from you, than that what you have carried out elsewhere by this means, you will likewise attempt here, little by little, once you have gathered sufficient strength?"

units.la: Intuli quoque sermonem de ipsius vocatione; cuius rei occasio fuit, quod conscientiam suam informatam esse Dei verbo diceret. Quaesiui, qua conscietia ipse, cum nec à Deo vocatus esset, nec ab hominibus, qui potestatem eius rei haberet, huius vrbis ciuibus subrepsisset? Nō est, inquam, in hac celebri ac populosa vrbe, vel vnus homo, qui non habeat suum Pastorem, per legitimæ vocationis viam à Deo constitutū: Inter quos & ego meque, licet omnium infimum, connumero. Nobis igitur, qui Pastores in hac vrbe sumus, creditæ sunt, ac commissæ oues huius gregis; quibus diuini verbi, ac Sacramentorum pabulum hactenus ministrauimus: Eam ad rem, per Dei gratiam, tua, tuique similium opera non indigemus. Quomodo igitur in iudicio Dei facinus hoc defendes, quod, cum peregrinus sis, nec legitimè vocatus, oues nostras dissipas, easque contra Magistratus Edicta in angulum conuocatas, à nobis auertis? Tu quod nos, qui legitimi Pastores sumus, in conuenticulis istis traducis, quin absentes calumnijs ac mendacijs oneras, & nec admonitos, nec auditos condemnas? Quod si nos, qui Coloniæ curam animarum gerimus, non recte fungeremur officio nostro, tuarum partium fuisset, nos admonere prius, & redarguere, quàm ad eum modum, contra Senatus voluntatem, prohibitos conuentus agere. Hæc ego; Ille vero ne verbo quidem vnquam conatus est, vel nostrā vocationem oppugnare, vel tueri suam.
units.tr: I also turned the talk to his own calling; the occasion for this was that he said his conscience was informed by the Word of God. I asked by what conscience he himself had crept in among the citizens of this city, since he had been called neither by God nor by men who had the authority in this matter? "There is not," I said, "in this famous and populous city a single person who does not have his own minister, appointed by God by the way of lawful calling; among whom I too count myself, though the lowest of all. To us, therefore, who are ministers in this city, the sheep of this flock have been entrusted and committed; to them we have up to now supplied the food of the divine Word and the Sacraments. For this task, by the grace of God, we do not need your work or that of your like. How, then, will you defend before the judgment of God this wrong, that, being a stranger and not lawfully called, you scatter our sheep and turn them away from us, when they have been gathered into a corner against the edicts of the magistrate? Why do you slander us, who are the lawful ministers, in these little conventicles, and burden us with calumnies and lies while we are absent, condemning us unadmonished and unheard? If we who have the cure of souls in Cologne were not performing our office rightly, it would have been your part first to admonish and refute us, rather than to hold forbidden meetings in this way, against the will of the Senate." These were my words; but he never once attempted, even by a word, either to assail our calling or to defend his own.

units.la: Adiunxi demum & illud; Ipsos aduersarios non ferre, vt quisquam inter eos huiusmodi furtiuos conuentus agat, vel secreto docendi auctoritatem vsurpet. Et Lutherus quidem, inquam, consulit, vt tenebriones illi, qui passim repunt per domos, & contra magistratus voluntatem, inscijs veris pastoribus, clam aliud doctrinæ genus spargunt, quàm publicè viget, non tolerentur vllo pacto; imò si desistere nolint, demum magistro Hansoni (quo nomine carnificem designat) commendentur. Atque hoc non tantùm intelligi vult de seductoribus, qui prauis dogmatibus simpliciorum animos imbuunt, verùm de ijs quoque, qui veri doctores sunt, ac doctrinam Euangelij profitetur: Hos, inquit, tametsi vel Angeli sint, vel meri Gabrieles de cœlo, tamē, si contra vtriusq; magistratus, Ecclesiastici nimirum, & ciuilis, voluntatem clam docere instituant, coercendos esse ac puniendos; Etiam cum inter Papistas, ut ipse loquitur, aut haereticos, huiusmodi quid tentare volunt. Quae ratio à Lutheranis etiā hactenus observatur: Quemadmodum demonstrari potest exemplis Principum, ac urbium quarundam in Imperio, quae publice Lutheri doctrinam, sub Augustanae Confessionis nomine, profitentur. Haec omnia ille, quemadmodum & superiora, silentio transmittebat.
units.tr: Finally I added this too: that the adversaries themselves do not tolerate anyone among them conducting such furtive gatherings or assuming the authority to teach in secret. "Luther himself," I said, "advises that those rogues who creep about everywhere through houses, and against the will of the magistrate, without the knowledge of the true ministers, spread secretly a kind of teaching other than that which flourishes publicly, must not be tolerated in any way; indeed, if they refuse to desist, they should at last be commended to Master Hans (by which name he designates the executioner). And he wishes this to be understood not only of seducers who imbue the minds of simple people with depraved doctrines, but also of those who are true teachers and profess the doctrine of the Gospel: these, he says, even if they were angels or mere Gabriels from heaven, yet if they undertake to teach secretly against the will of both magistrates, the ecclesiastical and the civil, must be restrained and punished; even when they wish to attempt such a thing among the Papists, or heretics, as he himself puts it. This rule has been observed by the Lutherans even until now, as can be shown from the examples of princes and certain cities in the Empire which publicly profess Luther's doctrine under the name of the Augsburg Confession." He let all these things pass in silence, as he had the preceding ones.

units.la: Sub finem iterum sermo incidit de Edictis Magistratus nostri, deque rebus iis, quas ipsius indicio scire vellet Amplissimus huius urbis Senatus; quē tacitè, si in sententia sua persistat, tyrannidis ab eo accusari, Doctor Crantius aperte demonstrabat: Ad cuius verba ille, rugata nonnihil fronte, quàm amarulentè, inquit, de hac re loquitur D. Doctor: Nunquam ego tyrannidis Amplissimū Senatū insimulatui. Eam hominis insolentiam indignè ferens Doctor Crantius, humaniter tamen respondit, Iniquè sibi amarulentiam obijci: Non hoc se dicere, quod expressis verbis Senatum tyrannidis accusarit; Verum id ex ipsius actionibus & verbis necessario sequi: Quam rem idem Doctor Cratius ad eum modum declarauit, ut ille contra ne mutire quidem potuerit.
units.tr: Towards the end the talk again fell on the edicts of our magistrate, and on those matters which the most distinguished Senate of this city wished to learn from his own information; Doctor Crantz clearly showed that if he persisted in his opinion, he would accuse the Senate of tyranny by implication. At these words he, his brow wrinkled somewhat, said: "How bitterly the Doctor speaks on this matter! I have never accused the most distinguished Senate of tyranny." Doctor Crantz, taking ill this insolence of the man, yet answered courteously: that it was unfair to charge him with bitterness; he was not saying that he had accused the Senate of tyranny in express words, but that this necessarily follows from his actions and words. Doctor Crantz explained this matter in such a way that the other could not so much as murmur in reply.

units.la: Obieci ego denuò & illud, (quod antea quoque per occasionem attigeram) Concionatores istius partis, de quorum numero & ipse sit, in huiusmodi conuenticulis, graui admodum iniuria nos afficere; cùm absentes acerbe ac contumeliosè traducant, & Religionem Catholicam, quam profitemur, velut impiā, & foeda cū Idololatria coniunctā, abominandū in modū detestentur: Quod tametsi iam expressè fateri nolit, nequeat tamen inficiari, nisi conscientiae testimonio reclamare velit. Eā verò criminatione, non ad nos pertinere tātum, verùm nostros etiam, eosdemque ipsorum maiores, à quibus Catholica Religio ad nos peruenerit, simul nobiscum inuoluere. Et quia nobis absentibus tam atrox iniuria inferatur, ut adeo
units.tr: I objected again, too, (as I had touched on this before in passing) that the preachers of that party, of whose number he himself is, treat us with very grave injury in such gatherings, since they slander us in our absence bitterly and insultingly, and detest the Catholic religion, which we profess, as impious and joined with foul idolatry, in an abominable manner. Although he now refuses to admit this openly, he cannot deny it unless he wishes to contradict the testimony of his own conscience. And by this accusation they involve not only us but also our people, and their own forefathers, from whom the Catholic religion has come down to us, along with us. And since so grave an injury is done to us in our absence, that we cannot in this way defend our innocence and that of our forefathers against such calumnies and lies, the whole matter must be entrusted to God, the just avenger of all wrongs, by whom assuredly at some time the most grievous...

units.la: Fol. 157 a / Fol. 346 b: folio references printed in the left margin. adeò nostram, maiorumque nostrorum innocentiam, aduersus huiusmodi calūnias ac mendacia tueri nequeamus, rem totam quidem Deo, iusto iniuriarum omnium vindici, committendam esse; cui proculdubio grauissimam aliquādo rationem hoc nomine sint reddituti.
units.tr: ...that we cannot defend our innocence, or that of our forefathers, against such calumnies and lies; the whole matter must be committed to God, the just avenger of all wrongs, to whom they will assuredly one day have to render a most grievous account for this.

units.la: Hæc ego, & id genus alia quædam in eandem sententiam cùm dicerem, ille se nonnihil repressit: Tādem vero, Non dissiteor, inquit, Religionem vestram, tanquam erroneam, à nobis reprehendi: Quod si hac parte in errore sum, instrui cupio; præbebo me docilem, tu te præbeas doctorem. Respōdi, Nescire me, an cum in finem à Magistratu vocatus sim. Præterea tempus colloquendo iam effluxisse, (imminebat enim vespera) vt si in hunc campum ingrediendum sit, id nunc, vel hoc etiam nomine fieri non possit. Iam & alios esse me doctiores, tum in facultate Theologica, tum inter Pastores quoque confratres meos, qui commodius ac melius agere doctorum partes, ac errantem instituere possint. Quanquam ego quidem non existimem, quod hac parte candidè, atque ex animo loquatur. Si enim ea mente esset, vt syncerè cuperet instrui, potuisse iampridem illum toto illo tempore, quo hic cōmoratus fuerit, vel me, vel alium quempiam è Pastoribus hoc nomine conuenire. Tādem à præsentibus Dominis humaniter & amicè monebatur, vt deliberaret secum in diem crastinum, ac posita demum per uicacia, legitimè ad interrogata responderet. Ille ad hæc suo more tergiuersari, ac prætendere cōscientiam suam, & legem charitatis de non lædendo proximo: Mea conscientia, inquit, hoc non fert; alius fortasse posset facere, ego non possum. Deinde repetita protestatione, qua initio quoque fuerat vsus, excusauit timiditatem suam; atq; ita hac vice dimissus est, & reductus in carcerem.
units.tr: When I said these things and others of the same kind to that effect, he restrained himself somewhat. At last he said: "I do not deny that our religion condemns yours as erroneous. But if I am in error on this point, I wish to be instructed; I will show myself teachable, and you should show yourself a teacher." I replied that I did not know whether I had been summoned for this purpose by the magistrate. Besides, the time for talking had already run out, for evening was coming on, so that if we were to enter upon this field, it could not be done now, or at least not for this reason. Moreover, there are others more learned than I, both in theology and among my fellow ministers, who could play the part of a teacher more conveniently and better, and instruct one who is in error. Yet I did not think he was speaking candidly and from his heart on this point. For if he had truly desired to be instructed, he could have asked me, or some other of the ministers, for this purpose at any time during the whole period he had stayed here. Finally, the gentlemen present advised him kindly and in a friendly way that he should consider the matter with himself until the next day, and then, once the arguments had been set out, answer the questions put to him properly. He, in his customary way, evaded this and pleaded his conscience and the law of charity not to harm one's neighbour: "My conscience," he said, "does not allow this; another man perhaps could do it, but I cannot." Then, repeating the protest he had also used at the beginning, he excused his timidity; and so he was dismissed for this time and led back into prison.

units.la: Postea visum quibusdam fuit, non futurum abs re, (modò de voluntate Amplissimi Senatus fieri possit) si de vno atque altero Religionis capite, amica cum illo collatio institueretur; præsertim, quia fe docile futurû promisisset. Dixi ego, si publico nomine Magistratus, atq; ex professo cum homine fit agendū, necessariū esse, vt id fiat ordinaria via, de consilio Theologicæ facultatis; vel per Dominum Suffraganeum, qui vnum atque alterum è Pastoribus assumere possit. Existimatum fuit, satius esse, vt quemadmodum iam factum fit, obiter atque priuatim, per modum amicæ collocutionis tentetur, an reipsa præstare velit, quod verbis præ se tulisset. Ad eam igitur rem ego quidem operam meam detuli; verum hac conditione, vt quicquid huius futurum esset, id fieret præsentibus viris aliquot fide dignis: propterea quod non semel talium hominum calumnias ac mendacia post huiusmodi priuatas collocutiones, expertus eram. Placuit igitur, vt, si ea res Amplissimo Senatui non displiceret, postridie ad horam secundam pomeridianam, eodem loco rursum conueniremus. Atque hæc fere primi diei collatio fuit.
units.tr: Afterwards it seemed good to some that it would not be out of place (provided it could be done with the consent of the most distinguished Senate) if a friendly conference were held with him on one or two heads of religion, especially since he had promised that he would be teachable. I said that if the matter was to be dealt with formally, in the name of the magistrate and openly with this man, it was necessary that it be done by the ordinary way, with the advice of the theological faculty, or through the lord superintendent, who could take one or two of the ministers along. It was judged better, as has already been done, to try informally and privately, by way of a friendly discussion, whether he was really willing to do what he had said in words. I therefore put my own effort into this business, but on this condition: that whatever came of it should take place in the presence of several trustworthy men, because I had more than once experienced the calumnies and lies of such men after private conversations of this kind. It was therefore agreed that, if the matter did not displease the most distinguished Senate, we should meet again in the same place the next day at two o'clock in the afternoon. And this was roughly the account of the first day's conference.

units.la: ALTERIVS DIEI COLLATIO.
units.tr: ALTERIVS DIEI COLLATIO.

units.la: POstridie, qui fuit vndecimus Aprilis, hora secundā pomeridiana, vti constitutum erat, ad carcerem redij. Conuenerunt eò, qui pridie adfuerat; (excepto Ioanne Lennepio) & præter eos Balthafar à Berchem, Theodorus Plöger, Michaël Ludgen, Hermannus à VViddig, Senatorij ordinis viri; tum Anthonius Rinck, patritius Coloniensis. Vocatus iterum est Ioannes Badius Minister Caluinianus; Cumque suo loco consedisset, Doctor Hacksteinius inter cætera, quæ breuiter illi proposuit Amplissimi Senatus nomine, illa quoque verba repetijt, quod pridie docilem se fore promisisset, si ego doctoris partes agerem. Existimatum igitur fuisse, non futurum abs re, si fieret eius rei periculum. In eum itaq; finem me, Pastorem D. Cuniberti, nunc denuo vocatum adesse, vt placida scilicet, atque amica inter nos de Religione collatio institueretur.
units.tr: On the following day, which was the eleventh of April, at two o'clock in the afternoon, as had been arranged, I returned to the prison. Those who had been present the day before gathered there (except John Lennep), and in addition Balthasar von Berchem, Theodor Plöger, Michael Ludgen and Hermann von Widdig, men of the senatorial order; also Anthonius Rinck, a patrician of Cologne. John Badius, the Calvinist minister, was called again; and when he had taken his seat, Doctor Hacksteinius, among other things which he briefly put to him in the name of the most distinguished Senate, also repeated those words, that the day before he had promised to be teachable if I played the part of the teacher. It was therefore thought that it would not be out of place to make a trial of this. To that end I, the pastor of St. Cunibert, now summoned again, was present, so that a calm and friendly discussion about religion might be conducted between us.

units.la: Ego deinde Badium hortabar, vt eam sumeret in colloquendo libertatem, qua vsurus esset, si vel Heidelbergæ mecum ageret, vel alibi in medio Palatinatu. Faciebã illi quoque potestatẽ deligendi, quam vellet, materiam, de qua collatione instituì cuperet. Demũ, vt inter colloquendũ vtras vellet, siue opponẽtis, siue respondentis partes agere, id illi quoq; liberum relinquebã. Ille deligebat Articulum de Cœna Domini. Rogaui, Quia multiplex esset de hoc Articulo controuersia, quam istius materiæ partem inter nos disceptari cuperet? Respondit eam, in qua de veritate quæritur, vt quæ primaria esset. Dixi, Magni quoque momenti disputationem esse de Sacrificio, ac Sacerdotio; cur non illam desumeret? Badius ad hæc, Placere nunc priorem, quam dixerit; altera illam postea quoque discutiendam sumi posse. Itaq; ego hac in parte ipsius voluntati acquieui.
units.tr: I then urged Badius to take the same freedom in conversing that he would use if he were dealing with me at Heidelberg, or elsewhere in the middle of the Palatinate. I also gave him the choice of whatever subject he wished to have discussed in our conference. Finally, I left it free to him, during the conversation, to take whichever role he wished, that of opponent or that of respondent. He chose the article on the Lord's Supper. I asked, since there was a manifold controversy about this article, which part of this subject he wished to be debated between us. He replied that it was the part in which the question is about truth, as being the primary one. I said that the disputation about sacrifice and priesthood was also of great importance; why did he not take that one? To this Badius replied that he preferred the first one he had named; the other could be taken up afterwards as well. So in this matter I yielded to his wish.

units.la: Et principio quidẽ à me petijt, vt se Dominis præsenti bus excusarem; quos diebus superioribus dicto quodam de pane Eucharistico videretur offendisse. Cum enim de Eucharistia sermo per occasionem inciderit, eos nõ admodum æquis animis accepisse, quod veteres communi pane, ad hoc mysterium peragendum vsos fuisse dixerit.
units.tr: And at the outset he asked me to excuse him to the gentlemen present, whom he seemed to have offended in the previous days by a certain remark about the Eucharistic bread. For when the discussion of the Eucharist had come up by chance, they had not taken it very calmly that he had said the ancients used ordinary bread to carry out this mystery.

units.la: Respondi, Non existimare me, quod eo dicto quenquam offenderit; quando Catholicorum omnium consensu satis constet, panem illum, qui ad altare defertur, antequam consecretur, omnino communem esse: Post consecrationem vero iam non amplius dici, vel esse communem panem, sed verum Christi corpus.
units.tr: I replied that I did not think anyone had been offended by that remark, since it is sufficiently established by the agreement of all Catholics that the bread which is brought to the altar, before it is consecrated, is indeed ordinary bread; but after consecration it is no longer called, or be, ordinary bread, but the true body of Christ.

units.la: Ille sermone continuato, ad confirmandum ea, quæ dixerat, Græcorum etiam morem adducebat, quos notum est, vti pane fermentato, cum sacra mysteria peragunt. Ex quibus verbis intelligebam, quod communis panis nomine, cuiuscunq; generis panem domesticum intelintelligeret, siue fermentatus is sit, siue non sit. Respondebam igitur ad exemplum Græcorum; Aliam esse consuetudinem Ecclesiæ Latinæ, quæ scilicet azymo pane ad sacrificium peragendum uteretur: Eam vero consuetudinem, procul dubio in ipsius Christi Seruatoris exemplo fundari, quem satis certe costaret azymo pane vsum, cum hoc mysterium instituęret; quando Iudæis eo tempore, quo Paschalem agnum comedebant, fermētatum panem in domibus habere non licuerit.
units.tr: Continuing his speech, to confirm what he had said, he also brought forward the custom of the Greeks, who, as is well known, use leavened bread when they celebrate the sacred mysteries. From these words I understood that by the name of ordinary bread he meant bread for domestic use of whatever kind, whether it is leavened or not. I therefore replied, following the example of the Greeks, that the Latin Church has another custom, namely that it uses unleavened bread to carry out the sacrifice; and that this custom is undoubtedly founded on the example of Christ the Saviour himself, who certainly is known to have used unleavened bread when he instituted this mystery, since at the time when the Jews ate the Paschal lamb it was not lawful for them to have leavened bread in their houses.

units.la: Excepit rursum, & nominato D. Gregorio, tum Paulo quoque Diacono, de pane nummulario mentionem intulit, in eū finem, opinor, vt quemadmodum azymi panis vsum, adducto Græcorum more, arroscrat, ita formā quoque rotundam eiusdem Eucharistici panis improbaret. Dixi, talia nihil admodū facere ad rem; præstare igitur, vt missis ijs, quæ minutiora essent, ad causam ipsam aggrederetur. Idem hortabatur Domini Syndici; qui & illud adijciebant, Se nequaquam indigne tulisse, quod pridie de communis aut fermentati panis vsu dixerit; verum id sibi mirum accidisse potius, quod citauerit pro se D. Gregorium, cum quo reuera tamen in Religione nihil haberet commune.
units.tr: He again took up the matter, and after naming Gregory the Great, and then Paul the Deacon too, he made mention of the bread of coins, I suppose with the aim that, just as he had rejected the use of unleavened bread by bringing in the custom of the Greeks, so he might also disapprove of the round shape of the same Eucharistic bread. I said that such things had nothing much to do with the matter; he should therefore, leaving aside those things which were of less importance, approach the cause itself. The gentlemen of the Senate urged the same; and they added that they had not taken it amiss at all that he had spoken the day before about the use of ordinary or leavened bread; rather, what seemed strange to them was that he had cited Gregory in his support, although in religion he really had nothing in common with him.

units.la: Igitur cum sermonem in pauca contulisset, propius tandem ad rem ipsam accessit, & pro libertate sibi concessa quæsiuit, quæ mea esset de Eucharistia sententia? Respondi, credere me cum vniuersa Ecclesia Catholica, in Eucharistiæ Sacramento, verū illud, ac naturale Christi corpus esse, quod de Virgine natum sit, ac pro nobis in mortem traditum. Atque hanc fidei meæ professionem fundaui super ipsius Christi verbis, quæ sunt: Accipite, & manducate, hoc est Corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur: Cum satis constet, non panem, sed illud idem corpus pro nobis esse traditū, quod antea natū est ex Maria Virgine. Ille, Se nequaquam id credere, aperte profitebatur. Tu ego; Ergo hic oritur contradictio, dum, quod ego constanter affirmo, tu verum esse negas. Cæterùm, quia ego partem affirmantem defendo, tu negantem; tuarum partium erit, idipsum, quod à me constitutum est, & quasi defixum, rationibus in medium prolatis oppugnare.
units.tr: So, when he had brought the discussion down to a few points, he at last came closer to the matter itself, and, using the freedom granted to him, asked what my opinion of the Eucharist was. I replied that I, with the whole Catholic Church, believe that in the Sacrament of the Eucharist is the true and natural body of Christ, which was born of the Virgin and delivered to death for us. And I founded this profession of my faith upon the very words of Christ, which are: Take, eat; this is my body, which is given for you. Since it is quite certain that it is not bread but that same body which was given for us, which was previously born of the Virgin Mary. He openly declared that he did not believe this at all. I said: "Then here a contradiction arises, since what I firmly affirm you deny to be true. But since I defend the affirmative side and you the negative, it will be your part to oppose, with reasons brought forward, the very thing that I have set down and, as it were, fixed firmly."

units.la: Postulauit deinde, vt declararem mentem meam, quo nimirum modo Christi verũ corpus in Eucharistia præsens esse crederem? Eo, inquam, quem dilucida ipsius Christi verba; Hoc est Corpus meum, quod pro vobis tradetur; in vero natiuoque sensu, secundum τὸ ἐντὸν accepta postulant. Ergo statuis, inquit, fieri transubstantiationem panis in Christi corpus? Tum ego; Imò vero; Credo fieri quod ipsa Christi verba requirunt, siue id cum Ecclesia Catholica transubstantiationem, siue transelementationem, vel conuersionem appelles.
units.tr: He then asked that I declare my mind: in what precise way did I believe the true body of Christ to be present in the Eucharist? "In the way," I said, "which the plain words of Christ themselves require: This is my body, which is given for you; they demand to be taken in their true and natural sense, according to the τὸ ἐντὸν." "So you hold," he said, "that the bread is changed by transubstantiation into the body of Christ?" Then I said: "Indeed; I believe that what the very words of Christ require takes place, whether you call it transubstantiation with the Catholic Church, or transelementation, or conversion."

units.la: Interrogauit deinde, qua virtute huiusmodi transubstantiationem fieri crederem? Dixi, virtute verborum Christi Seruatoris, quæ iuxta D. Ambrosij dictum, in hoc mysterio operatoria essent, vt efficerent, quod Christus ijs pronunciaret. Respondit ille, Si ita crederem, dissentire me à Concilio Tridentino, quod Transubstantiationem non Christi verbis, sed benedictioni tribueret. Excepi ego, nequaquam à Concilio Tridentino me dissentire, verùm idem prorsus dicere ac profiteri, quod ab eo sit definitum. Ille contra in sententia persistebat; cumque hoc vrgeret prolixius, aliâ scilicet esse meam hac de re, quàm Concilij Tridentini sententiam; Ego demum, prouoco, inquam, ad ipsius Concilij definitionem. Separas tu benedictionē à Christi verbis, quam ego iuxta mentē Concilij, cum ijs esse coniunctam affirmo. Ergo, inquit ille, tibi nō constas, cùm antea solis Christi verbis transsubstantiandi virtutem tribueris, quam nunc verbis simul ac benedictioni adscribis. Respondi: Ego verò benedictionem à verbis Institutionis nunquam separaui, quemadmodum tu fraudulenter ac veteratorie colligis, quasi dum conuersionis vim Christi verbis attribuo, ea rebenedictionem ab ijsdem seiungam; quod salsissimum esse contendo.
units.tr: He then asked by what power I believed such a transubstantiation to take place. I said, by the power of the words of Christ the Saviour, which, according to the saying of St. Ambrose, are operative in this mystery, so as to effect what Christ pronounces. He replied that if I believed so, I dissented from the Council of Trent, which ascribed transubstantiation not to the words of Christ but to the blessing. I objected that I did not dissent from the Council of Trent at all, but said exactly the same thing and professed what it had defined. He persisted in his opinion, and when he pressed this at greater length, saying that my view on this matter was other than the opinion of the Council of Trent, I at last challenged him, I said, to the definition of the Council itself. You separate the blessing from the words of Christ, whereas I affirm, according to the mind of the Council, that it is joined with them. "Therefore," he said, "you are not consistent, since before you ascribed the power of transubstantiation to the words of Christ alone, and now you ascribe it to the words together with the blessing." I replied: "I have never separated the blessing from the words of institution, as you craftily and deceitfully infer, as if, by attributing the power of conversion to the words of Christ, I thereby separated the blessing from them; which I maintain to be most absurd."

units.la: Rogauit denuo: Qua tandem igitur virtute conuersio panis in Christi corpus fieri dicerem? Respondi, virtute verborum Christi, velut antea quoque asseruerim, quibus perficiatur benedictio vel consecratio, concurrente omnipotentia Dei, quae nimirum efficiat, ut verum sit, quod ijsdem verbis pronunciatur. Repetij dictu B. Ambrosij, Christi sermonem in hisce mysteriis operatorium esse dicentis. Ad quae ille nihil amplius, nisi scio, inquit, Ambrosium id dicere in libris de Sacramentis.
units.tr: He asked again: by what power, then, did I say the conversion of the bread into the body of Christ takes place? I replied, by the power of the words of Christ, as I had already asserted, by which the blessing or consecration is completed, with the omnipotence of God concurring, which of course brings it about that what is pronounced in those words is true. I repeated the saying of St. Ambrose, who says that the word of Christ is operative in these mysteries. To this he replied nothing more than: "I know that Ambrose says this in the books On the Sacraments."

units.la: Deinde, cum paululum, quasi deliberandus, siluisset, adiecit & illud, dissentire me quoque a Pontificijs Doctoribus, quorum nonnulli, (nominabat vero Ambrosium Catharinum) non solis Christi verbis, sed toti actioni complexim, transubstantiandi virtutem tribuerent. Addere Catharinum, multa hoc modo deuitari posse incommoda, quae suboriantur, si solis Christi verbis conuersionem panis in Christi corpus effici dicas.
units.tr: Then, after he had been silent for a little while, as if he needed time to deliberate, he added also that I dissented from the Papist teachers as well, some of whom (he named Ambrose Catharinus) ascribed the power of transubstantiation not to the words of Christ alone but to the whole action taken together. He added that Catharinus said that many inconveniences which arise if you say that the conversion of the bread into the body of Christ is effected by the words of Christ alone can be avoided in this way.

units.la: Respodi, Catharinum de summa rei nequaquam dissentire a Concilio Tridentino. Ipsum credere procul dubio, quod verum Christi Iesu corpus, ac verus sanguis, per conuersionem panis ac vini, reuera in Eucharistiae Sacramento adsint; tum quod eadem conuersio benedictioni vel consecrationi fit adscribenda. Caeterum quibus verbis illa Eucharistiae consecratio praecise fiat, an ad ea praeter verba Christi, alia quoque, quae in Canone praecedunt, necessario requirantur, id a Theologis nonnullis disputari quidem; verum ea moderatione, ut substantialia tamen huius articuli nihil laedantur. Instabat ille, disceptationem hanc ad substantialia quoque pertinere. Id vero, quia simpliciter afferebat, eodem modo, ac totidem pene verbis a me negatum est.
units.tr: I replied that Catharinus does not in substance disagree with the Council of Trent at all.
