Undoubtedly he believes that the true body and true blood of Christ Jesus are really present in the Sacrament of the Eucharist through the conversion of the bread and wine, and that this conversion is to be ascribed to the blessing or consecration. As for the precise words by which that consecration of the Eucharist is effected, and whether other things besides the words of Christ, such as those that precede them in the Canon, are necessarily required, some theologians do indeed dispute this, but with such moderation that the substance of this article is not harmed. He insisted that this dispute also touched the substance. But since he asserted this without qualification, I denied it in the same way and in almost the same words.

units.la: Atque hoc loco parum abfuit, quin in aliam disputationem ingrederemur; cum ille per hanc occasionem, priuata Catholicorum quorundam Theologorum certamina mihi obijceret, in primis vero illud, quod ante Concilium Tridentinum, inter viros doctissimos Dominicum à Soto, & Ambrosium Catharinum fuisse, vtriusque scripta testantur. Ad quam ipsius obiectionem respondi: Hanc semper in Ecclesia consuetudinem hactenus viguisse, vt quoties controuersia surgeret inter doctos, quae ad Religionis substantiam pertineret, eam vtraque pars ad cognitionem Ecclesiae, ac Conciliorum generalium definitionem reijceret; Sin vero leuior esset, quàm vt Religionis fundamenta contingeret, tum salua fidei vnitate, atque Ecclesiae obedientia, ita velitatam, vt licet vtraque pars abundaret in suo sensu, neutra tamen contra Ecclesiam insurgeret. Exempli loco disceptationem adduxi, quae de mendacio quondam inter D D. Hieronymum & Augustinum exorta est; tum eam quoque, quae ante complures annos, inter quosdam Theologos, de virtute atque operatione Baptismatis in infantibus exarsit. Excepit ille; Catharinum, quamuis in Concilio Tridentino praesens fuerit, tamen post Concilij definitionem in sententia sua, de Eucharistiae consecratione perstitisse. Tum ego; si verum hoc sit, opinionem esse priuatam hominis, quae rei summam in hoc articulo, veram scilicet corporis Christi praesentiam, & transubstantiationem non euertat.
units.tr: At this point we came close to entering upon another dispute, since he used this occasion to throw at me the private quarrels of certain Catholic theologians, above all the one that, as the writings of both men testify, took place before the Council of Trent between two very learned men, Dominicus à Soto and Ambrosius Catharinus. To this objection of his I replied: in the Church it has always been the custom hitherto that whenever a controversy arises among learned men which touches the substance of religion, each side refers it to the judgment of the Church and of the general councils. But if the question is too slight to touch the foundations of religion, then, with the unity of the faith and obedience to the Church preserved, it is thrashed out in such a way that, although each side holds fast to its own opinion, neither rises up against the Church. By way of example I cited the dispute that arose long ago between the holy doctors Jerome and Augustine about lying, and also the one that flared up some years ago among certain theologians about the power and operation of baptism in infants. He took this up and said that Catharinus, although he was present at the Council of Trent, nevertheless persisted after the Council's definition in his own view about the consecration of the Eucharist. I replied: if that is true, it is the private opinion of one man, which does not overturn the sum of the matter in this article, namely the true presence of Christ's body and transubstantiation.

units.la: Demum, misso Catharino, veram ac Catholicam de Eucharistia sententiam, quam ego profes-sus eram, oppugnare coepit; idq; duplici via; partim argumentando, partim vero suo more pressius examinando verba Christi, super quibus ego meam, & Ecclesiae Catholicae sententiam fundaram.
units.tr: Finally, setting Catharinus aside, he began to attack the true and Catholic view of the Eucharist, which I had professed, and he did so in two ways: partly by arguing, and partly by examining the words of Christ, on which I had founded my own view and that of the Catholic Church, in his own manner, more closely.

units.la: Formabat igitur huiusmodi argumentum: Verum Christi corpus factum est ex Maria Virgine: At corpus Christi, quod vos in Eucharistia praesens esse dicitis, fit ex pane. Ergo non est verum Christi corpus. Ego resumpto arguproferret quicquam, interrogaui demum ego: An non Amplissimum Senatum Colonienscm, pro vero huius vrbis magistratu agnosceret? Respondit, quanquam cun ctabundus, Ita. Quaesiui denuo: An non, dum in hac vrbe vixisset, obedientia sese eidem legitimo magistratui debere, ex conscientiae obligatione putaret? Respondit, Ita, si nihil contra Deum mandaret; Alioquin Deo magis obediendum esse, quàm hominibus. Quaesiui tertio: An igitur Amplifs. huius vrbis Senatus, vnquam ipsi mandarit aliquid, quod legi charitatis, aut diuino mandato contrarium fuerit? Ad hanc quaestionem subticuit.
units.tr: He therefore framed an argument of this kind: The true body of Christ was made from the Virgin Mary; but the body of Christ, which you say is present in the Eucharist, is made from bread; therefore it is not the true body of Christ. I took up the argument again, and when he still could not bring forward anything further, I finally asked him: Did he not acknowledge the most distinguished Senate of Cologne as the true magistracy of this city? He answered, though with hesitation, "Yes." I asked again: Did he not think that, while he lived in this city, he owed obedience to this lawful magistracy from an obligation of conscience? He answered, "Yes, provided it commanded nothing against God; otherwise God must be obeyed rather than men." I asked a third time: Had the most distinguished Senate of this city ever commanded him anything contrary to the law of charity or to a divine command? To this question he kept silent.

units.la: Admonitus aliquoties à Dominis Syndicis, vt aperiret syncere mentem suam, ac causas proderet pertinacis illius silentij, quo iam aliquamdiu Magistratum elusisset; Nihil amplius protulit, nisi, proximum suum laedi, & voluntati Senatus obtemperaret: Neque vero hac in re opus esse suo indicio, posse Magistratum omnia, quae ex ipso scire vellet, aliunde resciscere. Facturum se contra conscientiam, si ea proderet, per quae deinde proximo suo detrimentum adferri sciret. Itaque rogare se, ne hac parte grauius vrgeretur.
units.tr: Many times the lords syndics urged him to disclose his mind sincerely and to state the reasons for the stubborn silence with which he had for some time been eluding the magistrate. He brought forward nothing more than this: that his neighbour was being harmed, and that he must obey the will of the Senate. Nor was there any need for his own testimony in this matter, since the magistrate could learn elsewhere everything that it wished to know from him. He would be acting against his conscience if he disclosed things through which he knew his neighbour would then suffer harm. Therefore he asked that he not be pressed more heavily on this point.

units.la: Quaesiui ego rursum: An Senatus, quem pro legitimo huius vrbis magistratu agnoscceret, ipsius quoque proximus esset, nec ne? Respondit, esse. Cur igitur, inquam, quando proximi tui rationem habere vis, magis respiciendum putas ad paucos quosdam priuatos, qui magistratui debitam obedientiam negant, quàm ad eos, quos ad Reipublicae gubernacula collocauit Dominus, quorum interest ad conseruandam pacem publicam, ea scire, quae à te quaeruntur.
units.tr: I asked him again: Was the Senate, which he acknowledged as the lawful magistracy of this city, also his neighbour or not? He answered that it was. "Why then," I said, "when you wish to have regard for your neighbour, do you think one should give more heed to a few private individuals who deny the obedience owed to the magistracy, than to those whom the Lord has placed at the helm of the commonwealth, whose concern it is, for the preservation of public peace, to know the things you are being asked about?"

units.la: Respondit ille, Non pendere Reipublicae salutem ex hoc negocio, neq; laedi Senatus auctoritatem, si non prodat ea, quae Magistratus ipsius indicio scire vellet. Imò vero, inquam, laeditur. Antea fassus es, obedientia te debere Magistratui huius vrbis, nisi quid contra Deum mandet. Igitur vel obtemperandum nunc est, vel certè demon-strandū, mandari aliquid, quod cum diuina lege pugnet: iam & salus Reipublicæ læditur, quando nimirum occultantur ea consilia, ęque actiones, quibus perturbari pacem publicam, ac seditiones excitari, aliarum vrbium exempla testantur: Et tu quidem tacitè Senatum huius vrbis accusas impietatis atq; tyrannidis, impiettatis quidem, quod eam Religionem foueat, quam tu cum Idololatria coniunctam esse sentis, quæ summa est, & omnium maxima impietas; tyrannidis vero, quod Edicta sanciat, quibus Idololatria & impietas stabiliatur, ac subditi, ab ea alieni, per vim opprimantur; quæ, quin germana tyrannis sit, negari non potest.
units.tr: He replied that the safety of the commonwealth did not depend on this affair, nor was the authority of the Senate harmed if he did not disclose what the magistrate wished to know from his own testimony. "On the contrary," I said, "it is harmed. You admitted earlier that you owe obedience to the magistracy of this city, unless it commands something against God. So either you must now obey, or you must clearly demonstrate that something is being commanded which conflicts with divine law. And the safety of the commonwealth is harmed when those plans and actions are concealed by which, as the examples of other cities attest, public peace is disturbed and seditions are stirred up. And you, in effect, are silently accusing the Senate of this city of impiety and tyranny: of impiety, because it fosters the religion which you judge to be joined with idolatry, which is the greatest and worst of all impieties; and of tyranny, because it sanctions edicts by which idolatry and impiety are established, and subjects who are alien to it are oppressed by force. That this is genuine tyranny cannot be denied."

units.la: Excepit ille, Nequaquam se tyrannidis aut impietatis accusare Senatum. Posse fieri, vt magistratus ex sinistra persuasione iudicio nonnunquam aberret, dum hæc aut illa, præter æquitatis rationem statuit: Quemadmodum euenerit Constantino Magno Imperatori, quem Arriani quondam in Athanasium vehementer concitarint. Neque vero huiusmodi lapsus eorum, qui in magistratu sunt, impietatis ac tyrannidis nomine censendos esse, quando non accedit habitus.
units.tr: He answered that he did not accuse the Senate of tyranny or impiety at all. It can happen that a magistrate, through a mistaken persuasion, sometimes errs in judgment, when he decides this or that contrary to the reason of equity, as happened to the Emperor Constantine the Great, whom the Arians once stirred up greatly against Athanasius. Nor should such lapses of those who hold office be counted under the name of impiety or tyranny, when there is no settled habit of that kind.

units.la: Ego, cùm Constantini mentionem faceret, narraui ex historia Ecclesiastica, qua strophapissimus Imperator, cùm magno concordiæ farciendæ studio flagraret, ab Arrio circumuentus, in Arrianos aliquando propensior factus fit. Quam historiam hoc loco brevitatis studio omitto. Subiunxi deinde, Eum hoc exemplo non sufficienter ab huius vrbis Senatu tyrannidis atque impietatis crimè remouere: Quandoquidem omnia, quæ Senatus hac parte contra Sectarios ageret, non temerè, vel ex informatione sinistra, sed maturo consilio, ac deliberato ageret; imò, (quemadmodum Syndici suggerebant) hanc tuendæ Religionis Catholicæ rationem, à pijs maioribus per manus traditam haberet: Vt adeò hæ actiones, proeul dubio, ex habitu quodam administrandæ Reipu-blicæ proficiscantur. Itaq; non esse, quod imprudentem Constantini credulitatem ac lapsum, cum maturis huius magistratus actionibus comparet.
units.tr: When he made mention of Constantine, I related from ecclesiastical history how that most crafty emperor, though burning with a great zeal for restoring concord, was won over by Arius and at one time became more inclined toward the Arians. I omit that story here for the sake of brevity. I then added that by this example he did not sufficiently clear the Senate of this city of the charge of tyranny and impiety, since everything the Senate did in this matter against the sectarians was done not rashly or on the basis of false information, but with mature counsel and deliberation; indeed, as the syndics pointed out, it had received this manner of defending the Catholic religion handed down by hand from its pious forefathers. So these actions undoubtedly proceed from a settled habit of governing the commonwealth. Therefore there is no reason for him to compare the imprudent credulity and lapse of Constantine with the mature actions of this magistracy.

units.la: Hortabatur cum inter conferendum Doctor Hack-steinius, vt nunc proferret D. Cypriani sententiam, quam ad causæ suæ defensionem, in examine superiori protu-lisset; Vrgebam idem & ego. Verùm ille perpetuò, quic-quid diceremus, tergiuersatus est, nec vnquā vel D. Cy-priani nomen appellare voluit. Demum ego, quia nihil afferebat, Cyprianus, inquā, nulla in re tibi suffragatur. Fuit is Episcopus Catholicus, & causam egit coram ma-gistratu gentili. Si quid eo rerum statu dixit, id ad te ni-hil pertinet: Quando inter D. Cyprianum, & te; tum in-ter Senatum huius vrbis Catholicum, & magistratum illum gentilem, nulla penitus est comparatio.
units.tr: Meanwhile, in the course of the conference, Doctor Hackstein urged him to now bring forward the opinion of St. Cyprian, which he had put forward in the earlier examination in defence of his cause. I pressed the same request. But he kept evading whatever we said, and never once wished even to name St. Cyprian. At last, since he offered nothing, I said: "Cyprian, I tell you, supports you in nothing. He was a Catholic bishop, and he pleaded his cause before a pagan magistrate. If he said anything in that state of affairs, it has nothing to do with you. Between St. Cyprian and you, and between the Catholic Senate of this city and that pagan magistrate, there is no comparison at all."

units.la: Vrgebant eum, cum ita perpetuò restitaret, alijs quoq; rationibus, Consul Hardenradius & Syndici. Quærebāt, cur ad eum modum tergiuersaretur? Quid huiusmodi subterfugijs Amplissimum Senatum ac seipsum quoque distineret? Ipsum fateri hoc pertinaci silentio, quod male fecerit. Nam si bene se fecisse putaret, cur tantopere de fugeret lucem? Cur actiones suas secretas esse vellet, eas-que tanto studio celare contenderet? Imo quo magis hac parte subterfugeret, eo graviores habere causas Senatū, vt consilia contra Reipublicæ salutem in ijs conuenticu lis agitata suspicetur. Neque vero eam suspicionem om-nino vanam esse, quando per huiusmodi clancularios conuentus, insignes nonnunquam Respublicæ penitus euersæ sint. Hæc, & id genus alia cùm obijcerentur, ille ni hil admodum respondit; nisi quod diceret, se suos audi-tores semper ad obedientiam, ac pacem colendam hor-tatum fuisse, neque hoc spectasse vnquam, vt seditionem concitaret.
units.tr: Since he kept resisting in this way, Consul Hardenradius and the syndics pressed him with other arguments as well. They asked why he evaded in such a manner. Why did he distract the most distinguished Senate and himself with such subterfuges? By this stubborn silence he was confessing that he had done wrong. For if he thought he had acted well, why did he so greatly shun the light? Why did he want his actions to be secret, and strive so eagerly to hide them? Indeed, the more he evaded on this point, the stronger the grounds the Senate had for suspecting that plans against the safety of the commonwealth were being discussed in those conventicles. Nor was that suspicion altogether groundless, since commonwealths have sometimes been utterly overthrown through such secret little gatherings. When these and similar things were put to him, he answered hardly anything, except that he had always exhorted his hearers to obedience and to cultivating peace, and had never aimed at stirring up sedition.

units.la: Ad quàm vocem Dominus Hardenradius Consul,
units.tr: At this remark Lord Hardenradius, the consul,

units.la: scilicet,inquit,id fatis experimur in vestri sodalitij homi nibus,qui ita fe gerunt erga Senatum, vt omnia illorum inobedientiam spirare videantur: Vnde liquido con- stare potest,quid agatur in vestris coetibus, & qualia in ijs consilia pertractentur:In quibus proculdubio inter alia Senatum falsò, & contra conscientiam traducitis, quasi Christo Seruatori praecludat viam, & Idololatriam in hac vrbe foueat;vt scilicet causam habere videatur,cùm sese magistratui ad eum modum opponunt. Ad quae ille paululum submurmuras,nihil amplius respondit,quàm quod antea quoque dixerat, quod nunquam publi- cos excitare motus in animo habuerit.
units.tr: "Indeed," he said, "we experience this in the men of your fellowship, who conduct themselves toward the Senate in such a way that all of them seem to breathe disobedience. From this it can be clearly established what is being done at your meetings and what kinds of plans are discussed there. In them, without doubt, among other things, you falsely and against your own conscience slander the Senate, as if it blocks the way to Christ the Saviour and fosters idolatry in this city, so that you may seem to have a cause when you set yourselves against the magistrate in this manner." To this he muttered briefly and replied nothing more than what he had said before, that he had never intended to stir up public disturbances.

units.la: Tum ego,vt hoc,inquam,concedatur,quod tu conci- tare auditores tuos contra Senatum non intenderis, cer- tum est tamen experientia magistra, vbicunque contra magistratus Edicta, huiusmodi secreti conuentus à ve- ftris habiti sunt,ibi semper perturbationem publicae pa- cis, ac magistratus oppressionem demum subsecutam. Quod exempla florentissimarum vrbium in vicino Bel- gio fatis testificantur. Addidit Dominus Confulb Suder- mannus exemplum vrbis Aquisgranensis, quae eadem via in magnas difficultates coniecta fit. Et in Belgio quidem, (inquit Dominus Consul) voluistis omnes, vti vobis vi- debatur, à iugo Romani Pontificis eximere. At quid fa- ctum est? Scilicet vestris conatibus multò profundius, quàm vnquam antea,Belgas in Pontificis Romani feru- tutem coniecistis.Itaque nihil valent conatus vestri, ne- que tolerari debent,aut possunt. Admonemur ex omni parte,multas in vrbe nostra Sectas pullulare; neceffariū esse,vt diligenter prospiciamus rebus nostris, ne quid ab ijs detrimenti Reipublicae nostrae inferatur.
units.tr: Then I said: "Granted that you did not intend to stir up your hearers against the Senate. Experience, the teacher of all things, nonetheless makes it certain that wherever secret assemblies of this kind have been held by your people against the edicts of the magistrate, there a disturbance of public peace and eventually the oppression of the magistrate have always followed. The examples of the most flourishing cities in the nearby Netherlands bear ample witness to this." Lord Consul Sudermannus added the example of the city of Aachen, which was thrown into great difficulties by the same route. "And in the Netherlands indeed," said the Lord Consul, "you all wished, as seemed good to you, to free yourselves from the yoke of the Roman Pontiff. But what happened? Clearly, by your efforts you have cast the Belgians into the servitude of the Roman Pontiff far more deeply than ever before. Therefore your efforts are worth nothing, and cannot or should not be tolerated. We are warned from every side that many sects are sprouting up in our city, and it is necessary that we look carefully to our affairs, lest any harm come to our commonwealth from them."

units.la: Ad haec verba ego,rogata venia,interlocutus,quod de Sectis dicitur,inquam,id verisimum est; quemadmodū fatis experimur,qui curam animarum in hac vrbe geri- mus.Lutherani rariores sunt,& deficiunt indies;quidam illoillorum ad nos redeunt, quidam vero paulatim in naf- fam pertrahuntur à Caluinistis; Qui numero superat Lu- theranos. Iam & Svvenckfeldiani quoq; incrementa su- munt. Anabaptistarum vero gens etiam augetur. Quin & Domus charitatis, quæ ex Anabaptiftarū fecibus, tan- quam riuus quidam, promanauit, pedé in hac vrbe iam- pridem fixit.
units.tr: To these words I replied, with leave asked: "As to what is said about sects, I say that it is very true, as we experience well enough who have the care of souls in this city. The Lutherans are fewer and are dwindling day by day; some of them return to us, while others are gradually drawn into the net by the Calvinists, who now outnumber the Lutherans. Already the Schwenckfeldians too are increasing. The race of Anabaptists is indeed growing as well. Moreover, the House of Charity, which flowed out of the dregs of the Anabaptists like a certain stream, has long since set foot in this city."

units.la: Excepit Ioannes Lennepius, & Currum quoque ster- corum, (id nouum quoddam Libertinorum genus est) huc aduectum dixit, quemadmodum à fide dignis acce- perit. Tum Dominus Sudermannus Consul, Bene, in- quit, Si igitur nos quemlibet pro libitu suo agere patere- mur, & demum aliqua fieret in Religione mutatio; quid Cæsarea Maiestas, quid Rex Hispaniarum, quid Ponti- sex, quid Iuliacensis Princeps, vicinus nostrer dicturus es- set? Procul dubio hoc pacto ciuitas nostra in plurima pe- ricula conijceretur. Hæc à Domino Consule cum vehe- mentia quadam dicebantur; Ille vero omnia silentio transmittebat.
units.tr: John Lennep took up the matter and said that a cart of dung (this is a new kind of Libertine) had also been brought here, as he had heard from trustworthy sources. Then Lord Sudermann, the consul, said: "Good. If we were to allow each person to act as he pleases, and some change in religion were eventually made, what would his Imperial Majesty, what would the King of Spain, what would the Pope, what would the Prince of Jülich, our neighbour, say? Without doubt in this way our city would be thrown into the greatest dangers." These things were said by the Lord Consul with a certain vehemence; but he let everything pass in silence.

units.la: Inter colloquendū, cum obijceretur, huiusmodi clan- cularios conuentus semper motus publicos, ac seditio- nes subditorum contra magistratum peperisse; atque ille nonnihil obmurmuraret, quæsiuit ex illo Ioannes Len- nepius, vt vel vnicum proferret exemplum, vbi secus ac- cidisset? Ad quam vocem, oculis in finum defixus, peni- tus obmutuit. Tum ego, quid igitur, inquam, magistratus huius vrbis aliud à vobis exspectare potest, quàm vt, qd' alibi per hoc medium perpetraftis, idem & hic quoque conemini paulatim, vbi satis virium accreuerit?
units.tr: During the conversation, when it was objected that such secret assemblies had always produced public disturbances and seditions of subjects against the magistrate, and he was muttering something in protest, John Lennep asked him to produce even one single example where things had turned out otherwise. At this, with his eyes fixed on his lap, he fell completely silent. Then I said: "What else, then, can the magistrate of this city expect from you, than that you try here too, gradually, once you have gathered enough strength, what you have carried out elsewhere by this same means?"

units.la: Intuli quoque sermonem de ipsius vocatione; cuius rei occasio fuit, quod conscientiam suam informatam esse Dei verbo diceret. Quæsiui, qua conscientia ipse, cum nec à Deo vocatus esset, nec ab hominibus, qui potestatem eius rei haberet, huius vrbis ciuibus subrepsisset? Nō est, inquam, in hac celebri ac populosa vrbe, vel vnus homo, qui mo, qui non habeat suum Pastorem, per legitimæ vocationis viam à Deo constitutū: Inter quos & ego mequeque, licet omnium infimum, connumero. Nobis igitur, qui Pastores in hac vrbe sumus, creditæ sunt, ac commissæ oues huius gregis, quibus diuini verbi, ac Sacramentorum pabulum hactenus ministrauimus: Eam ad rem, per Dei gratiam, tua, tuique similium opera non indigemus. Quomodo igitur in iudicio Dei facinus hoc defendes, quod, cum peregrinus sis, nec legitimè vocatus, oues nostras dissipas, easque contra Magistratus Edicta in angulum conuocatas, à nobis auertis? Tu quod nos, qui legitimi Pastores sumus, in conuenticulis istis traducis, quin absentes calumnijs ac mendacijs oneras, & nec admonitos, nec auditos condemnas? Quod si nos, qui Coloniæ curam animarum gerimus, non recte fungeremur officio nostro, tuarum partium fuisset, nos admonere prius, & redarguere, quàm ad eum modum, contra Senatus voluntatem, prohibitos conuentus agere. Hæc ego; Ille vero ne verbo quidem vnquam conatus est, vel nostra vocationem oppugnare, vel tueri suam.
units.tr: I also brought up the subject of his own calling. The occasion for this was that he said his conscience was informed by the Word of God. I asked by what conscience he himself, since he had been called neither by God nor by men who had the authority in this matter, had crept in among the citizens of this city. "There is not," I said, "in this famous and populous city, even one single person who does not have his own minister, appointed by God through the lawful way of calling. Among these I count myself too, though the lowest of all. Therefore to us, who are the ministers in this city, the sheep of this flock have been entrusted and committed, and to them we have hitherto supplied the food of the divine Word and the Sacraments. For this purpose, by the grace of God, we do not need your work or the work of those like you. How, then, will you defend before God's judgment this crime, that, though a stranger and not lawfully called, you scatter our sheep and, contrary to the edicts of the magistrate, lead them away from us, gathered into corners? And why do you slander us, who are the lawful ministers, in these little conventicles, and burden us with lies and calumnies while we are absent, and condemn us without having admonished or heard us? If we who have the care of souls in Cologne did not discharge our duty rightly, it would have been your task to admonish and rebuke us first, rather than to hold forbidden assemblies in this way, against the will of the Senate." These were my words. He, however, never even once tried, by a single word, either to attack our calling or to defend his own.

units.la: Adiunxi demum & illud; Ipsos aduersarios non ferre, vt quisquam inter eos huiusmodi furtiuos conuentus agat, vel secreto docendi auctoritatem vsurpet. Et Lutherus quidem, inquam, consulit, vt tenebriones illi, qui passim repunt per domos, & contra magistratus voluntatem, inscijs veris pastoribus, clam aliud doctrinæ genus spargunt, quàm publicè viget, non tolerentur vllo pacto; imò si desistere nolint, demum magistro Hansoni (quo nomine carnificem designat) commendentur. Atque hoc non tantum intelligi vult de seductoribus, qui prauis dogmatibus simpliciorum animos imbuunt, verùm de ijs quoque, qui veri doctores sunt, ac doctrinam Euangelij profitetur: Hos, inquit, tametsi vel Angeli sint, vel meri Gabrieles de cœlo, tamē, si contra vtriusq; magistratus, Ecclesiastici nimirum, & ciuilis, voluntatem clam docere instituant, coercendos esse ac puniendos; Etiam cum inter Papistas, vt ipse loquitur, aut haereticos, huiusmodi quid tentare volunt. Quae ratio a Lutheranis etiam hactenus observatur: Quemadmodum demonstrari potest exemplis Principum, ac urbium quarundam in Imper-io, quae publice Lutheri doctrinam, sub Augustanae Confessionis nomine, profitentur. Haec omnia ille, quemadmodum & superiora, silentio transmittebat.
units.tr: Finally I added this also: that your own adversaries do not allow anyone among them to hold such furtive meetings or to assume the authority of teaching in secret. "And Luther indeed," I said, "advises that those shadowy fellows who crawl about everywhere through houses, and against the will of the magistrate, without the knowledge of the true ministers, secretly spread a kind of teaching other than what is publicly in force, should on no account be tolerated; indeed, if they refuse to desist, they should at last be handed over to master Hanson (by which name he designates the executioner). And he wishes this to be understood not only of seducers, who imbue the minds of simple people with depraved doctrines, but also of those who are true teachers and profess the doctrine of the Gospel. These, he says, even if they are angels or mere Gabriels from heaven, nevertheless, if they set about teaching secretly against the will of both magistrates, the ecclesiastical and the civil, must be restrained and punished; and this holds even when they want to attempt such a thing among Papists, or heretics, as he himself puts it. This principle has also been observed by the Lutherans up to now, as can be shown by the examples of princes and certain cities in the Empire that publicly profess Luther's doctrine under the name of the Augsburg Confession." He let all these things pass in silence, as he had the earlier ones.

units.la: Sub finem iterum sermo incidit de Edictis Magistratus nostri, deque rebus iis, quas ipsius indicio scire vellet Amplissimus huius urbis Senatus, quae tacite, si in sententia sua persistat, tyrannidis ab eo accusari, Doctor Crantius aperte demonstrabat: Ad cuius verba ille, rugata nonnihil fronte, quam amarulente, inquit, de hac re loquitur D. Doctor: Nunquam ego tyrannidis Amplissimum Senatu insimulavi. Eam hominis insolentiam indigne ferens Doctor Crantius, humaniter tamen respondit, Inique sibi amarulentiam obijci: Non hoc se dicere, quod expressis verbis Senatum tyrannidis accusarit; Verum id ex ipsius actionibus & verbis necessario sequi: Quam rem idem Doctor Cratius ad eum modum declarauit, vt ille contra ne mutire quidem potuerit.
units.tr: Near the end the conversation turned again to the edicts of our magistrate, and to those matters which the most distinguished Senate of this city would wish to know from his own report, and which Doctor Crantius openly showed would be charged against him as tyranny, if he persisted in his opinion. At these words he, his brow somewhat wrinkled, said bitterly: "The Doctor speaks of this matter bitterly. I never accused the most distinguished Senate of tyranny." Doctor Crantius, taking this insolence ill, nevertheless answered calmly that bitterness was unjustly imputed to him: he did not say that he had expressly accused the Senate of tyranny, but that this necessarily follows from his actions and words. Doctor Crantius explained this matter in such a way that the other could not even mutter a word against it.

units.la: Obieci ego denuo & illud, (quod antea quoque per occasionem attigeram) Concionatores istius partis, de quorum numero & ipse sit, in huiusmodi conuenticulis, graui admodum iniuria nos afficere; cum absentes acerbe ac contumeliose traducant, & Religionem Catholicam, quam profitemur, velut impiam, & foeda cū Idololatria coniunctā, abominandū in modū detestentur: Quod tametsi iam expresse fateri nolit, nequeat tamē inficiari, nisi conscientiae testimonio reclamare velit. Ea vero criminatione, non ad nos pertinere tātum, verum nostros etiam, eosdemque ipsorum maiores, à quibus Catholica Religio ad nos peruenerit, simul nobiscum inuoluerc. Et quia nobis absentibus tam atrox iniuria inferatur, vt adeo adeò nostram, maiorumque nostrorum innocentiam, aduersus huiusmodi calūnias ac mendacia tueri nequeamus, rem totam quidem Deo, iusto iniuriarum omniū vindici, committendam esse; cui proculdubio grauissimam aliquādo rationem hoc nomine sint reddituti.
units.tr: I again objected also that (as I had touched on earlier in passing) the preachers of that party, of whose number he himself is, treat us with very grave injury in these little assemblies, since they cruelly and insultingly slander us in our absence, and abominably denounce the Catholic religion which we profess as impious and joined with foul idolatry. Although he is now unwilling to admit this openly, he cannot deny it unless he wishes to contradict the testimony of his own conscience. And by this accusation they involve not only us but also our forebears, and even their own, from whom the Catholic religion has come down to us, together with us. And since such an atrocious injury is inflicted on us in our absence, so that we cannot defend our innocence and that of our forebears against such calumnies and lies, the whole matter must indeed be committed to God, the just avenger of all injuries; to whom, without doubt, they will one day render a most grievous account of this.

units.la: Hæc ego, & id genus alia quædam in eandem sententiam cum dicerem, ille se nonnihil repressit: Tādem vero, Non dissiteor, inquit, Religionem vestram, tanquam erroneam, à nobis reprehendi: Quod si hac parte in errore sum, instrui cupio; præbebo me docilem, tu te præbeas doctorem. Respōdi, Nescire me, an cum in finem à Magistratu vocatus sim. Præterea tempus colloquendo iam effluxisse, (imminebat enim vespera) vt si in hunc campum ingrediendum sit, id nunc, vel hoc etiam nomine fieri non possit. Iam & alios esse me doctiores, tum in facultate Theologica, tum inter Pastores quoque confratres meos, qui commodius ac melius agere doctorum partes, ac errantem instituere possint. Quanquam ego quidem non existimem, quod hac parte candidè, atque ex animo loquatur. Si enim ea mente esset, vt syncerè cuperet instrui, potuisse iampridem illum toto illo tempore, quo hic cōmoratus fuerit, vel me, vel alium quempiam è Pastoribus hoc nomine conuenire. Tādem à præsentibus Dominis humaniter & amicè monebatur, vt deliberaret secum in diem crastinum, ac posita demum per uicacia, legitimè ad interrogata responderet. Ille ad hæc suo more tergiuersari, ac prætendere cōscientiam suam, & legem charitatis de non lædendo proximo: Mea conscientia, inquit, hoc non fert; alius fortasse posset facere, ego non possum. Deinde repetita protestatione, qua initio quoque fuerat vsus, excusauit timiditatem suam; atq; ita hac vice dimissus est, & reductus in carcerem.
units.tr: I was saying these things and others of the same sort to the same effect, when he restrained himself somewhat. At last he said: "I do not deny that your religion is criticised by us as erroneous. If I am in error on this point, I wish to be instructed. I will show myself teachable; you show yourself a teacher." I replied that I did not know whether I had been summoned by the magistrate for this purpose. Moreover, the time for conversation had already run out, since evening was coming on, so that if we were to enter upon this field, it could not now be done, not even for this reason. There were also others more learned than I, both in theology and among my fellow ministers, who could play the part of teachers more fittingly and effectively and instruct one who is in error. Yet I did not think he was speaking candidly and from the heart on this point. For if he were minded to be sincerely instructed, he could have asked me, or some other minister, to meet him for this purpose at any time during the whole period he had stayed here. Finally, the gentlemen present urged him kindly and in a friendly way to consider the matter with himself until the next day, and then, once the conditions had been set out, to answer the questions put to him properly. To this he responded in his usual manner, evading and pleading his conscience and the law of charity, not to injure one's neighbour: "My conscience does not allow it," he said; "another man perhaps could do it, but I cannot." Then, repeating the protest he had also used at the beginning, he excused his timidity, and so he was dismissed for this occasion and led back to prison.

units.la: Postea visum quibusdam fuit, non futurum abs re, (modò de voluntate Amplißimi Senatus fieri possit) si de vno atque altero Religionis capite, amica cum illo collatio instituere tur; praesertim, quia se docile futurū promisisset. Dixi ego, si publico nomine Magistratus, atq; ex professo cum homine sit agendū, necessariū esse, vt id fiat ordinaria via, de consilio Theologicæ facultatis; vel per Dominum Suffraganeum, qui vnum atque alterum è Pastoribus assumere posset. Exi stimatum fuit, satius esse, vt quemadmodum iam factum sit, obiter atque priuatim, per modum amicæ collocutionis tentetur, an reipsa præstare velit, quod verbis prę se tulisset. Ad eam igitur rem ego quidem operam meam detuli; verum hac conditione, vt quicquid huius futurum esset, id fieret præsentibus viris aliquot fide dignis: propterea quod non semel talium hominum calumnias ac mendacia post huiusmodi priuatas collocutiones, expertus eram. Placuit igitur, vt, si ea res Amplissimo Senatui non displiceret, postridie ad horam secundam pomeridianam, eodem loco rursum conuenieremus. Atque hæc fere primi diei collatio fuit.
units.tr: Afterwards it seemed good to some that it would not be out of place (provided it could be done with the will of the most distinguished Senate) to hold a friendly conference with him on one or two heads of religion, especially since he had promised he would be teachable. I said that if the matter were to be handled in the name of the magistrate and openly with the man, it was necessary that it be done in the ordinary way, with the advice of the theological faculty, or through the Suffragan, who could take one or two of the ministers to assist him. It was judged better, as has now been done, to try informally and privately, by way of a friendly discussion, whether he is really willing to do what he had professed in words. I therefore offered my services for this purpose, but on this condition: that whatever came of it should take place in the presence of several trustworthy men, because I had more than once experienced the slanders and lies of such men after private conversations of this kind. It was agreed, then, that if the Most Distinguished Senate did not object, we should meet again in the same place the next day at two o'clock in the afternoon. And this was more or less the conference of the first day.

units.la: ALTERIVS DIEI COLLATIO.
units.tr: THE CONFERENCE OF THE SECOND DAY.

units.la: POstridie, qui fuit vndecimus Aprilis, hora secunda pomeridiana, vti constitutum erat, ad carcerem rediij. Conuenerunt eò, qui pridie adfuerāt; (excepto Ioanne Lennepio) & præter eos Balthasar à Berchem, Theodorus Plòger, Michaël Ludgen, Hermannus à VViddig, Senatorij ordinis viri; tum Anthonius Rinck, patritius Coloniensis. Vocatus iterum est Ioannes Badius Minister Caluinianus; Cumque suo loco consedisset, Doctor Hackfteinius inter cætera, quæ breuiter illi proposuit Amplissimi Senatus nomine, illa quoque verba repetijt, quod pridie docilem se fore promisisset, si ego doctoris partes agerem. Existimatum igitur fuisse, non futurum abs re, si fieret eius rei periculum. In eum itaq; finem me, Pastorem D. Cuniberti, nunc denuo vocatum adesse, vt placida scilicet, atque amica inter nos de Religione collatio institueretur.
units.tr: On the next day, which was the eleventh of April, at two o'clock in the afternoon, as had been arranged, I returned to the prison. Those who had been present the day before gathered there (except John Lennep), and besides them Balthasar von Berchem, Theodor Pleger, Michael Ludgen, Hermann von Widdig, men of the senatorial order, and also Anthony Rinck, a patrician of Cologne. John Badius, the Calvinist minister, was summoned again; and when he had taken his seat, Doctor Hackfteinius, among other things he briefly put to him in the name of the most distinguished Senate, repeated also those words, that he had promised to be teachable if I were to play the part of teacher. It was therefore judged that it would not be out of place to try the matter. To this end I, the minister of St Cunibert's, now summoned again, am present, so that a calm and friendly conference about religion may be held between us.

units.la: Ego deinde Badium hortabar, vt eam sumeret in colloquendo libertatem, qua vsurus esset, si vel Heidelbergæ mecum ageret, vel alibi in medio Palatinatu. Faciebā illi quoque potestatē deligendi, quam vellet, materiam, de qua collatione instituì cuperet. Demū, vt inter colloquendū vtras vellet, siue opponētis, siue respondentis partes agere, id illi quoq; liberum relinquebā. Ille deligebat Articulum de Cœna Domini. Rogaui, Quia multiplex esset de hoc Articulo controuersia, quam istius materiæ partem inter nos disceptari cuperet? Respondit eam, in qua de veritate quæritur, vt quæ primaria esset. Dixi, Magni quoque momenti disputationem esse de Sacrificio, ac Sacerdotio; cur non illam desumeret? Badius ad hæc, Placere nunc priorem, quam dixerit; alterā illam postea quoque discutiendam fumi posse. Itaq; ego hac in parte ipsius voluntati acquieui.
units.tr: I then urged Badius to take the same freedom in conversation that he would use if he were dealing with me at Heidelberg, or elsewhere in the midst of the Palatinate. I also gave him the power to choose whatever subject he wished for the conference. Finally, I left it to him to take whichever part he wished during the discussion, that of opponent or that of respondent. He chose the article on the Lord's Supper. I asked him, since there was much controversy over this article, which part of this subject he wished us to dispute. He replied that it should be the part concerning the question of truth, as this was the primary one. I said that the dispute about sacrifice and priesthood was also of great importance; why not take that one? To this Badius replied that he preferred the first subject he had named, and that the other could be discussed afterwards. So in this matter I yielded to his wish.

units.la: Et principio quidē à me petijt, vt se Dominis præsenti bus excusarem; quos diebus superioribus dicto quodam de pane Eucharistico videretur offendisse. Cùm enim de Eucharistia sermo per occasionem incidesit, eos nō admodum æquis animis accepisse, quod veteres communi pane, ad hoc mysterium peragendum vsos fuisse dixerit.
units.tr: And at the beginning he asked me to excuse him to the gentlemen present, whom he seemed to have offended in the previous days by a certain remark about the Eucharistic bread. For when the Eucharist came up in conversation by chance, they had not received very calmly his statement that the ancients used common bread to perform this mystery.

units.la: Respondi, Non existimare me, quod eo dicto quenquam offenderit; quando Catholicorum omnium consensu satis constet, panem illum, qui ad altare defertur, antequam consecretur, omnino communem esse: Post consecrationem verò iam non amplius dici, vel esse communem panem, sed verum Christi corpus.
units.tr: I replied that I did not think anyone had been offended by that remark, since it is sufficiently established by the agreement of all Catholics that the bread brought to the altar, before it is consecrated, is indeed common bread; but after consecration it is no longer called or regarded as common bread, but the true body of Christ.

units.la: Ille sermone continuato, ad confirmandum ea, quæ dixerat, Græcorum etiam morem adducebat, quos notum est, vti pane fermentato, cùm sacra mysteria peragunt. Ex quibus verbis intelligebam, quod communis panis nomine, cuiuscunq; generis panem domesticum intelintelligeret, siue fermentatus is sit, siue non sit. Respon-debam igitur ad exemplum Græcorum; Aliam esse consuetudinem Ecclesiæ Latinæ, quæ scilicet azymo pane ad sacrificium peragendum vteretur: Eam vero consuetudinem, procul dubio in ipsius Christi Seruatoris exemplo fundari, quem satis certè cõstaret azymo pane vsum, cùm hoc mysterium instituisset; quando Iudæis eo tempore, quo Paschalem agnum comedebant, fermētatum panem in domibus habere non licuerit.
units.tr: Continuing his speech to confirm what he had said, he also cited the custom of the Greeks, who, as is well known, use leavened bread when they celebrate the sacred mysteries. From these words I understood that by "common bread" he meant the household bread of any kind, whether leavened or not. I replied, following the example of the Greeks, that the Latin Church has a different custom, namely that it uses unleavened bread to perform the sacrifice; and that this custom is undoubtedly founded on the example of Christ the Saviour himself, who is certainly known to have used unleavened bread when he instituted this mystery, since at the time when the Jews ate the Passover lamb it was not lawful for them to have leavened bread in their houses.

units.la: Excepit rursum, & nominato D. Gregorio, tum Paulo quoque Diacono, de pane nummulario mentionem intulit, in eũ finem, opinor, vt quemadmodum azymi panis vsum, adducto Græcorum more, arroserat, ita formā quoque rotundam eiusdem Eucharistici panis improbaret. Dixi, talia nihil admodū facere ad rem; præstare igitur, vt missis ijs, quæ minutiora essent, ad causam ipsam aggrederetur. Idem hortabātur Domini Syndici; qui & illud adijciebant, Se nequaquam indignè tulisse, quod pridie de communis aut fermentati panis vsu dixerit; verum id sibi mirum accidisse potius, quod citauerit pro se D. Gregorium, cum quo reuera tamen in Religione nihil haberet commune.
units.tr: He took up the argument again, and after naming Gregory, and then also Paul the Deacon, he mentioned coin-shaped bread, I suppose with the aim that, just as he had criticised the use of unleavened bread by appealing to the Greek custom, so he might likewise disapprove of the round shape of the same Eucharistic bread. I said that such things had nothing much to do with the matter; he should therefore set aside these minor points and come to the cause itself. The gentlemen Syndics urged the same thing, and they added that they had not taken it amiss at all that on the previous day he had spoken about the use of common or leavened bread; rather, what seemed strange to them was that he had cited Gregory in his support, though in religion he really had nothing in common with him.

units.la: Igitur cum sermonem in pauca contulisset, propius tandem ad rem ipsam accessit, & pro libertate sibi concessa quæsiuit, quæ mea esset de Eucharistia sententia? Respondi, credere me cum vniuersa Ecclesia Catholica, in Eucharistiæ Sacramento, verū illud, ac naturale Christi corpus esse, quod de Virgine natum sit, ac pro nobis in mortem traditum. Atque hanc fidei meæ professionem fundaui super ipsius Christi verbis, quæ sunt: Accipite, & manducate, hoc est Corpus meum, quod pro vobis tradetur: Cum satis constet, non panem, sed illud idem corpus pro nobis esse traditū, quod antea natū est ex Maria Virgine. Ille, Se nequaquā id credere, aperte profitebatur. Tu ergo; Ergo hic oritur contradictio, dum, quod ego constanter stanter affirmo, tu verum esse negas. Cæterum, quia ego partem affirmantem defendo, tu negantem; tuarum partium erit, idipsum, quod à me constitutum est, & quasi defixum, rationibus in medium prolatis oppugnare.
units.tr: So when he had reduced the discussion to a few points, he at last came closer to the matter itself, and, using the freedom granted to him, asked what my view of the Eucharist was. I replied that I, with the whole Catholic Church, believe that in the sacrament of the Eucharist there is the true and natural body of Christ, the body that was born of the Virgin and delivered to death for us. I based this profession of my faith upon the very words of Christ, which are: Take, eat; this is my body, which is given for you. Since it is quite clear that it was not bread but that same body, which was born of the Virgin Mary before, that was given for us. He openly declared that he did not believe this. You, then, said I: here arises a contradiction, since what I firmly affirm, you deny to be true. But since I defend the affirmative side and you the negative, it will be your part to attack, with arguments brought forward, the very thing that has been laid down by me and, as it were, fixed firm.

units.la: Postulauit deinde, vt declararem mentem meam, quo nimirum modo Christi verũ corpus in Eucharistia præsens esse crederem? Eo, inquam, quem dilucida ipsius Christi verba; Hoc est Corpus meum, quod pro vobis tradetur; in vero natiuoque sensu, secundum τὸ ῥητὸν accepta postulant. Ergo statuis, inquit, fieri transsubstãtiationem panis in Christi corpus? Tum ego; Imò verò; Credo fieri quod ipsa Christi verba requirunt, siue id cum Ecclesia Catholica transsubstantiationem, siue transelemētationem, vel conuersionem appelles.
units.tr: He then asked me to explain my view, namely in what way I believed the true body of Christ to be present in the Eucharist. I said: in the sense that the plain words of Christ himself require, This is my body, which is given for you, taken in their true and natural meaning, according to the literal sense [τὸ ῥητὸν]. "So you hold," he said, "that the bread is changed into the body of Christ by transubstantiation?" I replied, "Certainly. I believe that what Christ's own words demand takes place, whether you call it transubstantiation with the Catholic Church, or transelementation, or conversion."

units.la: Interrogauit deinde, qua virtute huiusmodi transsubstantiationem fieri crederem? Dixi, virtute verborum Christi Seruatoris, quæ iuxta D. Ambrosij dictum, in hoc mysterio operatoria essent, vt efficerent, quod Christus ijs pronunciaret. Respondit ille, Si ita crederem, dissentire me à Concilio Tridentino, quod Transsubstantiationem non Christi verbis, sed benedictioni tribueret. Excepi ego, nequaquam à Concilio Tridentino me dissentire, verum idem prorsus dicere ac profiteri, quod ab eo sit definitum. Ille contra in sententia persistebat; cumque hoc vrgeret prolixius; aliâ scilicet esse meam hac de re, quàm Concilij Tridentini sententiam; Ego demum, prouoco, inquam, ad ipsius Concilij definitionem. Separas tu benedictionē à Christi verbis, quam ego iuxta mentē Concilij, cum ijs esse coniunctam affirmo. Ergo, inquit ille, tibi nō constas, cùm antea solis Christi verbis transsubstantiandi virtutem tribueris, quam nunc verbis simul ac benedictioni adscribis. Respondi: Ego verò benedictionem à verbis Institutionis nunquam separaui, quemadmodum tu fraudulenter ac veteratorie colligis, quasi dum conuersionis vim Christi verbis attribuo, ea rebenedictionem ab ijsdem seiungam; quod falsissimū esse contendo.
units.tr: He then asked by what power I believed such a transubstantiation to be effected. I said: by the power of the words of Christ our Saviour, which, according to the saying of St Ambrose, are operative in this mystery, so that they effect what Christ pronounces. He answered that if I believed this, I dissented from the Council of Trent, which ascribed transubstantiation not to the words of Christ but to the blessing. I objected that I did not dissent from the Council of Trent at all; rather I said and professed exactly what it had defined. He persisted in his view, and when he pressed this at length, insisting that my opinion on this matter was other than the judgement of the Council of Trent, I at last appealed, I said, to the Council's own definition. You separate the blessing from the words of Christ, whereas I affirm, in keeping with the mind of the Council, that the two are joined. "Then," he said, "you are not consistent, since you earlier ascribed the power of transubstantiating to the words of Christ alone, and now you attribute it to the words together with the blessing." I answered: I have never separated the blessing from the words of institution, however craftily and deceitfully you draw that conclusion, as though, in ascribing the power of conversion to the words of Christ, I thereby separated the blessing from them. I maintain that this is utterly false.

units.la: Rogauit denuò: Qua tandem igitur virtute conuersio nem panis in Christi corpus fieri dicerem? Respondi, vir tute verborum Christi, velut antea quoque asseruerim, quibus perficiatur benedictio vel consecratio, cōcurren te omnipotentia Dei, quæ nimirum efficiat, vt verum sit, quod ijsdem verbis pronunciatur. Repetij dictū B. Am- brosij, Christi sermonem in hisce mysterijs operatorium esse dicentis. Ad quæ ille nihil amplius, nisi scio, inquit, Ambrosium id dicere in libris de Sacramentis.
units.tr: He asked again: by what power, then, did I say the conversion of the bread into the body of Christ is effected? I answered: by the power of the words of Christ, as I had already asserted, by which the blessing or consecration is accomplished, with the omnipotence of God concurring, which of course makes true what is pronounced in those words. I repeated the saying of St Ambrose, who says that the word of Christ is operative in these mysteries. To this he replied nothing more than: "I know that Ambrose says this in his books On the Sacraments."

units.la: Deinde, cùm paululum, quasi deliberandus, siluisset, adiecit & illud, dissentire me quoque à Pontificijs Docto ribus, quorum nonnulli, (nominabat vero Ambrosium Catharinum) non solis Christi verbis, sed toti actioni co- plexim, transubstantiandi virtutem tribuerent. Addere Catharinum, multa hoc modo deuitari posse incommo da, quę suboriantur, si solis Christi verbis conuersionem panis in Christi corpus effici dicas.
units.tr: Then, after he had been silent for a little while, as if he were weighing his answer, he added that I also dissented from the Papist teachers, some of whom (he named Ambrose Catharinus) ascribed the power of transubstantiation not to the words of Christ alone but to the whole action taken together. He said that Catharinus pointed out that many inconveniences which arise can be avoided in this way, if you say that the conversion of the bread into the body of Christ is effected by the words of Christ alone.

units.la: Respodi, Catharinum de summa rei nequaquam dis- sentire à Concilio Tridentino. Ipsum credere procul dubio, quod verum Christi Iesu corpus, ac verus sanguis, per conuersionem panis ac vini, reuera in Eucharistiæ Sacramento adsint; tum quod eadem conuersio benedi- ctioni vel cōsecrationi fit adscribenda. Cæterùm quibus verbis illa Eucharistiæ consecratio præcisè fiat, an ad eā præter verba Christi, alia quoque, quæ in Canone præce- dunt, necessario requirantur, id à Theologis nonnullis disputari quidem; verùm ea moderatione, vt substantia- lia tamen huius articuli nihil lædantur. Instabat ille, disceptationem hanc ad substantialia quoque pertinere. Id vero, quia simpliciter asserebat, eodem modo, ac toti- dem pene verbis à me negatum est.
units.tr: I replied that Catharinus in the substance of the matter by no means dissents from the Council of Trent. Without doubt he believes that the true body and true blood of Christ Jesus are really present in the sacrament of the Eucharist through the conversion of the bread and wine; and also that this same conversion is to be ascribed to the blessing or consecration. As for the question which words precisely effect that consecration of the Eucharist, or whether other words besides the words of Christ, those that precede them in the Canon, are necessarily required for it, this is indeed debated by some theologians, but with such moderation that the substantial points of this article are not harmed at all. He insisted that this dispute also touched on the substantial points. But since he merely asserted this, I denied it in the same way, and in almost as many words.

units.la: Atque hoc loco parum abfuit, quin in aliam disputa- tionem ingrederemur; cùm ille per hanc occasionem, pripriuata Catholicorum quorundam Theologorum certamina mihi obijceret, in primis vero illud, quod ante Concilium Tridentinum, inter viros doctissimos Dominicum à Soto, & Ambrosium Catharinum fuisse, vtriusque scripta testantur. Ad quam ipsius obiectionem respondi: Hanc semper in Ecclesia consuetudinem hactenus viguisse, vt quoties controuersia surgeret inter doctos, quae ad Religionis substantiam pertineret, eam vtraque pars ad cognitionem Ecclesiae, ac Conciliorum generalium definitionem reijceret; Sin vero leuior esset, quàm vt Religionis fundamenta contingeret, tum salua fidei vnitate, atque Ecclesiae obedientia, ita velitatam, vt licet vtraque pars abundaret in suo sensu, neutra tamen contra Ecclesiam insurgeret. Exempli loco disceptationem adduxi, quae de mendacio quondam inter D D. Hieronymum & Augustinum exorta est; tum eam quoque, quae ante complures annos, inter quosdam Theologos, de virtute atque operatione Baptismatis in infantibus exarsit. Excepit ille; Catharinum, quamuis in Concilio Tridentino praesens fuerit, tamen post Concilij definitionem in sententia sua, de Eucharistiae consecratione perstitisse. Tum ego; si verum hoc sit, opinionem esse priuatam hominis, quae rei summam in hoc articulo, veram scilicet corporis Christi praesentiam, & transubstantiationem non euertat.
units.tr: At this point we came close to entering upon another dispute, since he, on this occasion, threw in my face the quarrels of certain Catholic theologians, above all the one that, before the Council of Trent, arose between the most learned men Dominic de Soto and Ambrose Catharinus, as the writings of both attest. In answer to this objection I said: it has always been the custom in the Church, whenever a controversy arises among learned men concerning something that belongs to the substance of religion, for each side to refer the matter to the judgement of the Church and the definition of the general councils. But if the question is too slight to touch the foundations of religion, then, with the unity of the faith and obedience to the Church preserved, it is left open in such a way that, although each side may abound in its own sense, neither rises up against the Church. By way of example I cited the dispute that once arose between the doctors Jerome and Augustine over lying, and also the one that some years ago flared up among certain theologians concerning the power and operation of baptism in infants. He took up the point: Catharinus, though he was present at the Council of Trent, nevertheless persisted after the Council's definition in his view about the consecration of the Eucharist. I replied: if that is true, it is a private opinion of one man, which does not overturn the substance of the matter in this article, namely the true presence of the body of Christ and transubstantiation.

units.la: Demum, missò Catharino, veram ac Catholicam de Eucharistia sententiam, quam ego profes-sus eram, oppugnare coepit; idq; duplici via; partim argumentando, partim vero suo more pressius examinando verba Christi, super quibus ego meam, & Ecclesiae Catholicae sententiam fundaram.
units.tr: At last, leaving Catharinus aside, he began to attack the true and Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist which I had professed. He did this in two ways: partly by argument, and partly by examining the words of Christ, on which I and the Catholic Church's teaching are founded, more closely, in his usual manner.

units.la: Formabat igitur huiusmodi argumentum: Verum Christi corpus factum est ex Maria Virgine: At corpus Christi, quod vos in Eucharistia praesens esse dicitis, fit ex pane. Ergo non est verum Christi corpus. Ego resumpto arguargumento, Respondi, Cùm Christi corpus ex Maria Virgine factum dicitur, id intelligendum esse de assumptione humanæ naturæ, vel de factura corporis illius, quod ante Verbi incarnationem reuera non fuit: At cùm ex pane, per substantiæ conuersionem Christi corpus fieri asseritur, non intelligi corpus aliquod nouum, quod antea non extitit; sed illudipsum, quod assumptum est, ac natum ex Virgine, proq; nobis in mortem traditum.
units.tr: He therefore framed the argument in this form: The true body of Christ was made from the Virgin Mary; but the body of Christ which you say is present in the Eucharist is made from bread; therefore it is not the true body of Christ. I took up the argument again and replied: when it is said that the body of Christ was made from the Virgin Mary, this must be understood of the assumption of human nature, or of the formation of that body which in fact did not exist before the incarnation of the Word. But when it is asserted that the body of Christ is made from bread by a conversion of substance, one should not understand some new body which did not previously exist, but that very body which was assumed and born of the Virgin, and given into death for us.

units.la: Tum ille, vt argumentum suum contra responsionem meam tueretur, quærebat ex me, An non Christum illud mulieris semen esse crederem, quod post lapsum hominis promissum est in paradiso? Respondi, Quid ni verò? Instabat igitur, Aliud esse corpus illud, quod secundum Dei promissionem, ex semine mulieris factum fateret; & aliud quoque, quod ex pane factum, in Eucharistia præsens esse crederem. Ego vicissim demonstrabam, ipsum fraudem struere in voce, factum, vel fieri; quæ non vno modo vteretur. Longè aliud esse, cùm dicitur, Christi corpus, quod ante non fuit, factum vel assumptum est ex semine mulieris: Et cùm dicitur, Panis in Eucharistia conuertitur in illud Christi corpus, quod iam antea extitit, vtpote assumptum ex Virgine, & in cruce pro nobis traditum in mortem. Conclusi demum, Christi corpus, quod in Eucharistia præsens esse credimus, nō nouum aliquod esse corpus, (quemadmodū ipse fraudulenter comminisceretur) sed illud ipsum plane, quod ex Maria Virgine natum est, proque nobis crucifixum.
units.tr: Then he, in order to defend his argument against my reply, asked me whether I did not believe that the Christ was that seed of the woman which was promised in paradise after the fall of man. I answered: why not? He pressed on: the body which, according to God's promise, is acknowledged to be made from the seed of the woman is one thing, and the body which I believe to be present in the Eucharist, made from bread, is another. I in turn showed that he was practising a fraud on the word "made" or "to be made", which he used in more than one sense. It is quite different when we say that the body of Christ, which did not exist before, was made or assumed from the seed of the woman; and when we say that the bread in the Eucharist is changed into that body of Christ which already existed, as assumed from the Virgin and given into death for us on the cross. I concluded that the body of Christ which we believe to be present in the Eucharist is not some new body (as he fraudulently invented), but plainly that very body which was born of Mary the Virgin and crucified for us.

units.la: Postea cœpit examinare propositionem illam, Hoc est corpus meum: Et quia nota ipsi erant, (quemadmodum ex Colloquio deprehendi) quæ disputantur in hac controuersia, de Pronomine demonstratiuo; Touto, Hoc; placuit illi, scilicet vt aliquod acuminis sui specimē daret, ad eas quoq; subtilitates diuertere. Quæsiuit igitur, Quid per Pronomen, Hoc, demonstrari crederem? Dixi, Id, quod tum in manu habuerit Christus. Instabat rursum, vt defi-
units.tr: Afterwards he began to examine that proposition, This is my body. And since he knew well (as I gathered from the conversation) the points disputed in this controversy concerning the demonstrative pronoun, touto, hoc, he chose, to show something of his keenness, to turn aside to these subtleties too. So he asked: what did I believe the pronoun hoc to demonstrate? I said: that which Christ then had in his hand. He pressed again, to define what this was: was it bread, or the body of Christ itself?

units.la: {a} Marginal note at left: "Cen. 3." (as printed, beside the paragraph "Tum ille"). vt definirem, quidnam illud fuerit, panis ne, an ipsius Christi corpus? Respondi, quod primum acceperit Dominus, procul dubio panem fuisse; Eū vero per consecrationem, & verba Christi conuersum in verum ipsius corpus; Vt adeo, vere quodam loco dixerit B. Augustinus, Dominum in vltima coena seipsum in manibus suis tulisse. Ille dictū Augustini repetebat, addita voce; quodammodo; quam non eo tamen, quem ego citabam, verum alio quodam loco D. Augustinus habet: quanquam nec ea sensui à me intento quicquam officit. Ego vocem illam in partes resolui, ex quibus componitur; quodam modo; alio scilicet, quàm quo visibilis isthic in cospectu discipulorum sedebat Dominus.
units.tr: {a} Marginal note at left: "Cen. 3." (as printed, beside the paragraph "Tum ille"). He then asked me to define what that was: bread, or the body of Christ itself? I replied that what the Lord first took was undoubtedly bread, but through the consecration and the words of Christ it was changed into his true body. So St Augustine rightly said somewhere that the Lord carried himself in his own hands at the last supper. He repeated Augustine's saying, adding the word "in a certain way" (quodammodo), which St Augustine does not have in the place I cited but in some other place; yet this does nothing to hinder the sense I intended. I broke that word into the parts of which it is composed: "in a certain way", that is, in another way than that in which the Lord visibly sat there in the sight of the disciples.

units.la: Vrgebat interim vocem; τοῦτο, Hoc; rogans an non ea subiectum esset in propositione, σῶμα vero, vel corpus praedicatum? Volebat igitur, vt dicerem, quonam vocē; τοῦτο; referendam esse putarem, ad panem ne, an ad corpus? Dixi, ad corpus potius, quàm ad panem. Tum ille; Ergo facis propositionem identicam, quemadmodum si dicam; gladius est ensis: petra est lapis. Ego vero identicam nūquam dixi: Caeterum quod per τοῦτο demonstrari corpus asserui, corpus sumpsi pro re, vel substantia, sub externa panis specie contenta, de qua (licet ipsa corpus Domini reuera sit) τὸ σῶμα tamē, tanquam de subiecto, ritè praedicari potest.
units.tr: Meanwhile he pressed the word "this" [τοῦτο], asking whether it was not the subject of the proposition, while "body" [σῶμα] was the predicate. He wanted me to say to which word, "this" [τοῦτο], I thought it referred: to the bread or to the body? I said, to the body rather than to the bread. Then he said: So you make an identical proposition, as if I were to say "a sword is a blade" or "a rock is a stone." But I never called it identical. As for my assertion that the body is demonstrated by "this" [τοῦτο], I took "body" to mean the thing or substance contained under the outward appearance of bread, of which (although it really is the body of the Lord) "the body" [τὸ σῶμα] can rightly be predicated as of a subject.

units.la: Hoc loco mihi contradictionem obiecit, quasi prono mine; τοῦτο, nunc panem, nunc Christi corpus demonstrari dixerim: Quorum neutrum eo sensu, in quo ipse panem, ac corpus accipiebat, à me dictum est vnquam. Itaque cum hoc dixit, mihi sane fecit iniuriam. Asserui, panem esse in principio; verum per consecrationem, aut Christi sermonem operatorium, eum ipsum panem in Christi corpus conuerti; id autem fieri modo quodam ineffabili atque incomprehensibili.
units.tr: Here he charged me with a contradiction, as if I had said that the pronoun "this" [τοῦτο] sometimes demonstrates the bread and sometimes the body of Christ. I never said either of these in the sense in which he understood bread and body. So when he said this, he certainly did me an injustice. I asserted that bread is there at the beginning, but that through the consecration, or Christ's operative word, that same bread is converted into the body of Christ; and this happens in a certain ineffable and incomprehensible manner.

units.la: Instabat nihilominus de propositione; Hoc est Corpus meum; meum; Et enumeratis aliquot propositionum generibus, quaerebat demum, qualem hanc esse dicerem? Tum ego; Respondeat tibi Philippus tuus, ad cuius sententiam de Eucharistia provocasti. Is, cum videret huiusmodi propositiones ad communes Logicę formas redigi non posse, inuſitatas appellavit. Nos hac supernaturalem dicimus, qua non liceat vel revocare ad humanae rationis iudicium, vel ad eum modum expendere, quem in rebus naturalibus sequimur. Ad haec ille, Non ignorare se, quae Philippi sententia fuerit de Eucharistia. Verum in eo contradictionem esse, quod eandem Propositionem, quam identicam antea fecissem, nunc supernaturalem nominare. Ego vero quemadmodum iam ante dictum est, identicam nunquam appellavi; neque ille huiusmodi quid per legitimam consequentiam ex verbis meis conficere potuit. Caeterum perstiti in eo, quod supernaturale esse propositionem asserui, cum id, quod hac ipsa enunciatur, nec percipi sensibus, nec humano intellectu comprehendi possit.
units.tr: He nevertheless kept pressing the proposition "This is my body; my", and after listing several kinds of propositions, he finally asked what kind I said this one was. Then I said: let your Philip answer you, to whose opinion on the Eucharist you appealed. Seeing that propositions of this sort cannot be reduced to the common forms of logic, Philip called them unusual. We call this one supernatural, which may be neither referred to the judgment of human reason nor weighed in the manner we use for natural things. To this he replied that he was not unaware what Philip's view of the Eucharist was. But there was a contradiction in my calling the same proposition, which I had earlier made identical, now supernatural. Yet, as has already been said, I never called it identical, and he could not draw such a conclusion from my words by any legitimate inference. However, I persisted in asserting that the proposition is supernatural, since what it states can be perceived neither by the senses nor grasped by the human intellect.

units.la: Demum misso propositionis examine, struebat quoddam sophisma, quo veritati offundere nebulam ac perspicua verba Christi Servatoris, a vero natiuoque sensu detorta, evertere conabatur. Christus, inquit, accepit panem, eundemque panem benedixit, fregit, ac tandem discipulis dedit manducandum; quemadmodum constat ex iis locis, quibus institutio describitur. Igitur nihil aliud dedit, quam quod primum accepit in manus, panem scilicet. Unde sequitur, non esse verum Christi corpus in Eucharistia.
units.tr: Finally, having dropped the examination of the proposition, he built a certain sophism by which he tried to cast a mist over the truth and overturn the plain words of Christ the Saviour, twisting them away from their true and natural sense. Christ, he said, took bread, blessed that same bread, broke it, and at last gave it to the disciples to eat, as is clear from the passages in which the institution is described. Therefore he gave nothing other than what he first took into his hands, namely bread. From this it follows that there is no true body of Christ in the Eucharist.

units.la: Respondi; Atqui Christus deinde quoque dixit, Accipite, & manducate, Hoc est corpus meum. Ergo si verum hac parte dixit, certe non panem (uti tu asseris) sed corpus suum discipulis manducandum obtulit. Accepit ille quidem principio panem; verum eundem, antequam porrexit discumbentibus, virtute benedictionis, ac verborum, quae operatoria recte ria recte dicuntur,in corpus suum conuertit.Quam rem, vt humano intellectu assequamur, nunquam futurum est.Itaq; Domino id afferenti simpliciter credendum est, ac cogitandum,quod Christus & veritas ipsa sit, vt mentiri vel fallere nequeat; & non homo tantum, sed verus quoque Deus,apud quem non est impossibile omne verbum:de quo Scriptura:Ipse dixit, & facta sunt.
units.tr: I replied: But Christ also said afterwards, "Take and eat; this is my body." Therefore, if he spoke truly in this part, he certainly offered his disciples to eat not bread (as you assert) but his own body. He indeed took bread at the start, but before he handed it to those reclining at table, by the power of the blessing and of the words, which are rightly called operative, he changed the same bread into his body. We shall never grasp how this is done by the human intellect. Therefore, when the Lord affirms it, we must simply believe and think that Christ is truth itself, so that he can neither lie nor deceive; and that he is not only man but also true God, with whom no word is impossible. Of him Scripture says: "He spoke, and they were made" [Ipse dixit, & facta sunt].

units.la: Adiecit & aliud: Si corpus Christi praesens fuit, antequam verba prolata sunt;sequitur,verborum virtute conuersionem non fieri: Si vero per verba fit conuersio; Ergo propositio illa; Hoc est Corpus meum,in principio falsa est; quandoquidem affirmat iam esse,quod primu in fine propositionis futurum erat. Hoc tortuoso ac clumbi sophismate Christo struebat insidias, eiusque veritatem oppugnabat. Quod cum propositisset, quaesiui ego, An punctum a me scire vellet, aut momentum temporis, in quo conuersionem panis in verum Christi corpus fieri credimus?Respondit, Se hoc non agere; sed expendere verba institutionis,atque ex ijs scrutari huius articuli veritatem. Atque hoc cum dixit, satis suum ipsius sophisma confutauit.Nam si momentum temporis, quo panis in Christi corpus conuertitur,precise non queras,(quod ille se quaerere disertis verbis negauit) reuera nullus est huius sophismatis visus. Itaque ego contra nihil aliud obieci,quam fidei nostrae simplicitatem, qua conscientias nostras,contra prophanas huiusmodi naenias,munire consueuimus.Christi verba,inquam,procul dubio verissima sunt,atque idipsum, quod sonant, assistente diuina virtute potenter operantur:Ideoq; super illis,non super intellectu, vel sensibus humanis, fides nostra de Eucharistiae mysterio, simpliciter ac solide fundata consistit. Atque ea fides, quoniam infallibili veritatis aeternae verbo nititur, securas reddit conscientias nostras; vt adeo nihil moremur iudicium rationis humanae, ex qua huiusmodi sophismata, contra simplicem veritatem infinita formari possunt; quæ nulla re certius ac facilius, quàm adhærendo planis, veris, ac solidis Christi verbis eluduntur. Quod si mysteria Religionis nostræ ad humani cerebri normam revocare velis, neque quicquam credere, nisi cum ea quadret, futurum est, vt nō hunc articulum modò, verùm & alios quosdam magni momenti, puta de mysterio S. Trinitatis, de incarnatione Verbi, de resurrectione carnis, eadem via penitus euertas.
units.tr: He added another point: if the body of Christ was present before the words were spoken, it follows that the conversion does not take place by the power of the words; but if the conversion does take place through the words, then the proposition "This is my body" is false at the beginning, since it asserts that what was to come at the end of the proposition already is. With this twisted and clumsy sophism he laid snares for Christ and attacked his truth. When he had put this forward, I asked whether he wanted from me a point, or a moment of time, at which we believe the conversion of the bread into the true body of Christ takes place. He replied that he was not asking that, but weighing the words of institution and searching in them for the truth of this article. And when he said this, he himself sufficiently refuted his own sophism. For if you do not ask precisely for the moment of time at which the bread is converted into the body of Christ (which he expressly denied he was asking), then there is indeed no appearance of this sophism. So on the contrary I objected nothing other than the simplicity of our faith, by which we are accustomed to fortify our consciences against such profane trifles. Christ's words, I said, are without doubt most true, and by the presence of divine power they powerfully effect what they say. Therefore our faith concerning the mystery of the Eucharist rests simply and firmly upon those words, not upon the understanding or the human senses. And since that faith leans on the infallible word of eternal truth, it makes our consciences secure, so that we do not regard at all the judgment of human reason, from which endless sophisms of this kind can be framed against plain truth. Such sophisms are refuted by nothing more surely and easily than by adhering to the plain, true and solid words of Christ. But if you wish to bring the mysteries of our religion back to the measure of the human brain, and to believe nothing unless it squares with that, you will by the same route overturn not only this article but certain others of great importance too, such as the mystery of the Holy Trinity, the incarnation of the Word, and the resurrection of the flesh.

units.la: Ille ad hæc; Se nihil aliud habere propositum, quàm vt veram Christi verborum intelligentiâ inquirat. Tum ego; Imò hoc agis, inquâ, vt præsidio Physicarum rationum, verba Christi ab ipsius mente aliorsum detorqueas, & euertas. Asserit expresse Christus, id, quod in cœna manducandum discipulis dedit, fuisse corpus suum; atque idipsum quidem, quod pro nobis in mortem tradidit: tradidit autem in mortem, non panem, aut corpus quoddam symbolicum, sed verum illud ac naturale corpus, quod assumptum est, ac natu ex Maria Virgine. Tu vero Christum velut in faciem arguis mendacij, quasi non corpus suum, sed panem tantum ad manducandum porrexerit.
units.tr: To this he replied that he had no other aim than to seek the true meaning of Christ's words. Then I said: Indeed, you are doing this: under the shelter of physical reasons you twist Christ's words away from his mind and overturn them. Christ expressly asserts that what he gave the disciples to eat at the supper was his body, and indeed that same body which he delivered to death for us. He delivered to death not bread, nor some symbolic body, but that true and natural body which was assumed and born of the Virgin Mary. But you, as it were to his face, accuse Christ of lying, as though he had offered only bread to eat and not his body.

units.la: Hoc loco vultu nonnihil auersò, tanquam indignabundus, iniuriam sibi fieri protestabatur: Neque enim se mendacij arguere Christum, sed hoc spectare tantum, vt quo sensu verba cœnæ protulerit, liquidum ac manifestum euadat. Ad hæc ego: Sanè quidem, quod in cœna Christus disertis verbis asserit, Idipsum tu simpliciter negas; propterea, quod intellectus humanus citra fidei lumē, non assequitur, quomodo id verum esse possit. Itaq; animalis hominis ductum in hoc mysterio plane sequeris, & rationibus omnino Physicis oppugnas Christum, nec aliter eius verba tractas, quàm si non in ipsius Christi schola, sed in foro rerum naturalium versaremur. Si tu illud euiceris, nihil amplius in Religione credendum esse vel amplectendum, nisi quod percipere sensibus, aut ratione metiri, vel intellectu comprehendere possumus, nos quidem non solum in hoc Articulo de Eucharistia, verum etiam in alijs quibusdam, libenter manus dabimus. Verum id tu nunquam efficies. Constat enim fidem nostram in huiusmodi mysterijs, non dictamine rationis, aut humani cerebri ductu, sed norma veritatis, ac Dei verbo, dirigi oportere. Itaque si vere fideles sumus, preponimus coecę rationis iudicio Dei verbum, atque ea quoque in Religione nostra lubetibus animis amplectimur, quę sensuū experimento, ac iudicio rationis, etiam absurdissima videntur; vt D. Paulus non immerito fidem rerum non apparentium argumentum dixerit.
units.tr: At this point he turned his face somewhat away, as if indignant, and protested that he was being wronged: he did not accuse Christ of lying, he said, but only aimed to make clear the sense in which he uttered the words of the supper. To this I replied: Certainly, what Christ asserts in plain words at the supper, you simply deny, because the human intellect without the light of faith does not grasp how it can be true. So in this mystery you follow altogether the guidance of the natural man, and you attack Christ with wholly physical arguments, handling his words not as if we were in Christ's school, but in the marketplace of natural things.
