If you could succeed in that, nothing further would have to be believed or embraced in religion except what we can perceive by the senses, measure by reason, or comprehend by the intellect; and we would gladly give way not only in this article on the Eucharist but in certain others as well. But you will never accomplish that. For it is agreed that our faith in such mysteries ought to be directed not by the dictate of reason or the guidance of the human brain, but by the rule of truth and God's word. Therefore, if we are truly faithful, we set God's word above the judgment of blind reason, and in our religion we embrace with willing minds even those things which seem most absurd to the experience of the senses and the judgment of reason; as St Paul rightly called faith "the proof of things not seen" [argumentum non apparentium].

units.la: Haec ego: Ille vero sophisma suū, quod ad euertendam huius Articuli veritatē intorserat, identidem resumere, atque iterum vrgere conabatur. Quoniam igitur totis neruis eo dirigebat omnia, vt abditus post strophas physicas, vel putidis sophismatibus inuolutus, Caluinistarum more dilucidae veritati fumos offunderet, & coaceruatis absurditatibus, quas in hoc argumento philosophia suppeditat, Christo contumeliam inferret, abrupi demum prophanam hanc philosophandi rationem, atque homi-nem ab huiusmodi tricis, ac vanis sophismatibus, ad vera Theologiae Principia reuocaui: Quam rem ille quidem admodum aegre tulit. Dixi, Christū cum suis actionibus, naturae legibus nō subiacere; positum esse supra captum ingenij humani, quod hisce Christi verbis; Hoc est corpus meum, enunciatur. Itaque ea ipsa Christi verba, neq; praecise redigi ad Logicae formas, neq; praesidio philosophicarum rationum, vel naturalium principiorum, intelligi posse. Mitteret igitur nugas illas, neque Christum ad Aristotelis aut Platonis forum pertrahere, vel naturae legibus subdere conaretur. Philosophos Christo potius, quā Christum philosophis subijci oportere. Nimirum alio respiciēdum, si veram ac solidam Christi verborum intelligentiam assequi velimus.
units.tr: I said this. He, however, kept trying to repeat and press the sophism he had thrown up to overturn the truth of this article. Since he was straining every nerve to bury the plain truth under physical fancies and foul sophistries, as the Calvinists do, and to insult Christ by piling up the absurdities that philosophy supplies for this subject, I finally broke off this profane way of philosophising and called the man back from such tricks and empty sophistries to the true first principles of theology. He took this very badly. I said that Christ, with his actions, is not subject to the laws of nature, and that what is expressed in these words of Christ, This is my body, lies beyond the grasp of the human mind. So these very words of Christ cannot be reduced exactly to the forms of logic, nor understood with the help of philosophical arguments or natural principles. He should therefore drop those trifles and not try to drag Christ before the court of Aristotle or Plato, or subject him to the laws of nature. Philosophers ought to submit to Christ, not Christ to philosophers. Surely we must look elsewhere if we wish to reach the true and solid understanding of Christ's words.

units.la: Haec ego, & id genus alia quaedam: Ille vero manibus ac pedibus repugnabat, ne reductus ad Christi scholam, extra Platonis atque Aristotelis forum causam dicere cogeretur. Norunt enim Sacramentarij, quicquid in hoc articulo præsidij habent contra dilucida Christi verba, id totum in philosophorum armis consistere; quibus si exuantur, facile intelligunt, res suas admodum periclitari. Itaque reluctabatur Badius, quantum poterat, ne scilicet isto præsidio nudaretur. Negabat, se rationibus Physicis uti, sed Christi mentem in ipsius verbis indagare, atque id eo quidem modo, quem ipsi etiam Scholastici Pontificij, in disputationibus de Eucharistia sequerentur; à quibus aiebat hac in parte me dissidere.
units.tr: I said this and things of that kind. He, however, fought hands and feet against being led back to the school of Christ and forced to plead his case outside the court of Plato and Aristotle. The Sacramentarians know very well that whatever support they have in this article against the plain words of Christ rests entirely on the weapons of the philosophers, and that once they are stripped of these they quickly see their cause is in serious danger. So Badius struggled as hard as he could not to be stripped of this support. He denied that he used physical arguments, claiming that he was searching out the mind of Christ in his words, and doing so in the way that even the Scholastic Papists themselves follow in their disputations about the Eucharist. He said that on this point I dissented from them.

units.la: Respondi, Non disseri me, quin Scholastici Theologi materiam hanc, Dialecticæ beneficio certa ratione ac via pertractent: Verum id ita fieri, ut nusquam tamen à simplici verborum intelligentia, vel latum unguem discedant; Imò ubi ad summam rei ventum fuerit, tum vero eos, spretis Philosophorum placitis & iudicio rationis posthabito, captiuare omnem intellectum in obsequiū Christi, seque totos contra cæcæ rationis iudicium, æternæ veritati submittere. Ipsum vero longè aliam viam ingredi; hoc agere, scilicet, ut Christi verba reuocet ad humanæ rationis iudicium, eaque nomine Dialectices, ac physicarum, imò sophisticarum rationum præsidio, euertat potius, vel aliorsum detorqueat à Christi mente, quàm eorum sensum inquirat.
units.tr: I replied that I did not deny that the Scholastic theologians treat this matter with method, with the help of dialectic; but they do so in such a way that they never stray a hair's breadth from the plain sense of the words. Indeed, when they come to the heart of the matter, they set aside the opinions of the philosophers, put the judgement of reason in second place, take every understanding captive in obedience to Christ, and submit themselves entirely to eternal truth against the judgement of blind reason. He, on the other hand, went down a quite different road: he aimed to bring Christ's words back under the judgement of human reason, and, under the name of dialectic and of natural and even sophistical arguments, to overturn them, or rather to twist them away from the mind of Christ, instead of inquiring into their meaning.

units.la: Ille contra perfistebat in eo, se verba institutionis expendere, (ad rationis gnomonem scilicet) & veram illorum intelligentiam beneficio Dialectices indagare. Dixi, non defugere me Dialecticam conferendi rationem, modò ne in hac causa, quæ omnem naturæ captum transcenderet, argumentorum pondera, ac momenta rationum, ex naturæ principijs desumeret, & Dialecticæ nomine, ad velandam sophisticen, abuteretur.
units.tr: He, on the contrary, kept insisting that he was weighing the words of institution (by the measure of reason, that is) and was discovering their true meaning with the help of dialectic. I said that I did not reject dialectic as a way of comparing arguments, provided that in this cause, which goes beyond the grasp of all nature, he did not draw the weight of his arguments and the force of his reasons from the principles of nature, and did not misuse the name of dialectic to cover up sophistry.

units.la: Tum ille, Ego, inquit, rem ipsam ex scripturis desumo, modum vero tractandi ex Dialectica. Id quod ego constanter negaui; atq; totius rei iudicium ad eos reieci, qui præsentes erant. Imò sæpe postea mecum admiratus sum, qua fronte id dixerit; Quandoquidem reuera non ex sacris Scripturę fontibus, sed ex fœtidis humani cerebri ac philosophiæ lacunis hausit nænias, ac sophismata deprópsit, quibus in hoc mysterio clarissimam veritatis lucem, velutifumo quodam, inuoluere conabatur: Vt adeò nō iniuria prophanam illam, ac sophisticam philosophandi rationem, qua contra venerandam Eucharistiam ad gentilium prope morem, vtebatur, tandem abruperim, atque ipsum, quantumuis renitentem, (inuitus enim id fieri patiebatur) ad Christi scholam, & vera Theologiæ principia retraxerim.
units.tr: Then he said: "I take the matter itself from the Scriptures, and the method of handling it from dialectic." I firmly denied this, and I referred the whole judgement of the matter to those who were present. Indeed, I have often since wondered with amazement at the effrontery with which he said it. For in truth he drew his nonsense and dug out his sophisms not from the fountains of Holy Scripture but from the foul pits of the human brain and of philosophy, and with them tried to wrap the clearest light of truth in this mystery, as if in smoke. So I was not wrong to break off at last that profane and sophistical way of philosophising, which he used against the venerable Eucharist in something close to the manner of the heathen, and to draw him back, though he resisted (for he allowed it only unwillingly), to the school of Christ and the true principles of theology.

units.la: Quia vero ego, quemadmodum dictum est, ad auditorum iudicium prouocabam, cœperunt hoc loco quidā ex præsentibus interloqui, antequam ad sequentia progrederemur. Et Doctor Crantius quidem obiecit Badio, quod reuera rationibus naturalibus, ac sophisticis Eucharistiæ veritatem oppugnarit. Repetebat, exempli loco, primum illud argumentum, quod in forma syllogismi, contra præsentiam Christi corporis in Eucharistia produxerat, illiqué breuiter atque euidenter demonstrabat, quàm captiosè ac sophisticè lusisset in voce; Factum; cùm eam longè alio sensu in Maiore propositione vsurparit, quàm in Minore: Itaque resoluebat illi syllogismum in quatuor terminos; ac demum concludebat, negari non posse quin vitiosa ac fallaci argumentatione vsus sit. Idem confirmabat & alter Syndicorum Doctor Hacksteinius, atque explicata vocis; Factum, aut, Fit; diuersa significatione, demum, Ego, inquit, Minorem vel Conclusionem in syllogismo tibi negassem. Ille, cùm hæc dicerentur, victus euidentia rei, conticuit.
units.tr: Since I, as has been said, was appealing to the judgement of the hearers, some of those present began to speak at this point, before we moved on to what followed. Doctor Crantius indeed objected to Badius that he had in fact attacked the truth of the Eucharist with natural and sophistical arguments. By way of example, he took up again the first argument, which Badius had put forward in syllogistic form against the presence of Christ's body in the Eucharist, and he showed briefly and clearly how cunningly and sophistically he had played on the word; Factum, "made," since he had used it in the major premise in a quite different sense from the minor. So he reduced the syllogism to four terms, and in the end concluded that it could not be denied that Badius had relied on faulty and deceptive argument. Doctor Hacksteinius, the other of the syndics, confirmed this, and, after explaining the different meanings of the word Factum or Fit, said at last: "I would have denied you the minor premise or the conclusion in that syllogism." Badius, when these things were said, overcome by the plainness of the matter, fell silent.

units.la: Tum D. Hacksteinius; Huiusmodi captionibus ac sophismatibus, inquit, decipitis incautum vulgus, & simpliciores ciores, qui tales fallacias non intelligunt, irretitos à veritate ad dogmata vestra pertrahitis. Quanquam huius argumenti fraus adeo manifesta est, vt eam nos quoque, tametsi professione Theologi non sumus, sed laici, deprehendere possimus. Ad haec ille confusus, deiectis oculis obmutuit.
units.tr: Then Doctor Hacksteinius said: "By such tricks and sophisms you deceive the unwary crowd, and the simpler sort who do not understand such fallacies, and you draw them, caught in the net, away from the truth to your doctrines. Yet the fraud in this argument is so obvious that we too, although we are not theologians by profession but laymen, can detect it." At this, Badius, confused, lowered his eyes and said nothing.

units.la: Mouit D. Crantius & illud, quod obiecerat de modo, quem Scholastici Pontificij (vti loquebatur) in explicanda Eucharistiae controuersia sequerentur: Scholastici, inquit, disputant illi quidem diligenter & accurate de Eucharistiae mysterio; verum ita tamen, vt vbique maneant intra terminos, & demum, postquam omnia excusserint, repudiatis naturae principijs, atque intellectu captiuato, in simplici verborum Christi intelligentia, contra rationis iudicium, penitus acquiescant.
units.tr: Doctor Crantius also dwelt on what he had objected about the method which the Scholastic Papists (as he put it) follow in explaining the Eucharistic controversy. "The Scholastics," he said, "indeed debate the mystery of the Eucharist diligently and accurately; yet they do so in such a way that they always keep within the bounds, and at last, after they have examined everything, they reject the principles of nature, take the understanding captive, and rest entirely in the plain understanding of Christ's words, against the judgement of reason."

units.la: Caeterum Dominus Consul Hardenradius, & aliud quoddam repetebat ipsius argumetum, quod ex ijs locis formauerat, quibus prima Eucharistiae institutio describitur. Egregia vero, inquit, argumetandi ratio: Christus in vltima Coena panem in manus accepit; Ergo panem quoque discipulis dedit manducandum; Quasi frustra dixerit: Accipite, & manducate, Hoc est Corpus meum, eaque verba nullam omnino vim ad operandum habeant; vel quasi ea non esset Christi potentia, vt verum efficere possit, quod verbis pronunciat. Dedecus est, homines, qui Christi nomen profitentur, adeo contemptim ac prophane, de Religionis nostrae mysterijs philosophari, neque credere velle quicquam, nisi quod humanus intellectus verum esse iudicat. Ad eundem plane modum Ethnici quondam disputabant contra Christianos, eosque false ridebant, quod ea crederent, quae rationis humanae iudicio vel absurda, vel impossibilia videbantur.
units.tr: Then Lord Consul Hardenradius repeated another argument of his own, which he had drawn from those passages in which the first institution of the Eucharist is described. "What a splendid way of arguing!" he said. "Christ in the last supper took bread into his hands; therefore he also gave bread to the disciples to eat. As if he had spoken in vain: Take and eat; this is my body, and as if those words had no force at all for effecting anything, or as if it were not within Christ's power to make true what he declares in words. It is a disgrace that men who profess the name of Christ should philosophise so contemptuously and profanely about the mysteries of our religion, and be unwilling to believe anything except what human understanding judges to be true. In exactly the same way the heathen once argued against the Christians, and mocked them falsely because they believed things that seemed to the judgement of human reason either absurd or impossible."

units.la: Post haec ego, quemadmodum iam ante coeperam, disputationem nostram, à Physicorum subsellijs auocata, ad Christi scholam introducere perrexi: Atque id hoc quidem modo. Dixi, Quæstionem inter nos esse de verbis Cœnæ; Hoc est Corpus meum; quæ ego, tanquam sententiæ meæ fundamentum protuleram: Controuersiam vero in eo consistere, quia non vno modo ab omnibus eadem verba intelliguntur, quis verus germanusque sit illorum sensus. In hoc itaque versari studium nostrum, eoque, velut ad scopum, dirigi collationem oportere, vt veram scilicet verborum istorum intelligentiam assequamur. Eam vero ad rem opus esse medio quodam infallibili, per quod in hac, tũ in reliquis omnibus de Religione controuersijs, vbi de sensu quæstio est, vera scriptuæ sententia declaretur.
units.tr: After this, as I had already begun to do, I went on to lead our discussion away from the benches of the natural philosophers and into the school of Christ. I did it in this way. I said that the question between us concerned the words of the Supper, This is my body, which I had put forward as the foundation of my opinion. The controversy, however, consisted in this: since the same words are not understood by everyone in one way, which of them is the true and genuine sense. Our effort ought therefore to be directed to this, and our discussion ought to be aimed at it as at a goal, so that we may reach the true understanding of these words. For this purpose, I said, we need some infallible means, through which the true sense of Scripture may be declared, both in this controversy and in all the other controversies about religion where the question is one of meaning.

units.la: Excepit ille, Christi mentem è verbis ipsius hauriendam esse. At, inquam, id omnes facere conamur; & diuersos tamen, imò contrarios sensus è Christi verbis eruimus. Itaque medium ego requiro, per quod in hac opinionum ac sensuum diuersitate, verus & genuinus verborum sensus, à falsis opinionibus possit dijudicari. Hoc loco cunctabatur aliquantum: Repetebat deinde, quod ante dixerat, Ex ipsis Scripturæ verbis, si expendantur, Christi mentem satis intelligi posse. Ad quid enim aliud verba, nisi vt quidam mentis interpres sint?
units.tr: He replied that the mind of Christ must be drawn from his own words. "But," I said, "that is what we all try to do; yet from Christ's words we draw out different and even contrary senses. So I ask for a means by which, in this diversity of opinions and senses, the true and genuine sense of the words can be distinguished from false opinions." At this point he hesitated for a while. Then he repeated what he had said before: that if the words of Scripture are weighed, the mind of Christ can be understood well enough from them. "For what are words for," he asked, "except to be interpreters of the mind?"

units.la: Tum ego: Scio, verba dici & esse mentis interpretem; modò ea, quæ quis loquitur, in alienum à loquentis animo sensum non detorqueantur: Quod fieri necesse est, vbi de verborum quorundam intelligentia, pugnantes sententiæ inueniuntur; quemadmodum in hoc articulo de Eucharistia vsu venit. Atqui testis est experientia, controuersias eo modo non tolli, si quælibet dissidentium pars, se veram Christi, vel Spiritus S. mentem in Scripturis asse qui glorietur.
units.tr: Then I said: I know that words are the interpreter of the mind, provided that what someone says is not twisted into a meaning foreign to the speaker's intention. That is bound to happen when opposing opinions arise over the understanding of certain words, as happens in this article on the Eucharist. Yet experience shows that controversies are not settled this way, if each disputing party boasts that it alone has found the true mind of Christ or of the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures.

units.la: Cæterum hanc rem, quæ controuersiarum omnium, veluti summum caput est, & cardo quidam, euidentiæ causa, in hunc modum apertius demonstraui. Sint, inquam, exempli loco, in hac mensa diuersarum Religionum homines; Ego catholicus sum; tu Caluinianus; Sit & Lutheranus quispiam. Constituamus nunc in medio Scripturæ verba de Cœna; quæ ego cum vniuersa Ecclesia in eo sensu accipio, quem supra declaraui, & verum Christi corpus, per conuersionem panis in Eucharistia, præsens esse credo. Lutheranus eadem verba ita interpretabitur, vt manente panis substantia, verum Christi corpus, in, cum, & sub pane porrigi communicantibus, persuasum habeat. Tu vero, qui Caluinum sequeris, contradices vtrique nostrum, neque quicquam amplius, quàm panem, absentis corporis typum vel symbolum, in Eucharistia sumi, ex ijsdem Christi verbis colliges. Nunc quæro abs te, Quis hic sententiam feret, aut definiet inter nos, mea ne, an tua, an vero Lutherani illius intelligentia, veram Christi mentem exprimat?
units.tr: But I have shown this matter more clearly in the following way, since it is the chief point of all the controversies and, as it were, their hinge. Let us suppose, I said, that at this table there are people of different religions for an example: I am a Catholic, you are a Calvinist, and let there be some Lutheran too. Let us now put before us the words of Scripture about the Supper. I take them, with the whole Church, in the sense I explained above, and I believe that the true body of Christ is present in the Eucharist through the conversion of the bread. The Lutheran will interpret the same words so that, while the substance of the bread remains, he is convinced that the true body of Christ is offered to the communicants in, with and under the bread. But you, who follow Calvin, will contradict both of us and will conclude from the same words of Christ that in the Eucharist we receive nothing more than bread, a type or symbol of an absent body. Now I ask you: who here will pass judgment or decide between us, whether my understanding, or yours, or that of the Lutheran expresses the true mind of Christ?

units.la: Cum ad hæc ille nihil subticeret, Ego, intelligis opinor, inquam, oportere medium aliquod esse, per quod in hac de Cœna, tum in reliquis etiam controuersijs omnibus, veritas e scripturis eruatur. Hoc itaque medium abs te nominari mihi cupio. Ad hæc ille nihil admodum; nisi quod tergiuersabatur, & ad priorem illum philosophandi modum obliquè nonnunquam respectabat.
units.tr: When he kept silent in response to this, I said: You understand, I suppose, that there must be some means by which the truth is drawn from the Scriptures, both in this matter of the Supper and in all the other controversies. I want you to name this means for me. To this he replied with nothing much, except that he evaded the question, and now and then glanced sideways at his former manner of philosophizing.

units.la: Fundaui vero hanc rem, de medio veritatis e scripturis eruendæ, super dicto quodam D. Petri, quod & produxi: Hoc primum intelligentes, inquit Apostolus, quod omnis prophetia scripturæ propria interpretatione nonfit. In primis vrsi D. Petri verba, quæ sunt in contextu græco: ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως id est, priuata interpretatione vel resolutione non fit. Igitur si ego, inquam, si tu, vel alius quispiam priuatus, Scripturam interpretari pro suo captu velit, huiusmodi interpretationem, tanquam priuatam, reijcit D. Petrus; ea mente procul dubio, vt ad publicam quandam Scripturarum explicationem respiciedum esse doceat. Iam ego medium quæro, per quod audire liceat publicam hanc, eamq; veram Scripturarum interpretationem
units.tr: I based this point, about the means of drawing out the truth from the Scriptures, on a saying of St. Peter, which I also quoted: "Knowing this first, says the Apostle, that no prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation" [2 Pet. 1.20]. First I weighed the words of St. Peter, which in the Greek text are ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, that is, not of private interpretation or resolution. So, I said, if I, or you, or any other private person wishes to interpret Scripture according to his own understanding, St. Peter rejects such an interpretation as private. Without doubt his intention is to teach that we must look to a public explanation of the Scriptures. Now I seek a means by which we may hear this public and true interpretation of the Scriptures

units.la: *Pet. 1.6 nem, in qua pia mens tutò possit acquiescere. Quod si tu medium illud proferre nolis, ego proferam.
units.tr: Pet. 1.6 interpretation, in which a pious mind may safely rest. But if you are unwilling to put forward that means, I will put it forward.

units.la: Cùm aliquamdiu tergiuersatus esset, tandem, Bene, inquit, tu igitur proferas. Dixi, Spiritum sanctum, qui verus ac indubitatus auctor est Scripturæ, cùm de eiusdem Scripturæ sensu dissidium oritur, declarare mentem suâ per Conciliorum definitiones, ac perpetuum & vniuersalem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ consensum. Itaque generaliū Conciliorum definitiones, ac perpetuum in doctrina orbis Christiani consensum, sancti Spiritus quasi publicam vocem esse, qua Scripturas à se inspiratas interpretetur. Atque hoc esse medium, per quod in controuersijs de vero scripturæ sensu constare possit.
units.tr: After he had evaded the question for some time, at last he said: Well, then, you put it forward. I said that the Holy Spirit, who is the true and undoubted author of Scripture, when a disagreement arises about the meaning of the same Scripture, declares his mind through the definitions of Councils and through the perpetual and universal consensus of the Catholic Church. Therefore the definitions of the general Councils and the perpetual consensus of the Christian world in doctrine are, as it were, the public voice of the Holy Spirit, by which he interprets the Scriptures inspired by himself. This, I said, is the means by which agreement can be reached about the true meaning of Scripture in controversies.

units.la: Antequam vero medium hoc munire suis firmamentis aggrederer, hortatus sum Badium, vt si quid esset, quod putaret illud euerti posse; vel si quod aliud haberet medium, quo certius è Scriptura veritatem erui existimaret, id liberè proferret. Ille nihil admodum contra protulit; nisi quod Deum loquentem in scripturis audiendum diceret: Verbo Dei, vel Scripturis sanctis, tanquam certo κριτηρίῳ (ea enim voce vtebatur) dirimi Religionis controuersias oportere. Respondi, Dubium non esse quin Scripturæ sint audiendæ, & habendæ pro Dei verbo: Verùm quæstionem inter nos esse, de vero sancti Spiritus è Scripturis eruendo sensu; extra quem Dei Verbum, non Dei, sed hominum verbum non immeritò habeatur: Vt adeo, cùm de Religione controuersia surgit, frustra proferantur in medium Scripturæ, nisi de vera earundem intelligentia certò constet.
units.tr: Before I set out to fortify this means with its supports, I urged Badius that if he thought there was anything that could overturn it, or if he had some other means by which he believed the truth could be drawn more surely from Scripture, he should freely put it forward. He brought forward nothing much against it, except that he said God speaking in the Scriptures must be heard, and that the controversies of religion must be settled by the Word of God, or the holy Scriptures, as by a sure criterion (for that was the word he used). I replied that there was no doubt the Scriptures must be heard and held to be the Word of God. But the question between us was about drawing out the true sense of the Holy Spirit from the Scriptures; outside that sense, the Word of God is not rightly regarded as the Word of God, but as the word of men. So, when a controversy about religion arises, Scriptures are cited in vain unless the true understanding of them is certain.

units.la: Ille concedebat, necessariam esse veram Scripturarum intelligentiam; neque sacras litteras in iudicandis controuersiis aliter valere, nisi accipiantur in eo sensu, in quo, ductu sancti Spiritus, aliquando scriptæ sunt. Instabam igitur, vt medium illud, quod ego ad eundem sensum è Scripturis eruendum nominaram,
units.tr: He conceded that a true understanding of the Scriptures was necessary, and that the sacred writings could have no value in judging controversies unless they were taken in the sense in which they were at some time written under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. So I pressed him to refute, with solid arguments, the means which I had named for drawing out that same sense from the Scriptures,

units.la: vel oppugnaret firmis rationibus, vel pro legitimo amplecteretur ; vel demum aliud quoddam, magis ad eam rem idoneum adferret. Quia vero cunctanter admodū agebat; Ego sermonem prosecutus, duobus fundamentis stabiliui sententiam meam; quorum alterum e Scripturis desumpsi: alterum vero ab ipsorum Apostolorum exemplo, & perpetua Ecclesiæ Catholicæ praxi.
units.tr: or else to accept it as lawful, or finally to bring forward some other means better suited to the purpose. But since he was very hesitant, I pursued the discussion and supported my view on two foundations: one of which I took from the Scriptures, and the other from the example of the Apostles themselves and the perpetual practice of the Catholic Church.

units.la: Principio D. Petrum adduxi; qui cūm priuatam interpretationem Scripturæ reijcit, procul dubio requirit publicā, vti iam ante dictum est; quam non obscurè eidem Spiritui assc̈ribit, à quo inspirati locuti sunt sancti Dei homines; vt Apostolus ipse loquitur. Quemadmodum igitur non humana voluntate allata est aliquando Scriptura, sed à Spiritu sancto dictata atque contexta; Ita nec priuatim ab hominibus, sed ab eodem Spiritu sancto publicè resoluenda est atque interpretanda: Quod omniū certissimè per generalia Concilia, & perpetuum vniuersalis Ecclesiæ consensum fieri dixi. Aliud quoque protuli Scripturæ dictum ex Epistola D. Pauli ad Ephesios cap. 4. 4 . Ipse dedit quosdam quidem Apostolos, quosdam autem Prophetas, alios vero Euangelistas, alios autem Pastores ac Doctores, ad consummationem sanctorum, in opus ministerij, in ædificationem corporis Christi, &c. vt iam, inquit, nonsimus paruuli fluctuantes, & circumferamur omni vento doctrinæ, &c. Quamobrem, si quæritur doctrinæ certitudo, quæ ex vera Scripturarum intelligentia dependet, nimirum audiendi sunt Prophetæ illi, Pastores, atque Doctores, quos D. Paulus in eum finem à Deo datos asserit, vt non circumferamur omni vento doctrinæ, in nequitia hominum, in astutia ad circumuentionem erroris. Huiusmodi vero Prophetæ, Pastores, atque Doctores nunquam in Ecclesia defuerunt; vt semper iuxta D. Petri metem, publicam audire Spiritus sancti vocem, & veram Scripturarum intelligentiam habere licuerit.
units.tr: First I cited St. Peter, who, when he rejects private interpretation of Scripture, without doubt requires a public one, as has already been said. He plainly ascribes this public interpretation to the same Spirit by whom the holy men of God spoke when inspired, as the Apostle himself says. Just as Scripture was once brought forth not by human will but was dictated and composed by the Holy Spirit, so it is not to be explained and interpreted privately by men, but publicly by the same Holy Spirit. I said this is most certainly done through general Councils and the perpetual consensus of the universal Church. I also brought forward another saying of Scripture, from St. Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 4: "He gave some indeed to be Apostles, and some Prophets, and others Evangelists, and others Ministers and Teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ, etc., so that now, he says, we are no longer children tossed about and carried round by every wind of doctrine, etc." Therefore, if we seek certainty of doctrine, which depends on a true understanding of the Scriptures, then surely we must hear those Prophets, Ministers and Teachers whom St. Paul says God gave for this end, so that we are not carried round by every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, by cunning to deceive with error. Such Prophets, Ministers and Teachers have never been lacking in the Church, so that, in keeping with St. Peter's mind, it has always been possible to hear the public voice of the Holy Spirit and to have a true understanding of the Scriptures.

units.la: Addidi, secundo loco, ipsorum Apostolorū exemplū, per quos in Concilio Hierosolymitano congregatos, vti ex Actorum cap. 15. constat, idem Spiritus sanctus controversiam de Circucisione & Legalibus, ad hunc eundem modum publica voce definiuit. Ne vero quisquam dubitaret, illius Concilij sententiam, veram ac germanam Spiritus sancti vocem esse, Apostoli hac scribendi forma vti voluerunt: Visum est Spiritui sancto & nobis. Atq; hunc morem dijudicandi controversias, à Spiritu sancto per Apostolos demonstratum, Ecclesia postmodum in Concilio Niceno, Constantinopolitano, Ephesino, & reliquis item sequentibus, vsque ad hæc nostra tempora, perpetuò secuta est.
units.tr: Second, I added the example of the Apostles themselves, through whom, gathered in the Council of Jerusalem, as is clear from Acts chapter 15, the same Holy Spirit defined by public voice the controversy about circumcision and the legal observances in this same way. Lest anyone doubt that the judgment of that Council was the true and genuine voice of the Holy Spirit, the Apostles chose to use this form of writing: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us." And this custom of judging controversies, shown by the Holy Spirit through the Apostles, the Church afterwards consistently followed, at the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and the others that followed, right down to our own times.

units.la: Ad hæc ille: Non repugnare se, quin Concilia suo loco habeantur; modò vera sint, ac legitimè congregata. Respondi, Me de nullis aliis loqui Concilijs, quàm de ijs, quæ legitimè congregantur. Tum quidam ex præsentibus quærebat obiter; An non vllum posset Concilium nominare, quod legitimè congregatum existimaret? Ad quam vocem, quasi perculsus, subticuit. Mox conuersus in aliam partem, Concilia, inquit, declarare quidem illa Spiritus sancti mentem in Scripturis; Sed vt nouos articulos fidei cõderent, eam auctoritatem nunquã vsurpasse. Neq; vero licere Concilijs aliquid noui definire; sed illud ipsum, quod iam ante in Scripturis à Spiritu sancto definitum sit, Concilia per disquisitionem legitimam eruere, ac in lucem proferre. His verbis homo callidus diuerticulum quærebat, ad quod dissimulanter à causæ statu deflecteret. Neque enim hoc inter nos quærebatur; An Concilia nouos possint articulos fidei condere; Verum disceptabamus de medio, quod ego ad eruendam è Scripturis veritatem nominaram. Id vero medium ipsdem omnino verbis, quibus alio dilabi conabatur, vel imprudes probabat, dum Concilia veram Spiritus sancti mentem in Scripturis declarare fatebatur: Hoc enim idipsum erat, quod ego conabar obtinere.
units.tr: To this he replied that he did not object to the Councils being given their due place, provided they were true and lawfully gathered. I answered that I spoke of no Councils other than those lawfully gathered. Then one of those present asked in passing whether he could not name any Council which he judged to have been lawfully gathered. At this question, as if struck, he fell silent. Then, turning to another point, he said that Councils indeed declare the mind of the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures, but they never assumed the authority to frame new articles of faith. Councils are not permitted to define anything new; rather, they must bring to light through lawful inquiry only what the Holy Spirit has already defined in the Scriptures. With these words the crafty man was seeking a side path, by which he could covertly turn aside from the state of the question. For what was being asked between us was not whether Councils could frame new articles of faith; we were disputing about the means which I had named for drawing the truth from the Scriptures. Yet, either unwittingly or without thinking, he approved that very means in the same words by which he was trying to slip away elsewhere, when he admitted that Councils declare the true mind of the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures. For this was exactly what I was trying to obtain.

units.la: Quanquam vero nolui diuertentem à via sequi, respondi tamen breuiter, Concilia non declarare modo, vel interpretari Scripturas, verum etiam in controuersijs pro sua auctoritate decernere ac definire, quid verū sit, & quid falsum: Atque ijs definitionibus, tanquam publicæ voci sancti Spiritus, acquiescendum esse. Id confirmaui produĉtis Hierosolymitani Concilij verbis: Visum est enim Spiritui sancto, & nobis; quæ non modo ius declarandi Scripturas, verum & definiendi auctoritate præ se ferunt.
units.tr: Although I did not want to follow him off his path, I nonetheless replied briefly that councils not only declare or interpret the Scriptures, but also, by their own authority, decide and define in controversies what is true and what is false; and that these definitions are to be accepted as the public voice of the Holy Spirit. I confirmed this by citing the words of the Jerusalem Council: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us; words which carry with them the authority not only to declare the Scriptures but also to define.

units.la: Vrgebat ille, Apostolos diligenter expendisse Scripturas, atque ex ijs controuersiam, quæ fuerat exorta, decidisse. Eodem modo in reliquis etiam Concilijs subsequentibus actum esse: quæ semper è Scripturis, ac Dei verbo controuersias definierint. Ego lubens concessi, magnam fieri disquisitionem in Concilijs, diligenter examinari ac ponderari Scripturas, earumque mentem, ductu sancti Spiritus declarari: Verum eare non auferri Concilijs plenam illam definiendi ac constituendi auctoritatem, quam illi conciliet Spiritus sancti præsentia; quemadmodum ex Hierosolymitani Concilij verbis à me sit demonstratum.
units.tr: He pressed that the apostles had carefully weighed the Scriptures and settled the controversy that had arisen from them, and that the same procedure was followed in the later councils, which had always settled controversies from the Scriptures and the word of God. I gladly granted that there is a great deal of inquiry in councils, that the Scriptures are carefully examined and weighed, and that their meaning is declared under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. But I maintained that this does not take away from the councils that full authority to define and establish which the presence of the Holy Spirit gives them, as I had shown from the words of the Jerusalem Council.

units.la: Cæterum vt summam ac plenariam hanc auctoritatem, quam ego Concilijs generalibus integram esse volebam, arroderet, atque in dubium vocaret, aliam quoque rationem adduxit. Veterem Synagogam, inquit, procul dubio veram Ecclesiam fuisse, ac verū habuisse Dei cultum, vsque ad Christi mortem. Hanc ipsam vero Synagogam eo impietatis deuenisse, vt Hierosolymę in plenario Concilio, Christum innocentem publico decreto mortis reum pronunciarit: Quem omnium iudicio, gravissimum errorem fuisse constet. Simile quiddam in Ecclesia Noui Testamenti vsu venire posse, si tantam Ecclesiæ atque Concilijs auctoritatem tribuamus.
units.tr: Moreover, in order to undermine and call into doubt this full and complete authority, which I wanted to belong entire to the general councils, he brought forward another argument. The old synagogue, he said, was without doubt the true Church and had the true worship of God up until the death of Christ. Yet this same synagogue fell into such impiety that at Jerusalem, in a full council, it pronounced Christ, though innocent, guilty of death by public decree; which, by everyone's judgement, was clearly a most serious error. A similar thing, he said, could happen in the Church of the New Testament, if we grant such great authority to the Church and to councils.

units.la: Respondi: Quid autem, si ego demonstrare possim, decretum illud Iudæorum certa quadam ratione iustum fuisse, fuiffuisse? Quanquam non lubet id nunc pluribus. Certè, si Christi summam innocentiam, ac summam quoque Iudæorum malitiam spectes, iniquissimum fuit decretum; æquissimum verò, si Dei Patris dispensationem, ac culpā nostram attendas, quam ille luendam in se receperat, ideoque non tam suam, quàm totius humani generis personam repræsentabat. Atque eo quidem respectu tam iusta dici potest Iudæorum sententia, quàm verè post lapsum reus mortis fuit Adam, ac tota ipsius progenies, cuius tum personam sustinuit Christus: Vt huius rei consideratione iustum fuerit, ac calculo Spiritus sancti, per Caipham loquentis confirmatum illius Concilij decretum. At si tantum spectes intentionem ac malitiam Iudæorum, qui Christum innocentem morte damnarunt, certè generalia Concilia, quæ præsidem habent, ac gubernatorem Spiritum sanctum, cum hoc impio conventu non sunt comparanda.
units.tr: I replied: But what if I could show that the decision of the Jews was, for a certain reason, just? Though I do not wish to go into many details now. Certainly, if you look at Christ's supreme innocence and at the supreme wickedness of the Jews, the decree was most unjust; but it was most just if you consider the dispensation of God the Father and our guilt, which Christ had taken upon himself to pay, and so he represented not so much his own person as that of the whole human race. In this respect the sentence of the Jews can be called as just as it was true that Adam, and his whole progeny after the fall, were liable to death, whose person Christ then bore; so that, with this in view, the decree of that council was just, and was confirmed by the reckoning of the Holy Spirit speaking through Caiaphas. But if you look only at the intention and malice of the Jews who condemned innocent Christ to death, then certainly the general councils, which have the Holy Spirit as their president and governor, are not to be compared with that impious assembly.

units.la: Hæc ego; Quibus Dominus Hardenradius Consul & alia quædam adiecit: Ego quidem, inquit, non intelligo, quomodo hæc Synagogæ veteris, & Ecclesiæ comparatio subsistere possit. Erat enim hoc prædictum in Scripturis, futurum aliquando tempus, ut Dei populus Christum morte damnatum occideret. Contra verò Ecclesiæ (quam generalia Concilia repræsentant) iam ante promissus est Spiritus sanctus, ut illi adsit usque ad seculi finem, eamque perpetuò moderetur, & ab erroribus immunem conservet. Quemadmodum igitur Spiritus sanctus insignem illum Synagogæ veteris errorem in scripturis prædixit, ita plurima quoque extant eiusdem Spiritus sancti vaticinia, de insuperabili firmitate Ecclesiæ, nullis unquam errorum portentis expugnandæ. Quin Christus & Apostoli iam ante prædixerunt, futurum extremis temporibus, non ut ipsa Ecclesia, eiusque legitimi Præsides à veræ fidei doctrina deficerent, sed ut huiusmodi pseudopseudoprophetæ non vocati fraudulenter subreperent gregi dominico, ac contra communem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ sensum atque consensum, noua dogmata, sub ouinæ pellis velamine, simplicioribus obtruderent: Quos illi cauendos esse, solicite monuerunt. Ad hæc ille nihil respondit.
units.tr: So far I; to which Lord Hardenradius, the consul, added some other things as well: I, for my part, he said, do not see how this comparison between the old synagogue and the Church can hold. For it was foretold in the Scriptures that a time would come when the people of God would kill Christ, condemned to death. On the other hand, the Holy Spirit was promised in advance to the Church (which the general councils represent) so that he would be with it until the end of the age and would always govern it and keep it free from errors. Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit foretold in the Scriptures that remarkable error of the old synagogue, so there also exist many prophecies of the same Holy Spirit concerning the unconquerable firmness of the Church, which is never to be overthrown by any monstrous errors. Indeed, Christ and the apostles foretold beforehand that in the last times it would not be that the Church itself, and its lawful presidents, would fall away from the doctrine of the true faith, but that false prophets of this kind, not sent, would creep craftily into the Lord's flock and, against the common sense and consensus of the Catholic Church, would foist new dogmas on the simpler folk under the cover of sheep's skin; and they earnestly warned that these must be guarded against. To this he made no reply.

units.la: Quia vero præter Concilia, perpetuum ac vniuersalem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ consensum vrgebam, respondit; Incertam fieri sacrarum litterarum intelligentiam, si hoc argumento debeat æstimari. Posse enim & inter errantes aliquam esse consensionem. Fuisse præterea primis Ecclesiæ temporibus inter Doctores, qui suis opinionibus vniuersalem illum consensum turbarint: Papiam D. Ioannis Euangelistæ discipulum Chiliastarum errorem, sub Apostolicæ traditionis titulo, produxisse: in cuius erroris consortium & D. Irenæum, & cõplures alios pertractos esse constet; inter quos etiam consensus quidam fuerit. Iam & Tertullianum prauis quibusdam opinionibus imbutum fuisse, adeoque in Montani hæresin lapsum. Addidit & Origenē, & Cyprianum, quos docuisse quædam erronea, & suos etiam sectatores habuisse accepimus. Atque ex his omnibus (si recte mentem eius assecutus sum) duo conficere voluit. Primum est; Posse errantium etiam aliquam in propugnandis erroribus esse concordiam: Alterum vero, consensum Ecclesiæ perpetuum, quem ego vrgebam, quorundam Patrum hallucinationibus rumpi, vt adeo pro vero sensu diuini Spiritus haberi tutò nequeat.
units.tr: Because, besides the councils, I was insisting on the perpetual and universal consensus of the Catholic Church, he replied that the understanding of the sacred letters would become uncertain if it were to be judged by this argument. For there can be some agreement even among those who err. Moreover, in the earliest times of the Church there were teachers who disturbed that universal consensus by their opinions: Papias, a disciple of the apostle John, put forward the error of the Chiliasts under the title of apostolic tradition; and it is established that Irenaeus, and many others, were drawn into this error, and among these too there was a certain agreement. Also Tertullian was imbued with some wrong opinions, and so fell into the heresy of Montanus. He added that Origen and Cyprian, whom we have heard taught certain erroneous things, also had their followers. And from all these things (if I have rightly grasped his meaning) he wished to draw two conclusions. The first is that even those who err may have some agreement in defending their errors; the second, that the perpetual consensus of the Church, which I was urging, is broken by the delusions of certain Fathers, so that it cannot safely be held to be the true sense of the divine Spirit.

units.la: Respondi, Loqui me non de quouis, aut quorumuis consensu sub Christi nomine; sed de consensu illo generali, quem per vniuersum orbem Christianum, de summis Christianæ Religionis articulis, deque Scripturarum intelligentia, inter Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Doctores semper vigui sse, certis indicijs constet. Eum vero consensum, prouti dubio publicam esse Spiritus sancti vocem, quam perpetuo petuò in populo Dei, vel in Ecclesia Catholica sonàtem audire licuerit. Non inficiari me, quin inter errantes etiam concordia nonnunquam esse possit, verùm eam raro diuturnam esse, perpetuam pene nunquam; quemadmodum exemplis demonstrari queat. Neque verò priuatos quorundam patrum lapsus, huic admirabili atque perpetuo Christiani orbis consensui quicquam derogare. Hallucinatos esse procul dubio veteres illos, quos exemplicausa nominarit; at nunquam eò deueniisse tamen, vt errores suos contra legitimam Ecclesiae Catholicae, vel vniuersalis cuiusdam Concilij definitionem, ac publicam Spiritus Sancti vocem pertinaciter defenderint. Fuisse igitur priuatorum hominum priuatos lapsus, quibus ille publicus ac vniuersalis Doctorum in Ecclesia consensus, quem Spiritus Sanctus à temporibus Apostolorum, vsque ad hanc nostram aetatem, integrum atque illaesum conseruarit, nequaquam infringatur: Vt adeò si Papias errarisi, si Irenaeus, si Tertullianus, vel Cyprianus, aut alius quispiam aliquando sit hallucinatus, eam ob rem ne quaquam dicendum sit, orbis vniuersi consensionem in doctrina Religionis, & intelligentia Scripturae defecisse. Itaque nihil illum in huiusmodi exemplis, ad reijciendum orbis Christiani consensum, praesidij habere.
units.tr: I replied that I was not speaking of any consensus whatever, or of whatever people, under the name of Christ; but of that general consensus which, as is clear from certain indications, has always flourished throughout the whole Christian world, concerning the chief articles of the Christian religion and the understanding of the Scriptures, among the teachers of the Catholic Church. And this consensus, I said, is without doubt the public voice of the Holy Spirit, which may be heard sounding continually among the people of God, or in the Catholic Church. I did not deny that agreement can sometimes exist even among those who err, but that it is rarely lasting and almost never perpetual, as can be shown by examples. Nor do the private lapses of certain Fathers detract in any way from this wonderful and perpetual consensus of the Christian world. Those old writers whom he named as examples were no doubt deluded; yet they never went so far as to defend their errors stubbornly against the lawful definition of the Catholic Church or of some universal council, or against the public voice of the Holy Spirit. So the private lapses of private men do not overturn that public and universal consensus of the teachers in the Church, which the Holy Spirit has preserved whole and unharmed from the times of the apostles down to our own age. Therefore, even if Papias erred, or Irenaeus, Tertullian, or Cyprian, or some other person was at some time deluded, it must by no means be said that the consensus of the whole world in doctrine of religion and in understanding of Scripture has failed. Thus he had no support in such examples for rejecting the consensus of the Christian world.

units.la: Cùm ego ad hunc modum publicā in Ecclesia Scripturarum interpretationem vrgerem, & ille nonnunquam, quasi tergiuersabundus se reprimeret, dixi per occasionem inter reliqua; Quemadmodum Ecclesia Catholica Scripturam sanctam hactenus conseruarit, suoque testimonio atque auctoritate, libros canonicos à non canonicis discreuerit; Vt adeo Ecclesiae auctoritatem secuti, Prophetarum, Apostolorum atque Euangelistarū scripta, illorum reuera esse; tum quae illi scripserint, esse Dei verbum, indubitatò credamus: Ita nec aliunde, quàm ab eadem Ecclesia, veram eiusdem scripti verbi intelligentiam petendam. Caeterum eam ad rem non esse certitus medium, quàm si publicam Conciliorum vocem, & perpetuum orbis Christiani consensum audiamus.
units.tr: While I was urging in this way the public interpretation of the Scriptures in the Church, and he at times, as if making excuses, held himself back, I said, among other things and by way of occasion: just as the Catholic Church has hitherto preserved the holy Scripture, and by its testimony and authority has distinguished the canonical books from the non-canonical, so that, following the authority of the Church, we believe without doubt that the writings of the prophets, apostles and evangelists are truly theirs, and that what they wrote is the word of God; so also the true understanding of that written word must be sought from that same Church and from nowhere else. Moreover, I said, there is no surer means for this than if we hear the public voice of the councils and the perpetual consensus of the Christian world.

units.la: Hæc ego: Ille verò, vt vafer erat, ex oratione mea, via sibi ad elabendum sternere conatus est. Quæsiuit igitur ex me, An non Iudæi veteris Testamenti Scripturam, ex maiorum suorum testimonio pro Dei verbo habuerint? Cumque in affirmantem partem respondissem, quæsiuit iterum: An igitur Iudæorum quoque Cabala legitimum intelligendæ Scripturæ medium fuerit, propterea, quod ab ijsdem maioribus profecta erat, qui testimonium de libris canonicis ad posteros transmiserunt? Dixi, Medium illud inueniendæ veritatis in scripturis, quod à me prolatum sit, cum Iudæorum Cabala non esse conferendum. Ille verò contrarium probare nitebatur. Quod, inquit, Iudæis Cabala fuit præter diuinæ Scripturæ libros, id vobis est præter sacras litteras traditio, quam verbum Dei non scriptum appellatis. Ea verò non magis indigemus, quàm illa Cabala Iudæorum; cùm omnia, quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt, scripto Dei verbo abundè continentur. Hac stropha dissimulater à proposito, ad quæstionem de Traditionibus, & Verbo Dei non Scripto, deflectere voluit.
units.tr: So far I. But he, being crafty, seized on my speech and tried to find a way of escape. He therefore asked me whether the Jews did not hold the Scripture of the Old Testament to be the word of God on the testimony of their forefathers. When I answered in the affirmative, he asked again: then was the Cabala of the Jews also a lawful means of understanding Scripture, because it had come from those same forefathers who handed down to posterity the testimony about the canonical books? I said that the means of finding the truth in the Scriptures which I had put forward was not to be compared with the Cabala of the Jews. He, however, strove to prove the contrary. Just as, he said, the Jews had the Cabala besides the books of divine Scripture, so you have tradition besides the sacred letters, which you call the unwritten word of God. But we have no more need of that than of the Cabala of the Jews, since everything necessary for salvation is abundantly contained in the written word of God. By this turn he wished to slip away from the point, and to turn the question to traditions and the unwritten word of God.

units.la: Respondi, dubium nō esse, quin Apostoli quædam in Ecclesia viua voce tradiderint, quæ calamo non sint abipsis exarata; quemadmodum colligi possit ex illo Dꝰ Pauli: State, & tenete Traditiones, quas didicistis siue per sermonem, siue per Epistolam nostram. Quibus verbis Apostolus ea, quæ docuerit, se partim viua voce, partim scripto tradidisse testatur. Neque diffiteri nos, quin Verbum Dei quoddam nō scriptum agnoscamus; Certum esse, quod non omnia litteris consignata sint, quæ dixerit ac fecerit Christus. Quin & Symbolum Apostolorum nusquam in libris Scripturæ Canonicis inueniri, quod tamen nō modò Dei verbo cōforme sit, sed & ipsum, iuxta verborum seriem atque contextum, pro voce sancti Spiritus, & indubita-
units.tr: I replied that there is no doubt that the Apostles handed down in the Church, by living voice, certain things that were never written down by their own pen, as can be gathered from the words of St. Paul: Stand fast and hold the traditions which you have been taught, whether by word or by our epistle. By these words the Apostle testifies that he delivered what he taught partly by living voice and partly in writing. Nor do we deny that we acknowledge an unwritten word of God. It is certain that not everything Christ said and did was committed to writing. Indeed, the Apostles' Creed is nowhere to be found in the canonical books of Scripture, yet it not only agrees with the word of God but also, judging by the sequence and context of its words, must be regarded as the voice of the Holy Spirit and as an undoubted (indubita-)

units.la: 2. Thess. 2. dubitato Dei verbo non minus haberi oporteat, quàm id, quod Apostolorum atque Euángelistarum calamis exaratum legimus; cùm vtrumque ab vno eodemq; Spiritu profectum sit, qui hoc calamo quidem in charta; illud autem digito suo in Ecclesiæ corde descriptum, tradere ac conseruare voluerit. Iam si Symbolum illud Apostolicum, quod procul dubio contextum sit à Spiritu sancto, tũ Traditiones ab ipsis Apostolis profectas, quas teneri mandet D. Paulus, cum Iudæorum Cabala comparare velit, eam verò insignem esse contumeliam, quæ reuera in Spiritum sanctum redundet. Quanquam nolle me nunc in disputationem de Traditionibus, & Verbo non scripto profundius ingredi: Quæstionem inter nos esse de medio à me prolato, per quod verum germanumque sensum verbi scripti, vel sacrarum litterarum, in controuersijs erui, ac publica voce declarari oporteat. Ab huius itaque Quæstionis cardine non esse nunc deflectendum.
units.tr: (2 Thess. 2.) an indubitable word of God, and it ought to be held no less than what we read as written by the pens of the Apostles and Evangelists, since both proceeded from one and the same Spirit, who wished to deliver and preserve the one written on paper by this pen, and the other inscribed by his own finger on the heart of the Church. Now if that Apostolic Creed, which was undoubtedly composed by the Holy Spirit, then the traditions descended from the Apostles themselves, which St. Paul commands us to hold, Badius wishes to compare with the Cabala of the Jews. That would be a remarkable insult, one which in truth reflects upon the Holy Spirit. Yet I am not now willing to enter more deeply into a disputation about traditions and the unwritten word. The question between us concerns the means I have put forward, by which the true and genuine sense of the written word, or of the sacred letters, ought to be drawn out in controversies and declared by public voice. Therefore we must not now turn aside from the hinge of this question.

units.la: Post huiusmodi diuturnam concertationem, demum & ipse quoddam intelligendæ Scripturæ medium protulit; quod vt antea faceret, quamquam aliquoties à me monitus, non potuit induci. Scripturæ mentem, aiebat, per collationem locorum intelligi posse; si nimirum obscuriora loca, per alia, quæ magis dilucida sunt, ac plana, declarentur. Atque eam rationem, à D. Augustino, in libris de doctrina Christiana traditam esse. Excepi ego, agnoscere me D. Augustini regulam; nec infici ari, quin collatio Scripturarum, ad intelligendum loca difficiliora magno vsui sacrarum litterarum studiosis esse possit: Verùm si solam hac collationem, tanquam sufficiens ac infallibile medium protulerit, quo, cùm controuersia exoritur de Scripturæ sensu, veram Spiritus sancti mentem declarari oporteat, vehementer ipsum falli. Nec eam D. Augustini mentem vnquam fuisse.
units.tr: After such a long contention, at last he himself also put forward a certain means of understanding Scripture; though, although I had often urged him to do so earlier, he could not be persuaded to. The mind of Scripture, he said, can be understood by comparing passages: namely, if the obscure places are explained by others that are clearer and plainer. He added that this method was laid down by St. Augustine in his books On Christian Doctrine. I replied that I acknowledge St. Augustine's rule, nor do I deny that the comparison of Scriptures can be of great use to diligent students of the sacred letters in understanding more difficult passages. But if he were to put forward this comparison alone as a sufficient and infallible means by which, when controversy arises over the sense of Scripture, the true mind of the Holy Spirit ought to be declared, then he would be gravely mistaken. Nor was that ever St. Augustine's view.

units.la: Hoc loco monendum est, D. Augustinum non loqui de illa Scripturarum collatione, quæ fit in Concilijs generalibus auctoritate publica, per quam veritas diligenti conquisitione velut eliquata tandem solidatur, vtidem D. Augustinus alibi loquitur; sed de ea, quæ priuatim instituitur, studio atque industria doctorum virorū, qui Scripturis intelligendis atque explicandis operam nauant. Hanc solam non sufficere ad eruendam in controuersijs veritatem, rationibus quibusdā demonstraui.
units.tr: Here it must be noted that St. Augustine is not speaking of that comparison of Scriptures which is carried out in general councils by public authority, by which the truth, as if refined by diligent inquiry, is at last made firm, as St. Augustine speaks of elsewhere; he speaks of the comparison that is undertaken privately, by the zeal and industry of learned men who labour at understanding and explaining the Scriptures. I have shown by certain reasons that this private comparison alone is not sufficient for discovering truth in controversies.

units.la: Principio, inquam, huiusmodi collatio medium est reuera humanum: Homines enim sunt, qui conferunt Scripturas, easque per collationem declarant, vt ipsorū declarationi, tanquam infallibili, fidere non sit tutū. Ad eruendam vero Spiritus sancti mentem, opus est altiori quodā ac diuino medio, quod fallere nō possit, ad quod etiam, velut ad normam quandam, inter conferendum respicere oporteat; vt nimirum idem Spiritus mentem suam declaret in Scripturis, cuius instinctu eædem scriptæ sunt. Deinde Scriptura nō est priuatæ resolutionis vel interpretationis, quemadmodū D. Petrus testatur. Constat vero, collationem hanc, per quam Scriptura quasi resoluitur, priuatim fieri ab hoc, aut illo homine, vel à paucis quibusdam, priuatim tamen. Igitur ad Spiritus sancti mentem declarandā non sufficit. Accedit, quod nulla vnquam de Scripturæ sensu controuersia, per hoc medium cōpositā fuerit: Imò testatur experientia, quicunq; hoc solo collationis medio vtuntur, eos, si sententijs dissideant, non modò ad concordiam non redigi, verum etiam quo diutius Scriptu ras conferunt, eò longius à se mutuo dissilire. Cuius rei viuum exemplum in certaminibus horum temporum intueri licet. Conferunt Scripturas Lutherani, dum contra vos pugnant; confertis & vos contra illos, tum contra Anabaptistas quoque; Atq; hi contra vos vtrosque vicissim. At, quid aliud tandem efficitur, nisi vt grauius indies à vobis ipsis dissideatis?
units.tr: First, I said, such a comparison is really a human means. For it is men who compare the Scriptures and declare them by comparison, so that it is not safe to trust their declaration as if it were infallible. But to discover the mind of the Holy Spirit we need a higher and divine means, which cannot deceive, and to which one must also look, as to a certain rule, in comparing; so that the same Spirit may declare his mind in the Scriptures, by whose prompting they were written. Next, Scripture is not of private resolution or interpretation, as St. Peter testifies. It is clear, however, that this comparison, by which Scripture is as it were resolved, is carried out privately by this or that man, or by a few, yet privately. Therefore it is not sufficient for declaring the mind of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, no controversy about the sense of Scripture has ever been settled by this means. Indeed experience testifies that all who use this sole means of comparison, if they disagree in opinions, are not only not brought to concord, but the longer they compare the Scriptures, the further they leap apart from one another. A living example of this can be seen in the quarrels of our times. The Lutherans compare the Scriptures while they fight against you; you also compare them against them, and against the Anabaptists too; and these in turn against you both. But what else is finally brought about, except that you disagree with one another more gravely every day?

units.la: His dictis repressi me nonnihil, vt scilicet illi locum darem, si forte contra rationes meas quicquam in medium proferre vellet. Cum vero nihil adferret, ego sermonem prosecutus: Sic olim, inquam, Arriani quoque contulerunt Scripturas, ut errorem suum tuerentur; fecerunt idem in contrarium & Catholici pro veritate: Ea tamen re nec sopita est controversia, nec repressus error. Igitur cum Scripturæ ad hunc modum in fidei controversiis, hinc inde priuatim conferuntur, necesse est, ut sit iudex aliquis, qui publica voce definiat, vtrius partis collatio νομίμως ac rite, secundum analogiam fidei, ac Spiritus sancti mentem facta sit.
units.tr: Having said these things, I held myself back somewhat, so as to give him room, in case he wished to bring forward anything against my reasons. When he offered nothing, I went on with my speech: "Thus, I said, the Arians too once compared the Scriptures in order to defend their error; the Catholics did the same in the opposite direction for the truth. Yet by this means the controversy was neither calmed nor the error checked. Therefore, since in controversies of faith Scriptures are compared privately on both sides, it is necessary that there be some judge who, by public voice, may determine whether the comparison of either party has been made lawfully [νομίμως] and rightly, according to the analogy of faith and the mind of the Holy Spirit."

units.la: Ad hæc ille repetebat exemplum Apostolorum in Concilio Hierosolymitano, quos veritatem in Scripturis per diligentem collationem inuenisse, inuentamque declarasse affirmabat: quam eandem viam & Patres, aiebat, in sequentium quoque temporum Concilijs ingredi consueuisse. Atque hoc sane cum dixit, nihil dixit contra me; imo denuo sententiam meam confirmauit. Nam ego, vti supra monui, contra priuatam Scripturæ collationem agebam, quæ studio fit huius aut illius, vel paucorum hominum: Ille vero, ut caute declinaret rationes meas, respondebat de publica, quæ fit in Conciliis generalibus ministerio ac ductu sancti Spiritus, ex qua demum eorundem Conciliorum definitiones promanant. Quando igitur Badius hanc probauit, adeo nihil dixit alienum à sententia mea, vt eam vel imprudens amplexus sit, ac confirmarit.
units.tr: To this he kept repeating the example of the Apostles at the Council of Jerusalem, who, he asserted, had found the truth in the Scriptures through careful comparison, and had declared what they had found; and he said the Fathers too were accustomed to follow this same way in the councils of later times. Indeed, when he said this, he said nothing against me; rather, he confirmed my opinion once more. For I, as I warned above, was arguing against the private comparison of Scripture, which is made by the zeal of this or that man or of a few men. But he, in order to cautiously evade my reasons, answered about the public comparison, which is made in general councils under the ministry and guidance of the Holy Spirit, and from which at last the definitions of those councils proceed. Therefore, when Badius approved this, he said nothing so foreign to my view that he embraced it, and even confirmed it, though unwittingly.

units.la: Interea tamen aliquoties protestatus sum, me priuatam illam Scripturarum collationem, quam D. Augustini regula sacrarum litterarum studiosis præscribit, nequaquam repudiare, sed eam relinquere suo loco; modo legitime fiat secundum analogiam fidei, & ad publicam illam vbique dirigatur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, however, I have several times protested that I by no means reject that private comparison of Scriptures which St. Augustine's rule prescribes for students of the sacred letters, but leave it in its place, provided it is done lawfully according to the analogy of faith and is everywhere directed to that public judgment.

units.la: Quanquam vero Collationem suam reliquit indefessam, nondum tamen penitus acquiescere videbatur. Itaque que D. Crantius, Agite vero, inquit, date specimen aliquod istius collationis, & utrinque Scripturas de quoda Religionis articulo conferte, nimirum ut res tota per exemplum aliquod clarius elucescat. Placuit mihi conditio. Itaque ego huiusmodi collationem instituí.
units.tr: Although he had left off his comparison, unwearied, he did not yet seem fully satisfied. And so Crantius said: "Come now, give some specimen of that comparison, and both sides, compare the Scriptures on some article of religion, so that the whole matter may become clearer through an example." I agreed to the condition. And so I set about carrying out such a comparison.

units.la: Affero, inquam, Esse aliquod in Ecclesia Noui Testamenti visibile sacrificium ac sacerdotium, quod, vbi venerit, tollet Antichristus. Id vt probem ex scripturis, principio locum profero ex Genesis cap. 14. de Melchisedecho, qui Sacerdos fuit, & Rex, Christique figuram gessit. Adiungo locum alterum ex Psalmo 109. Iurauit Dominus, & non poenitebit eum, tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Cum his locis confero prophetiam Malachiae, cap. 1. de oblatione munda, ab ortu solis vsque ad occasum, in omni loco sacrificanda atque offerenda, eam quae de sacrificio Missae intelligendam esse contendo. Ex his locis inter se collatis hoc ipsum concludo, quod ante dixi, Esse nimirum externum aliquod sacerdotium ac sacrificium in Ecclesia: Christum sacerdotem aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech, idipsum sacerdotiu in vltima Coena non exercuisse modo, verum etiam reliquisse discipulis exercendum, toto terrarum orbe, vsque ad mundi finem. Oblationem vero istius sacrificij mundam esse, adumbratam per Melchisedechum, qui panem & vinum obtulit: cuius vmbrae veritas sit in sacrificio nostro, cum a sacerdote quopiam Christi gerente vices, sub speciebus panis ac vini, modo tamen incruento, Domini corpus & sanguis, in mortis eius memoriam Deo patri offertur. Adiungo compendij causa, haec scripturae collationem non meam esse solius, sed antiquorum etiam Patrum auctoritate niti: Quod adeo certum est, vt Caluinus ipse in libro de Scandalo sub finem, veteres in Coena sacrificium aliquod agnoscere fateatur.
units.tr: I assert, I said, that there is in the Church of the New Testament a visible sacrifice and priesthood, which Antichrist, when he comes, will take away. To prove this from Scripture, I first cite a passage from Genesis chapter 14 about Melchizedek, who was both priest and king and bore the figure of Christ. I add a second passage, from Psalm 109: The Lord has sworn, and will not repent: you are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. With these passages I compare the prophecy of Malachi, chapter 1, about the pure offering, to be sacrificed and offered in every place from the rising of the sun to its setting, which I maintain is to be understood of the sacrifice of the Mass. From these passages compared with one another I conclude precisely what I said before: namely, that there is in the Church an external priesthood and sacrifice, Christ being a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek, and that he not only exercised this priesthood at the last supper, but also left it to his disciples to exercise throughout the whole world until the end of the age. The pure offering of this sacrifice was foreshadowed by Melchizedek, who offered bread and wine; the truth of this shadow is in our sacrifice, when, by some priest acting in Christ's stead, under the appearances of bread and wine, yet in an unbloody manner, the body and blood of the Lord are offered to God the Father in memory of his death. I add, for brevity's sake, that this comparison of Scripture is not mine alone, but rests also on the authority of the ancient Fathers. This is so certain that Calvin himself, in his book On Scandal, toward the end, admits that the ancients acknowledged some sacrifice in the Supper.

units.la: Haec ego; Atque deinde locum dedi Badio, vt & ipse quandam Scripturae collationem institueret. Ille vero principio monuit, omisisse me primariu locu, quo Papistæ Missę sacrificium afferre niterentur; primam scilicet ipsius Cœnę Dominicę institutionem. Respōdi; Locu institutionis huius argumēti sedē esse, in qua Scripturę à me instituta collatio sua natura quasi pedem defixū habeat: Itaq; non fuisse necessarium, vt is seperatim proferretur.
units.tr: I said this, and then gave Badius the floor so that he too might set out some collation of Scripture. He first objected that I had left out the chief passage on which the Papists try to base the sacrifice of the Mass: the institution of the Lord's Supper itself. I replied that the account of the institution is the seat of this question, the place where my collation of Scripture, by its very nature, has its foot firmly fixed, so there was no need for it to be produced separately.

units.la: Postea locum Malachiæ Prophetæ, quem ego produxeram, non esse de huiusmodi externo sacrificio intelligendum afferebat, sed potius de sacrificio labiorum vel orationis, quod affirmabat à Propheta mundæ oblationis nomine designari; Neque id adeo mirum videri posse, quandoquidem & homines quidā mundi in Scripturis appellentur. Dixi, Eam interpretationem ipsorum met doctrinæ contrariam esse, cùm omnia etiam iustorum opera, quamdiu in hac vita sunt, immunda esse doceat. Et reuera nihil sub sole cogitari posse, cui melius quadret oblationis mūdę appellatio, quāsacrosanctā Eucharistiā, vt qua omnis munditiei fons & auctor continetur.
units.tr: Afterwards he argued that the passage of the prophet Malachi which I had cited should not be understood of this external sacrifice, but rather of the sacrifice of the lips, or of prayer, which he claimed the prophet meant by the name of a pure offering; and he said this was not so surprising, since some men too are called "pure" in Scripture. I replied that this interpretation was contrary to their own doctrine, since they teach that all the works of the righteous, for as long as they live in this life, are unclean. Indeed, nothing under the sun can be thought of to which the name "pure offering" fits better than the most holy Eucharist, which contains within itself every source and author of purity.

units.la: Adieci deinde locis à me citatis, & Danielis Prophetæ vaticinium de iugi sacrificio, auferendo per Antichristum: Demū & D. Pauli locū in Epistola ad Hebræos, applicatis Melchisedechi figuram ad Christum. Ille nonnihil obmurmurabat ad nomen D. Pauli, quem aiebat in Epistola ad Hebræos, nihil in hanc sententiā de sacrificio habere. Ego vero propterea D. Paulū adieci, quod is Melchisedechi figuram ad Christum applicet. Alioquin iam antea sententiam meam ex locis alijs inter se collatis exstruxeram: Quæ structura, tametsi D. Paulus ad eam nihil plane conferret (quod ego tamen non concessi) nihilominus ex reliquorum locorum collatione satis habet firmamenti, vt solidè consistat.
units.tr: I then added, to the passages I had cited, the prophet Daniel's prophecy about the continual sacrifice taken away by Antichrist, and finally the passage of St Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where he applies the figure of Melchizedek to Christ. He muttered somewhat at the name of St Paul, saying that the Epistle to the Hebrews contains nothing to this effect about sacrifice. But I had added St Paul precisely because he applies the figure of Melchizedek to Christ. Moreover, I had already built my argument beforehand from other passages compared with one another. Even if St Paul contributed nothing at all to it (which I did not concede), the comparison of the remaining passages is nonetheless firm enough to stand solidly on its own.

units.la: Quia verò Badius, nec quicquam attulit præterea contra collationem meam, nec specimen aliquod collationis pro parte sua dare voluit, quemadmodum ab ipso tamen requirebatur; repetij demum ego, quod antea quoque ra-
units.tr: Since Badius neither brought forward anything further against my collation, nor was willing to offer any specimen of a collation on his own side, although he was asked to do so, I finally repeated what I had also concluded earlier, with the reasons already given:

units.la: que rationibus allatis concluseram; Eam scilicet collat onem, per quam ille verum scripturae diuinae sensum rui oportere dixerat, non esse sufficiens medium in iu candis controuersijs, nisi vel generalium Concilioru definitionibus, vel vniuersalis Ecclesiae perpetuo co- sensu, tanquam publica Spiritus sancti voce, confirme- tur.
units.tr: namely, that the kind of collation by which he had said the true sense of divine Scripture must be sought is not a sufficient means of settling controversies, unless it is confirmed either by the decisions of general councils or by the perpetual common consent of the universal Church, as a public voice of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Caeterum cum ego ad hunc modum aliquoties Con- ciliorum definitiones, Spiritus sancti vocem appellare; Ille vero nihil adferret in contrarium, sed nescio quo consilio verba mea tacendo transmitteret; demum D. Consul Sudermannus, vt responsionem aliquam eliceret; Possim, inquit, ego diuinare quid cogitet; si metis arcanum fateri velit: Nimirum Episcopos, qui in Concilijs congregantur, Romano Pontifici iuramento deuinctos esse, vt nihil quicquam ausint definire, nisi quod eidem Pontifici placere, ac gratum esse intelligunt. Tum ad Badium conuersus est Dominus Consul, Satis scio, inquit, huiusmodi cogitationes in animo tuo versari. Quin igitur easdem libere profers? Ille vero ne sic quidem ad respondendum induci potuit. Dixi tamen ego, Non esse nunc quaestionem inter nos de Pontifice Romano, sed de Concil iorum definitionibus, deque perpetuo Ecclesiae Catholicae in scripturis intelligendis consensu. Aliud esse, si Pontificis auctoritas in quaestionem vocetur. Quoniam igitur ille nihil amplius afferebat, quo vel medium a me prolatum oppugnare, vel tueri suum niteretur, hic quidem collatio nostra finem habuit.
units.tr: Now, since I had several times called the decisions of the councils the voice of the Holy Spirit in this way, and he said nothing in reply but, for some reason I cannot fathom, let my words pass in silence, at last the honourable Consul Sudermann, to draw out some answer, said: "I can guess what he is thinking, if he wishes to reveal the secret: namely, that the bishops who gather in councils are bound by oath to the Roman Pontiff, so that they dare to define nothing except what they understand to be pleasing and acceptable to that same Pontiff." Then the Consul turned to Badius: "I know well that thoughts of this kind are in your mind. Why not then express them freely?" But he could not even be induced to answer in this way. I nevertheless said that the question between us was not now about the Roman Pontiff, but about the decisions of the councils and the perpetual consent of the Catholic Church in interpreting Scripture; it would be a different matter if the authority of the Pontiff were called into question. Since he then offered nothing further by which he might either attack the means I had put forward or defend his own, our collation came to an end at this point.

units.la: Antequam tamen eam concluderem, varij adhuc vltro citroque pro re nata, sermones inciderunt; de quibus ea notare placuit, quae ad praesens negocium facere videtur. Et ego quidem principio dixi; Quibus ille fundamentis in articulo de Eucharistia niteretur (ea vero sunt; Principia philosophiae naturalis & priuata Scripturae interpretatio, ad humanae rationis normam formata) ijsdem non minus Arrij blasphemiam de Christi diuinitate, tū aliorum hæreticorum nugas, quàm Sacramentariorum opinionem de Eucharistia superstrui posse. Quod Luthe-rus(inquam) sub initium huius controuersiæ de Cœna Domini, acutè vidit; quemadmodum testantur ipsius scripta contra Sacramentarios, quos ille iam tum monuit alere monstri quiddam; & Arrianismum in recessu habere. Neque verò Lutherus hac quidem in parte falsus est, quemadmodum euentus postea declarauit in Polonia, in Transyluania, tum ante paucos annos in Palatinatu quoque; Vbi Ioannes Syluanus, & Adamus Neuserus, primarij Caluinianæ Sectæ ministri, non tantùm ex Caluinianis Arriani facti sunt, & ex Arrianis porrò Mahometani, verùm etiam (quemadmodum mihi Ioannes Harenius, ex Caluiniano Ministro factus Catholicus, vir fide dignus, retulit) Concionatores aliquot sub Electore Palatino causæ suæ clam fauentes habuerunt: Quin & amicitiam contraxerunt cum Turcarum sacerdotibus, & datis acceptisque vltro citroque litteris, Mahometanam perfidiam in Germania quoque propagare conati sunt.
units.tr: Before I concluded it, however, various further conversations, spontaneous on both sides and arising as the matter required, took place. I thought it worth noting those points which seem to bear on the present business. And first I said this: the foundations on which he rests his position on the article about the Eucharist (these are the principles of natural philosophy and private interpretation of Scripture, shaped to the standard of human reason) can equally well support the blasphemy of Arius concerning the divinity of Christ, and the nonsense of other heretics, no less than the opinion of the Sacramentarians about the Eucharist. Luther, I said, saw this sharply at the beginning of this controversy about the Lord's Supper, as his writings against the Sacramentarians testify, in which he already then warned that they were nurturing a kind of monster and harboured Arianism in their hearts.
