Nor was Luther wrong on this point, as the outcome afterwards showed in Poland, in Transylvania, and a few years ago in the Palatinate too, where John Sylvanus and Adam Neuser, leading ministers of the Calvinist sect, not only turned from Calvinists into Arians, and from Arians further into Mahometans, but also (as John Harenius, a trustworthy man who went from being a Calvinist minister to being a Catholic, told me) had several preachers who secretly favoured their cause under the Elector Palatine. Indeed they also made friendship with the priests of the Turks, and by sending and receiving letters back and forth they tried to spread Mahometan perfidy in Germany as well.

units.la: Cùm ille adhæc omnia nihil responderet, ego sermone continuato; Ita nimirum fit, inquam, vt qui semel à veritate deflectunt, ij postea nusquam firmis vestigijs possint consistere. Quod reuera non vsque adeò mirandum est. Cùm enim quispiam in vno Religionis articulo locum dedit naturalibus principijs, Cur non & in alijs, qui sunt eiusdem generis, idem facere queat? Si propter rationis humanæ iudiciū cum Caluino negem, Christum in Eucharistia verè præsentem esse; quid obstet, quo minus eundem Christum cum Arrio quoq; verum Deum esse negem, cùm hoc posterius rationis iudicio non minus absurdum videatur, quàm prius illud? Neque verò minus quondam Arriani scripturæ sacrę præsidijs instru-cti fuerunt, ad oppugnandam Christi diuinitatem, quàm hoc tempore, ad negandā in Eucharistia corporis Christi præpræsentiam, instructi sunt ij, qui Caluini sententiam sequuntur. Imo certum est, Arrianos & plura, & magis in speciem plausibilia protulisse Scripturæ testimonia, quibus blasphemiam suam confirmarent; quàm Caluinistæ contra veram Christi præsentiam in Eucharistia vnquam proferre possunt.
units.tr: Since he made no reply to all this, I went on: "That is how it happens," I said, "that those who have once turned aside from the truth can afterwards nowhere stand on firm footing. And indeed this is not so very surprising. For when someone has given place to natural principles in one article of religion, why should he not do the same in others of the same kind? If, on the judgement of human reason, I deny with Calvin that Christ is truly present in the Eucharist, what prevents me from denying with Arius that the same Christ is true God, since this latter judgement of reason seems no less absurd than the former? Indeed the Arians were once equipped with the support of Scripture for attacking the divinity of Christ no less than those who follow Calvin's opinion are equipped today to deny the true presence of Christ's body in the Eucharist. In fact it is certain that the Arians put forward more passages of Scripture, and passages more plausible in appearance, to confirm their blasphemy, than the Calvinists can ever produce against the true presence of Christ in the Eucharist."

units.la: Adieci demum & illud; Anabaptistas etiam in ijsdem principijs habere patrocinium errorum suorum, dum Christum ex Maria Virgine veram assumpsisse corporis humani substantiam, id est, verum fuisse hominem, inficiantur; & (quod est ex eo consequens) resurrectionem in huius nostræ carnis substantia futuram negant.
units.tr: Finally I added this too: the Anabaptists also have support for their errors in the same principles, when they deny that Christ, from the Virgin Mary, assumed the true substance of human body, that is, that he was truly a man; and (which follows from this) they deny that the resurrection will be in the substance of this our flesh.

units.la: Hic ille; Error Anabaptistarum, inquit, de resurrectione, proficiscitur ex imperitia linguarum, quod vim scilicet græcè vocis ἀνάστασις non intelligunt. Respondi, fuisse quondam in eodem errore Ioannem Episcopum Hierosolymitanum, contra quem D. Hieronymus scripsit: Eum vero sine dubio græcæ linguæ fuisse peritissimum, ac vim istius voculæ satis perspectam habuisse; vt ignorantia linguæ vera huius erroris causa dici non possit. Rectius igitur & hanc hæresin communi omnium errorum principio adscribi.
units.tr: He replied: "The error of the Anabaptists about the resurrection arises from ignorance of languages, namely because they do not understand the force of the Greek word ἀνάστασις [anastasis]." I answered that John, Bishop of Jerusalem, was once in the same error, and St Jerome wrote against him; yet he was undoubtedly most skilled in the Greek language and had a sufficient grasp of the force of that little word, so that ignorance of language cannot be called the true cause of this error. It is therefore more correct to ascribe this heresy too to the common source of all errors.

units.la: Hæc ego; Alij vero hortabantur hominem ad resipiscentiam, vt scilicet induceret saniorem mentem, seque relictis erroribus ad Ecclesiam Catholicam adiungeret. In eum finem Anthonius Rinck, patritius Coloniensis, exemplum illi proponebat Georgij Cassandri, viri doctissimi, quem in religione Catholica hic Coloniæ mortuum esse narrabat. Ille, Cassandrum se magni facere, verbis ac nutu præse ferebat. Tu Anthonius Rinck; Eius igitur exemplu, inquit, ad imitandum tibi propone. Fuit is vir admodum mihi familiaris: Et habuit quidè opiniones suas; verum ijs relictis sub finem vitæ totus ad Ecclesiam Catholicam redijt, atque in fide maiorum, suscepta Catholico ritu Eucharistia, & Vnctionis extremæ Sacramento munimunitus, pie supremum diem clausit. Bene facies certè, si viri huius doctissimi vestigijs insistas, & ad Ecclesiæ Catholicæ communionem maturè reuertaris. Ille nihil ad hæc: Tum ego pauca quædam de Ecclesia, eiusque auctoritate subiunxi, Ecclesiam scilicet in fidei controuersijs audiendam esse, illiusque iudicio penitus acquiescendum: Alioqui futurum nunquam, vt vlla de Religione dissidia legitimè componantur. Cùm hæc, & id genus alia quædã, in eandem sententiam dicerentur, ille protestabatur, se magnifacere, ac habere summo loco Ecclesiam Dei, nec vnquam eius auctoritatem aspernatum. Interrogabam igitur ego; Qua in re Ecclesiam vnquam audiuisset? Ad quam vocem ille conticuit.
units.tr: So I said. Others, however, urged the man to repentance, so that he would be led to a saner mind, and, abandoning his errors, would join the Catholic Church. For this purpose Anthony Rinck, a patrician of Cologne, held up to him the example of George Cassander, a most learned man, who, he said, had died here in Cologne in the Catholic religion. He showed by his words and nods that he thought highly of Cassander. "You, Anthony Rinck," he said, "should therefore set his example before yourself for imitation. He was a man very familiar to me. He did indeed hold his own opinions, but at the end of his life he abandoned them and returned wholly to the Catholic Church, and in the faith of his fathers, having received the Eucharist in the Catholic manner and been strengthened with the sacrament of Extreme Unction, he piously closed his last day. You will certainly do well if you follow in the footsteps of this most learned man and return in good time to the communion of the Catholic Church." He made no answer to this. Then I added a few remarks about the Church and its authority: that the Church must be heard in controversies of faith, and that one must fully submit to its judgement, otherwise religious disputes could never be legitimately settled. When these and similar things were said to the same effect, he protested that he greatly valued the Church of God, held it in the highest regard, and had never once spurned its authority. I therefore asked him: "In what matter have you ever listened to the Church?" At this question he fell silent.

units.la: At Consul Hardenradius, veluti concludendo, & illud adiecit: Sibi hoc certum esse, atque omnino indubitatum, quod Christus Dominus, qui procul dubio æterna Veritas sit, & æterna Sapientia, nihil vnquam frustra dixerit. Eius verò hanc vocem esse; Si quis Ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus. Quisquis igitur in causa Religionis Ecclesiam audire renuit, quisquis illius interpretationi, vel collationi Scripturarum publicæ, priuatam suam vel opinionem, vel collationem anteponit, eum non alio, quàm ethnici ac publicani loco habendum. Tandem & ego Collationem nostram concluti, idque in hanc fere sententiam: Contulisse nos aliquamdiu de Eucharistiæ negocio, quam ille materiam delegisset: Et quia de vero germanoque verborum Christi sensu quæstio fuerit inter nos, medium aliquod quærendum fuisse, per quod in hac, tum in alijs quoque de Religione controuersijs, de vera Scripturarum intelligentia certò constare possit. Eā igitur ad rem me duplex medium protulisse; Conciliorum generalium definitionem scilicet, ac perpetuū in explicandis Scripturis Ecclesiæ Catholicæ consensum; quorum ipse, licet oppugnarit vtrumque, neutrum tamen euerterit. Protulisse quidem & ipsum me-dium. dium quoddam; verùm nec infallibile, nec ad eam rem sufficiens; quemadmodum à me demonstratum fit. Quo niam verò medium à me prolatum nec potuerit euerte re, nec amplecti tamen expresse velit, frustra porrò inter nos collationem fieri. Consistendum igitur hic esse, donec ille vel solidioribus rationibus euertat mea (quod nunquam futurū sit) vel veritati det locum. Cùm oritur de Religione disceptatio, oportere iudicium aliquod esse, in quo de vero germanoque sacrarum litterarum sensu, quasi lata sententia, pronuncietur. Quod Iudiciū cùm ipse defugiat, frustra sumi laborem, si deinceps conferamus; quādo procul dubio futurum esset, vt ego collationem omnem ad publicum illud, & legitimum Ecclesiæ Tribunal, quod à me constitutum sit, perpetuò reuocarem; Ille verò priuatam scripturarum intelligentiam sestando, iudicem alium de Scripturæ sensu ferre nollet, nisi seipsum, vel sui similes. Hoc igitur loco tantisper hę-rendum esse, donec aliam ille mentem induat.
units.tr: Then Consul Hardenradius, as if drawing a conclusion, added this: that it was certain to him and wholly beyond doubt that Christ the Lord, who is undoubtedly eternal Truth and eternal Wisdom, never said anything in vain. And his word is this: If he refuses to hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector. Therefore whoever refuses to hear the Church in a matter of religion, whoever puts his private opinion or private comparison of Scriptures before her interpretation or public comparison of Scripture, is to be regarded as nothing other than a heathen and a tax collector. Finally I too concluded our discussion, more or less to this effect: we had talked for some time about the matter of the Eucharist, which he had chosen as the subject. And since there was a question between us about the true and genuine sense of Christ's words, some means had to be sought by which the true understanding of Scripture could be settled with certainty, both in this controversy and in other religious controversies. For this purpose I had put forward a twofold means: namely, the decision of the general councils, and the constant consensus of the Catholic Church in explaining the Scriptures. Although he had attacked both, he had overthrown neither. He had indeed put forward some means of his own, but it was neither infallible nor sufficient for the purpose, as I had shown. Since he neither could overthrow the means I had put forward nor was willing to openly accept it, it was pointless for us to confer further. We must therefore stand firm here until he either overturns my position with more solid arguments (which will never happen) or gives way to the truth. When a dispute about religion arises, there must be some judgment by which the true and genuine sense of the sacred letters is pronounced, as it were by a settled sentence. Since he himself shuns this judgment, it is a wasted effort for us to confer any further; for without doubt I would always be referring the whole discussion back to that public and lawful tribunal of the Church which I had established, while he, defending his private understanding of Scripture, would refuse to accept any judge of the sense of Scripture except himself or men like himself. So at this point we must hold back for the time being, until he changes his mind.

units.la: Ad hæc ille; Non defugere se iudicium in causa Religionis, vbi sententiam suam è Scripturis protulerit. Tum ego, Reuera, inquam, tuam sententiam, non haustam è Scripturis, sed in Scripturas illatam potius, ac vestitam verbi Dei titulo. Ad eam vocem auerso vultu, velut indignabundus, respondit, Malitiosè à me torqueri verba; loqui se, non de priuato suo, sed de vero Scripturæ diuinę sensu. Excepi rursum, Iniuriam mihi hac parte fieri; Me nec torquere verba illius, nec ea maligně interpretari, verùm id dicere, quod ex ipsis verbis necessariò consequatur. Nam si publicum Ecclesiæ iudicium, de Scripturæ intelligentia, subire nolit; atque interea Scripturas tamen in priuato sensu, Caluinistarum more proferat, quid aliud existimandus sit proferre, quàm vel suam, vel alterius cuiusquam priuati opinionem, velatà verbi diuini nomine? Quamobrem non esse, quod ob eam vocem mihi succensēat.
units.tr: To this he replied that he did not shun judgment in a matter of religion, since he had set forth his opinion from the Scriptures. Then I said: "Indeed, your opinion is not drawn out of the Scriptures, but rather brought into them and clothed with the title of the Word of God." At this word he turned away, as if indignant, and answered that my words were twisted maliciously; that he was speaking not of his own private view but of the true sense of divine Scripture. I replied again that I was being wronged in this respect: I was neither twisting his words nor interpreting them spitefully, but saying what necessarily follows from his own words. For if he is unwilling to submit to the public judgment of the Church on the understanding of Scripture, and yet meanwhile puts forward Scriptures in a private sense, in the manner of the Calvinists, what else is he to be thought to be putting forward than his own or some other private person's opinion, veiled under the name of the divine Word? Therefore there is no reason for him to be angry with me because of that word.

units.la: Demum Consul Sudermannus, Satis apparet, inquit, non futurum, vt hac vice in eandem sententiam coeatis. Itaque actum hunc ego quidem concludendum censeo. Tum Badius assurgens, quemadmodum & pridie fecerat, iterum excusabat timiditatem suam ac <bl>ἀυσωπία</bl> (ea enim voce vtebatur, quae vitiosum ac inutile mpudorem significat) qua se dicebat quodam naturae vitio laborare, praesentesque Dominos rogabat, vt si hoc vitio impeditus, non omnia potuerit commode proferre, quae in mente haberet repos ita, ne id sinistre interpretari velint. Ad haec ego; Satis illum reipsa demonstrasse, quod ad declarandum mentis concepta nec animus illi defit, nec verba. Itaque mihi quidem excusationem illa toties iteratam, de <bl>ἀυσωπία</bl>, vel naturali timiditate, superuacanea videri. Adiecit D. Hardenradius, Friuolū est, & piget audire, quod huiusmodi timiditatem praetendis. Cum enim tot annis concionandi munus exercueris, & toties verba feceris in congregatione hominum, quis credere possit, te nunc priuatim in praesentia paucorum adeo timidum esse, vt animi sensa proferre nequeas? Imo vero excusatio haec occultam quandam superbiam redolet, quasi multa sint adhuc in animo tuo recondita, quae nondum prodideris. Interea, dum haec a D. Consule dicerentur, simul omnes surreximus. Atque ita collatio nostra finem habuit.
units.tr: Finally Consul Sudermannus said: "It is quite clear that you two will not agree on this occasion. So I think we should bring this business to a close." Then Badius rose, as he had also done the day before, and again apologised for his timidity and ἀυσωπία [ἀυσωπία] (for he used that word, which signifies a faulty and useless shamelessness), saying that he suffered from a certain natural defect, and he begged the gentlemen present that, if hindered by this defect he had not been able to express all that he had in mind, they would not wish to interpret it unfavourably. To this I replied that he had already shown in fact that he lacked neither the spirit nor the words to declare what he had conceived in his mind. So this excuse, repeated so often, of ἀυσωπία [ἀυσωπία] or natural timidity, seemed to me superfluous. Councillor Hardenradius added: "It is trivial, and it is tiresome to hear, that you plead such timidity. For since you have exercised the office of preaching for so many years, and have so often spoken before a gathering of men, who could believe that you are now so timid in the presence of a few people in private that you cannot express the sentiments of your mind? Indeed this excuse smells of some hidden pride, as if many things still lie hidden in your mind that you have not yet revealed." Meanwhile, while these things were being said by the Councillor, we all rose together. And so our discussion came to an end.

units.la: FINIS dium quoddam; verùm nec infallibile, nec ad eam rem sufficiens; quemadmodum à me demonstratum sit. Quo niam verò medium à me prolatum nec potuerit euerte re, nec amplecti tamen expresse velit, frustra porrò inter nos collationem fieri. Consistendum igitur hic esse, donec ille vel solidioribus rationibus euertat mea (quod nunquam futurû sit) vel veritati det locum. Cùm oritur de Religione disceptatio, oportere iudicium aliquod esse, in quo de vero germanoque sacrarum litterarum sen su, quasi lata sententia, pronuncietur. Quod Iudiciû cùm ipse defugiat, frustra sumi laborem, si deinceps conferamus; quàdo procul dubio futurum esset, vt ego collatio nem omnem ad publicum illud, & legitimum Ecclesiæ Tribunal, quod à me constitutum sit, perpetuò reuocarem; Ille verò priuatam scripturarum intelligentiam sefstando, iudicem alium de Scripturæ sensu ferre nollet, nisi seipsum, vel sui similes. Hoc igitur loco tantisper hę-rendum esse, donec aliam ille mentem induat.
units.tr: ...ium quoddam; but neither infallible nor sufficient for the purpose, as I demonstrated. Since, however, the means I put forward could neither be overthrown by him nor yet is he willing to embrace it openly, it is pointless for us to continue to confer. We must therefore stand firm here, until he either overturns my position with more solid arguments (which will never happen) or gives way to the truth. When a dispute about religion arises, there must be some judgment in which the true and genuine sense of the sacred letters is pronounced, as it were by a settled sentence. Since he himself shuns this judgment, it is a wasted effort to confer any further; for without doubt I would always be referring the whole discussion back to that public and lawful tribunal of the Church which I had established, while he, defending his private understanding of Scripture, would refuse to accept any judge of the sense of Scripture except himself or men like himself. So at this point we must hold back for the time being, until he changes his mind.
